documents.subtitle: Memory arithmetic, batching, kernels, quantization and serving diagnosis
documents.body:
# Understand the serving workload
Architecture: API admission and token budget -> bounded request queue -> tokenizer -> inference scheduler -> prefill -> iterative decode with KV cache -> detokenization and streaming. Observe queue time, token lengths, active sequences, memory and request outcomes together.
## Why use a GPU, and when is inference compute-bound or memory-bound?
Simple: GPUs perform many operations in parallel. Inference can be limited either by arithmetic throughput or by moving model data through memory.
Technical: Large matrix operations can exploit GPU parallelism, but achievable performance depends on batch shape, precision, kernels and memory bandwidth. Prefill often has high arithmetic intensity; small-batch autoregressive decoding often spends heavily on reading weights and KV state. These are workload tendencies, not guarantees. CPU work, tokenization and network delays can also dominate.
Example: If a short-output service has low GPU utilization but long queue times, inspect batching and CPU bottlenecks before buying more GPUs. If decoding bandwidth is saturated, simply increasing clock or theoretical FLOPS may not help much.
Follow-up: Why does peak TFLOPS not predict application tokens/second? | Peak values assume particular precisions and ideal kernels. Real serving includes memory movement, communication, variable sequences, scheduling and non-GPU work.
Follow-up: Can CPU inference be appropriate? | Yes, for small models, low request rates or latency-insensitive tasks when its measured cost and latency fit. GPU deployment is not automatically economical at low utilization.
Metrics: GPU utilization, memory bandwidth, kernel timing, queue time, TTFT, TPOT and completed output tokens/second.
## Prefill versus decode: what happens in each phase?
Simple: Prefill processes the prompt. Decode generates the answer one token step at a time for each sequence.
Technical: Prefill computes representations and key/value states for prompt tokens. Decode reuses cached keys/values and computes the next position, avoiding recomputation of the full prefix. The cache grows with sequence length. Prompt length primarily affects prefill work and stored state; output length adds sequential decoding steps. Batching changes the efficiency of both phases.
Example: A 12,000-token document with a 20-token answer stresses prefill differently from a 100-token prompt with a 2,000-token answer. Benchmark both rather than reporting one generic latency number.
Follow-up: Does KV caching make long-context decoding free? | No. New tokens still attend to prior state in ordinary attention models, and the cache occupies memory. Accessing a long cache can increase decode cost.
Follow-up: What is chunked prefill? | The scheduler processes long prompts in portions so they can coexist more fairly with other work. It can improve responsiveness under mixed workloads, with configuration-dependent throughput trade-offs.
Trade-offs: Optimizing long-prompt throughput can hurt short-request latency if scheduling does not provide fairness.
## Estimate model-weight memory before deployment.
Simple: Multiply the number of parameters by bytes per stored parameter, then reserve additional memory for runtime needs.
Technical: A 7-billion-parameter model at two bytes/parameter needs about 14 GB decimal for weights alone. Four-bit storage has a theoretical payload of 3.5 GB, but scales, zero points, unquantized layers, alignment and runtime workspaces add overhead. Serving also needs KV cache, activations, kernels and allocator headroom. Training adds gradients and optimizer state.
Example: A model whose weights nearly fill a 16 GB device may load but fail when requests allocate KV cache. Fit should be evaluated at the required concurrency and sequence lengths, not only at startup.
Follow-up: Is BF16 smaller than FP16? | Both commonly use 16 bits per value. They differ in exponent and mantissa allocation, affecting range and precision, not basic storage size.
Follow-up: Can I infer memory from the model name? | Not reliably. Check actual parameter count, architecture, quantization format, expert structure and loaded tensors. Some layers may remain higher precision.
Metrics: Peak allocated and reserved device memory, cache occupancy, OOM frequency and usable concurrency under the intended workload.
## Derive KV-cache memory and explain GQA/MQA.
Simple: The cache stores a key and a value for each retained token in each attention layer. More tokens and active sequences require more cache memory.
Technical: For a conventional decoder estimate bytes = 2 * layers * KV_heads * head_dimension * bytes_per_element * retained_tokens, summed across sequences. The factor 2 is keys plus values. Grouped-query attention uses fewer KV heads than query heads; multi-query attention commonly shares a single KV head. Cache layout, sliding windows, quantization and distributed placement can change actual allocation.
Example: With 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128 and FP16 cache, each token needs 131,072 bytes, or 128 KiB. A single 8,192-token sequence uses about 1 GiB of KV payload. Sixteen such sequences need about 16 GiB before paging overhead and weights. These are hypothetical dimensions, not a claim about your deployed model.
Follow-up: Should I use total attention heads in this formula? | Use KV heads, which can differ from query heads under GQA/MQA. Check the checkpoint configuration.
Follow-up: Does four-bit weight quantization also make the KV cache four-bit? | Not automatically. Weight and cache precision are separate configuration and kernel-support decisions.
Trade-offs: Smaller KV precision or fewer KV heads can reduce memory, but architecture and supported kernels constrain choices and quality must be validated.
## What are vLLM and PagedAttention?
Simple: vLLM is an LLM serving engine. PagedAttention organizes KV memory in blocks so variable-length requests can use memory more efficiently.
Technical: Logical sequence blocks map to physical cache blocks rather than requiring one large contiguous allocation per sequence. This reduces waste from over-reservation and fragmentation and supports efficient scheduling. It does not compress model weights or remove the mathematical need for token state. Its benefit depends on request lengths, sharing, scheduling and hardware.
Example: When one request finishes, its blocks can be reused for another request. This is more flexible than reserving each request's maximum context capacity from the start.
Follow-up: Is PagedAttention the same as an operating-system swap file? | No. The analogy is block-based address management; it is not a claim that GPU cache is automatically swapped to disk.
Follow-up: Does it guarantee faster single-request latency? | No. Its key advantages are memory management and serving efficiency. Measure latency and throughput under the intended concurrency rather than assuming every request gets faster.
Metrics: Cache utilization, concurrent token capacity, throughput at a latency SLO and OOM/preemption behavior.
## Static batching, dynamic batching and continuous batching: compare.
Simple: Static batching fixes a group of requests. Dynamic batching collects nearby arrivals. Continuous batching can change the active group as decoding proceeds.
Technical: Fixed batches waste capacity when short sequences finish before long ones. Continuous scheduling admits new work into freed capacity between decoding iterations, subject to token and memory budgets. Fairness, long prefills and variable output lengths still need management. Larger batches can improve throughput while worsening queueing or per-token latency.
Example: A batch with answers of 10, 20 and 1,000 tokens wastes resources if it waits as a rigid group. A continuous scheduler can replace completed sequences with new requests.
Follow-up: Why not set maximum batch size as high as possible? | Memory, latency and scheduling overhead impose limits. Optimize throughput subject to TTFT/TPOT and error constraints, not the batch-size number itself.
Follow-up: What is token-based admission? | Capacity is budgeted using prompt and expected/generated token work rather than treating every request as equal. It better captures the difference between tiny and long-context requests.
Trade-offs: Aggressive utilization can reduce interactive responsiveness. Separate latency-sensitive and batch workloads when their requirements conflict.
## Prefix caching, semantic caching and response caching: how do they differ?
Simple: Prefix caching reuses model computation for an identical token prefix. Response caching reuses a finished answer. Semantic caching reuses results for sufficiently equivalent queries.
Technical: KV-prefix reuse can reduce repeated prefill work but does not eliminate generation of new output tokens. Correct reuse depends on matching model, tokenizer, adapter and relevant execution configuration. Application response caches additionally need corpus and permission/version validity. Tenant separation and potential side channels require deliberate design.
Example: Many requests share a long stable system prompt. Prefix reuse may help. If the user-specific text appears first, fewer prefix tokens may be reusable. Reordering text only for caching must not break semantics or access controls.
Follow-up: Can prefix caching answer a new question without decoding? | No. It reuses prefix computation; the new answer still requires inference.
Follow-up: Can cached KV state bypass authorization? | Authorization must happen before protected content is included, and caches must be scoped appropriately. Cached computation is not permission to expose source data.
Metrics: Prefix hit rate, saved prefill tokens/time, TTFT improvement and isolation-test results.
## Tensor, pipeline, data and expert parallelism: when do you use them?
Simple: Tensor parallelism splits layer computation; pipeline parallelism splits layers; data parallelism runs replicas; expert parallelism distributes experts in suitable models.
Technical: Tensor-parallel workers exchange intermediate results and benefit from fast interconnects. Pipeline stages pass activations and can have bubbles or imbalance. Independent serving replicas can scale throughput when the model fits each replica. Expert routing adds communication and load-balancing considerations. Choose topology from model fit, workload and measured communication overhead.
Example: If a model fits on one device and traffic grows, replicas may be simpler than splitting it across devices. If it cannot fit, model parallelism becomes necessary, but a slower network can limit scaling.
Follow-up: Does two GPUs always mean twice the throughput? | No. Communication, scheduling, imbalance and bottlenecks can make scaling sublinear or even harmful for small workloads.
Follow-up: Is training data parallelism identical to serving replicas? | No. Training typically synchronizes gradients; serving replicas can handle independent requests without gradient synchronization. Use precise terminology.
Metrics: Scaling efficiency, interconnect utilization, per-stage idle time, throughput and tail latency.
## Quantization, FlashAttention, TensorRT and speculative decoding: what do they optimize?
Simple: These target different costs: numeric storage/compute, attention memory traffic, compiled execution and the number of serial generation steps.
Technical: Quantization reduces numerical precision with format- and kernel-dependent quality/performance effects. FlashAttention reorganizes exact attention computation to reduce memory traffic; it is distinct from KV-cache paging. TensorRT/TensorRT-LLM provide optimization and execution capabilities whose support depends on model and hardware. Speculative decoding proposes tokens with a draft mechanism and verifies them; correct algorithms preserve the target distribution under their assumptions.
Example: A draft model that rarely agrees with the target can add overhead rather than speed up generation. Measure acceptance rate and net latency. A quantized model may save memory but lose accuracy on numeric extraction.
Follow-up: Does FlashAttention make attention linear-time? | Ordinary full attention still has quadratic pairwise work; the optimization primarily changes memory access and intermediate storage. Do not confuse it with architectures that alter attention complexity.
Follow-up: Can I claim TensorRT and vLLM are one identical stack? | No. State which engine and kernels were actually used, for which model and benchmark. Do not combine tool names into an unsupported implementation claim.
Trade-offs: Faster kernels and lower precision improve only the bottlenecks they target. Pin compatible versions and rerun quality tests after optimization.
## Requests hit OOM or p95 rises sharply. What do you investigate?
Simple: Look at active tokens and queueing before assuming the model itself suddenly became slower.
Technical: Compare prompt/output distributions, concurrent sequences, KV occupancy, preemption, memory fragmentation and model copies. Check whether web workers each loaded an engine. Inspect CPU tokenization, network/provider latency and scheduler limits. Apply admission control, context/output caps, batching changes or additional capacity based on the identified cause.
Example: A new feature sends full chat history on every turn. Prompt lengths grow, KV memory increases and prefill delays interactive requests. Summarize or retrieve relevant history with provenance and validate that important constraints are retained.
Follow-up: Is reducing context length always safe? | No. It can remove evidence or user constraints. Measure quality on long-context tasks and reject oversized requests explicitly rather than silently truncating critical data.
Follow-up: How do you benchmark a fix? | Replay a representative sanitized workload with fixed versions, warm-up, offered load and timing boundaries. Include failed and cancelled requests, not only successful fast ones.
Metrics: TTFT/TPOT percentiles, completed RPS, token throughput, OOM rate, queue age and cost per accepted answer.
## How should you defend DGX Spark and GPU optimization on your resume?
Simple: Describe the exact machine, model, engine and experiment you used. Hardware branding alone is not evidence of optimization.
Technical: DGX Spark uses NVIDIA GB10 and a unified-memory design; do not describe it as a conventional discrete GPU with independently usable advertised VRAM. Verify OS/architecture, driver, framework, model and precision compatibility. A vendor maximum-model claim is a capacity statement under assumptions, not your measured serving throughput.
Example: Prepare an experiment ledger: checkpoint/revision, quantization, context limit, batch/token budget, engine/version, warm-up, workload, before/after latency and peak memory. Leave unknown values as evidence to collect rather than inventing them for the interview.
Follow-up: What if I used a hosted NVIDIA endpoint instead? | Say that clearly. Calling an endpoint is different from operating or optimizing a local GPU server. The current SQL Copilot provider report does not contain a completed NVIDIA benchmark.
Follow-up: What is the strongest optimization story? | One where profiling identified a bottleneck, a targeted change improved a measured metric, quality stayed within a defined bound and you can explain the new trade-off.
Metrics: Record reproducible baseline and optimized results; no throughput or speedup is asserted here for your hardware.
# GPU and serving definitions

## What are CUDA, ROCm and a GPU kernel?
Simple: CUDA and ROCm are GPU computing software ecosystems; a kernel is a function executed on a device.
Technical: Compatibility depends on hardware, drivers, runtime, framework build and the specific kernels needed by a model. CUDA and ROCm are not interchangeable labels. A framework may hide low-level calls, but deployment still depends on the supported stack.
Example: A quantization method supported on one NVIDIA device may lack an efficient implementation on a different platform.
Follow-up: Does having a GPU guarantee acceleration? | No. The operation must run on supported device kernels with enough parallel work to outweigh overhead.
Follow-up: What should you record in a benchmark? | Device, driver/runtime, framework/engine version, model revision, precision, sequence lengths and workload.

## What are FP32, FP16, BF16, INT8 and INT4?
Simple: They are numerical representations with different precision, range and storage costs.
Technical: FP32 uses 32 bits, FP16/BF16 16 bits, and integer quantization can store values in fewer bits with scales/other metadata. BF16 has a wider exponent range than FP16 but fewer fraction bits. Quantization schemes and kernel support determine actual speed and error.
Example: A four-bit weight format reduces nominal payload but may leave activations and KV cache in higher precision.
Follow-up: Is smaller precision always faster? | No. Dequantization and unsupported kernels can offset memory savings. Benchmark the complete workload.
Follow-up: Why test numeric tasks after quantization? | Small representation changes can affect rare tokens, numbers and reasoning behavior differently from average text quality.

## What is VRAM, unified memory and memory bandwidth?
Simple: Memory capacity is how much fits; bandwidth is how fast data can be moved. Unified-memory designs have a different sharing model from conventional separate CPU/GPU memory.
Technical: Capacity constraints and bandwidth constraints are distinct. A model can fit but decode slowly. Host/device transfers and shared-memory contention can dominate. Use the actual hardware architecture and runtime measurements rather than equating all advertised memory with dedicated GPU VRAM.
Example: DGX Spark requires discussing its unified-memory design; the same capacity number does not imply identical performance to another accelerator.
Follow-up: Why can a smaller model still be slow? | Low batch utilization, transfer overhead, CPU preprocessing or inefficient kernels may dominate.
Follow-up: Does adding RAM fix a KV-cache bottleneck? | Only if the serving design can use it within acceptable transfer/latency limits; more host RAM is not automatically more fast device cache.

## What is a warm-up run, and how do you benchmark inference fairly?
Simple: Warm-up lets initialization and compilation settle before measuring steady-state serving, while cold-start performance is measured separately.
Technical: Pin inputs, versions, output policy and concurrency. Report cold and warm behavior, successful and failed requests, prompt/output length distributions and timing boundaries. Compare engines under equivalent quality and sampling assumptions.
Example: Run a representative replay after loading the model, then separately measure startup and first-request latency.
Follow-up: Can I time only GPU kernels? | That helps diagnose compute but excludes tokenization, queues and network delivery. User-facing performance needs end-to-end timing too.
Follow-up: Why are averages insufficient? | Tail latency, overload and failures can be hidden. Report percentiles, offered/achieved load and errors.

# Adaptation choices
Architecture: Authorized corpus -> deduplicate and split by source/time -> tokenize -> baseline evaluation -> training objective and adapter configuration -> validation/early stopping -> held-out task evaluation -> versioned model/adapter -> serving compatibility and rollback.
## When do you use prompting, RAG, LoRA or full fine-tuning?
Simple: Use prompting for task instructions, RAG for external evidence, and training when the model needs more persistent behavioral or domain adaptation.
Technical: Diagnose the failure first. Missing current facts favor retrieval or tools. Poor format adherence or domain task behavior may justify supervised tuning. LoRA trains a compact parameter update while freezing the base; full fine-tuning updates the base parameters and requires more resources. Domain-adaptive pretraining uses an unsupervised language objective on domain text and is distinct from instruction tuning.
Example: If an assistant cites the wrong policy because indexing is stale, LoRA is the wrong first fix. If it consistently fails a specialized extraction format despite correct evidence, a labeled fine-tuning experiment may help.
Follow-up: Can training replace authorization? | No. Access decisions must remain in the application and data layers. Model weights can retain training information, so training-data governance matters.
Follow-up: How much data is enough? | It depends on task complexity, diversity, base model and objective. Count usable tokens/examples, assess coverage and learning curves; a document count alone is insufficient.
Trade-offs: Tuning adds dataset, training, evaluation and serving lifecycle work. Keep a prompt-only baseline to show incremental value.
## Explain LoRA mathematically and calculate parameter savings.
Simple: LoRA learns a small update to selected weight matrices instead of changing every original weight.
Technical: For W of shape d_out by d_in, represent the update as (alpha/r)BA, with A of shape r by d_in and B of shape d_out by r. Standard LoRA trains A and B while W stays frozen. Trainable parameters for this matrix are r*(d_in+d_out), instead of d_in*d_out. Implementations may use alternative scaling; report the actual configuration.
Example: For a 4096 by 4096 matrix, full tuning involves 16,777,216 weights. At rank 8, the two adapters contain 65,536 parameters, about 0.39% of that matrix. This is not the trainable fraction of the entire model unless every other choice is accounted for.
Follow-up: What does rank mean? | It bounds the rank/capacity of the learned update. Higher rank increases trainable parameters and possible expressiveness, but can overfit and does not guarantee a better model.
Follow-up: Can an adapter be merged? | Often the update can be added into compatible base weights for inference. Quantized formats and runtime support can complicate merging; validate numerical behavior and preserve the original base/adapter versions.
Metrics: Task quality, trainable parameter count, training memory, convergence and serving overhead.
## What is QLoRA, and how is it different from ordinary LoRA?
Simple: QLoRA trains adapters while keeping the frozen base model in a low-bit representation, reducing training memory further.
Technical: The QLoRA paper combines a four-bit base representation using NF4, double quantization of quantization constants and paged optimizers. Computation is not simply all four-bit arithmetic: weights are used through supported dequantization/compute paths, while adapters and other states use suitable higher precision. Gradients update adapters rather than the frozen quantized base.
Example: A model that does not fit with ordinary higher-precision base weights may fit for adapter training under QLoRA. Activations, sequence length and optimizer state still consume memory, so weight compression alone is not a complete capacity estimate.
Follow-up: Is QLoRA an inference engine? | No. It is an adaptation method. Serving the resulting adapter requires compatible base weights and runtime support, and its speed must be measured separately.
Follow-up: Does four-bit training guarantee no quality loss? | No. Quantization and adaptation can affect tasks differently. Evaluate the exact checkpoint on held-out cases, especially numeric, rare-domain and safety-sensitive outputs.
Trade-offs: Memory savings can enable larger models but add format/kernel constraints and quantization error.
## How do you choose rank, alpha, target modules and learning rate?
Simple: Start with a modest configuration, validate it and change one factor at a time.
Technical: Target modules determine where adaptation can act, such as attention projections and possibly feed-forward layers. Rank and scaling control update capacity and magnitude; dropout can regularize. Learning rate, batch size, schedule, sequence length and data quality interact. Names of target modules vary by model architecture, so inspect the model rather than copying a configuration blindly.
Example: Compare a small and a larger rank on the same data split and training-token budget. If training loss falls but validation performance worsens, additional capacity or training may be overfitting.
Follow-up: Why not tune every module at a high rank? | It increases memory, compute and overfitting risk. More adaptation is useful only if it improves the target task without unacceptable regressions.
Follow-up: What must be saved for reproducibility? | Base revision, tokenizer, adapter config and weights, data version/split, random seeds, optimizer/scheduler, library versions, steps and evaluation outputs.
Metrics: Validation task metrics, train-validation gap, loss curves, gradient norms, memory and wall-clock cost.
# BERT and training fundamentals
## How does masked-language modeling work in your BERT project?
Simple: Hide selected tokens and train the model to recover them using surrounding context.
Technical: BERT is a bidirectional encoder. The original procedure selects a subset of token positions, with mask/replacement/unchanged variants; implementations may use dynamic masking. Cross-entropy is evaluated on the selected target positions, with other positions ignored. Starting from a pretrained BERT checkpoint and continuing MLM on FSD documents is domain-adaptive pretraining, not training the architecture from scratch.
Example: 'The settlement cycle is [MASK]' illustrates contextual prediction, but evaluation must span representative domain text. Keep whole related documents or versions together in the split to avoid near-duplicate leakage.
Follow-up: Did I train on 1,000 people? | No. Your material says more than 1,000 documents. The important next details are token count, checkpoint, split, steps and objective.
Follow-up: Can MLM loss prove the chatbot improved? | No. It measures the pretraining objective. Evaluate downstream retrieval, classification, entity extraction or whichever task actually uses the encoder.
Trade-offs: Small domain corpora can teach terminology but also overfit or weaken general-language performance. Compare with the untouched base model.
## Pretraining from scratch versus continued pretraining versus task fine-tuning?
Simple: Scratch training starts without pretrained knowledge. Continued pretraining adapts a pretrained model using a language objective. Task fine-tuning trains for a specific labeled task.
Technical: Scratch training requires sufficient token diversity, compute and tokenizer/model design. Continued pretraining reuses existing representations and can adapt domain distributions. Task fine-tuning adds or trains a task head or response objective. Avoid calling every training run 'building a model from scratch'; the initialization and objective define the process.
Example: Load a pretrained BERT encoder, continue MLM on financial specifications, then train a classification head on labeled document categories. Those are two distinct adaptation stages with separate evaluations.
Follow-up: Why does 1,000 documents not determine feasibility? | Documents vary enormously in length and redundancy. Effective unique tokens, domain coverage and target performance matter more than the count alone.
Follow-up: What is catastrophic forgetting? | Adaptation can reduce capabilities learned previously. Use mixed-domain evaluation, conservative training and appropriate data mixing or regularization when needed.
Metrics: Held-out MLM loss, downstream task improvement, general-domain regressions and learning curves versus training tokens.
## Explain loss, gradients, backpropagation and an optimizer.
Simple: Loss measures how wrong the prediction is. Gradients show how parameter changes affect that loss. The optimizer uses gradients to update trainable parameters.
Technical: Cross-entropy for a target token is -log p(target); average it over the intended non-ignored positions. Backpropagation applies the chain rule through the computation graph. SGD uses gradient steps; Adam-type methods maintain moment estimates. Weight decay and learning-rate schedules affect optimization. Zero gradients deliberately to avoid accidental accumulation, unless accumulation is intended.
Example: If the target probability rises from 0.1 to 0.5, negative log loss falls from about 2.303 to 0.693 using natural logs. This does not directly translate into a percentage improvement in chatbot accuracy.
Follow-up: Why can training loss decrease while quality worsens? | Overfitting, data leakage, objective mismatch or evaluation noise can cause that. Use held-out task metrics and inspect errors, not just the loss curve.
Follow-up: What is gradient clipping? | It limits gradient magnitude to stabilize updates in some settings. It does not fix bad data or an inappropriate learning rate by itself.
## Batch size, gradient accumulation and mixed precision: explain.
Simple: Batch size controls examples per update. Gradient accumulation combines smaller microbatches. Mixed precision uses different numeric formats where appropriate to save resources.
Technical: Effective batch size is microbatch size times accumulation steps times data-parallel replicas, subject to the exact training scheme. Accumulation approximates a larger batch but can differ with normalization, stochastic layers and loss scaling. FP16 training may need gradient scaling to avoid underflow; BF16 often offers a wider exponent range but hardware and implementation still matter.
Example: A microbatch of 2, eight accumulation steps and two data-parallel workers gives an effective batch of 32 examples per optimizer update. Sequence length still strongly affects activation memory.
Follow-up: Does accumulation reduce total compute? | Not necessarily. It reduces peak batch memory while requiring several forward/backward passes before an update, often at a throughput cost.
Follow-up: What is activation checkpointing? | It saves memory by recomputing selected activations during backward rather than storing them all. It trades additional compute for lower memory use.
Metrics: Tokens per second, peak memory, loss stability, gradient overflow and validation quality at comparable training budgets.
## How do you prevent overfitting and evaluate a small domain model?
Simple: Keep a truly separate test set, watch validation performance and stop when more training no longer helps.
Technical: Deduplicate before splitting; group related document versions, templates and clients appropriately. Use early stopping, suitable regularization and data quality checks. Compare with the base model and a simple non-neural baseline when appropriate. Evaluate rare classes and out-of-domain inputs, not just the common training distribution.
Example: Randomly splitting chunks from one FSD into train and test can leak almost identical text. Split at the document family or time boundary, then tokenize each partition independently within the pipeline.
Follow-up: Is perplexity comparable between arbitrary tokenizers? | Not directly. Tokenization changes the units and likelihood decomposition. Compare under consistent tokenization/objectives or use task-level measures.
Follow-up: What if labels are scarce? | Use a smaller adjudicated evaluation set, weak supervision only with measured noise, and learning curves. Synthetic data requires validation and separation from test material.
Trade-offs: Strict splits can produce lower scores but better estimates of real generalization.
## Which classical ML concepts should a GenAI engineer still know?
Simple: Understand supervised learning, unsupervised learning, generalization, classification metrics and basic statistical reasoning. GenAI systems still depend on those foundations.
Technical: Supervised learning uses labeled targets; unsupervised learning seeks structure without those labels. Logistic regression models class probabilities through a linear score and link function; trees learn decision splits, and ensembles combine learners. Bias-variance describes different sources of generalization error. Feature scaling affects distance-based and many optimization-based methods, while tree splits are less sensitive to monotonic scaling.
Example: A lightweight classifier may route support queries more cheaply than an LLM. Compare it with keyword rules and an embedding-based classifier using macro-F1, calibration and inference cost.
Follow-up: Why does correlation not prove causation? | Shared causes, selection effects and temporal confounding can produce associations. A productivity claim needs a baseline, workload control and clear attribution, not just two averages.
Follow-up: What are drift and class imbalance? | Drift changes input or outcome distributions over time. Imbalance makes common-class accuracy misleading. Monitor slices, recalibrate thresholds and collect new labels when performance changes.
Metrics: Precision/recall/F1, calibration, confusion matrices, subgroup errors, drift indicators and business outcomes with uncertainty.
# ML fundamentals: objectives and generalization

## What are training, validation and test sets?
Simple: Training fits parameters, validation chooses settings, and test estimates final generalization after choices are fixed.
Technical: Split by the independent unit relevant to deployment, such as document family, customer or time. Repeated tuning on the test set turns it into validation. Fit preprocessing only on permitted training data when it learns distributional information.
Example: Keep near-duplicate FSD versions together so one version cannot teach the answer to a supposedly unseen test document.
Follow-up: Why not random-split every chunk? | Neighboring chunks share content and can leak topic/wording across splits.
Follow-up: Can I use cross-validation? | Yes when appropriate, with grouped/time-aware folds where necessary. Large model training may make repeated folds costly.

## What are overfitting, underfitting, bias and variance?
Simple: Overfitting memorizes training quirks; underfitting fails to capture useful structure. Bias and variance describe different sources of prediction error.
Technical: Inspect learning curves and held-out task metrics. More data, regularization or simpler models may reduce overfitting; more suitable features/capacity/training may address underfitting. These diagnoses are not interchangeable.
Example: Training accuracy rises while held-out intent classification declines after more epochs.
Follow-up: Does dropout always help? | No. It is one regularizer whose effect depends on architecture, data and training. Evaluate rather than adding it by habit.
Follow-up: Does low training loss prove success? | No. It may reflect memorization or a task objective that does not match downstream needs.

## What are cross-entropy, MSE and cosine loss used for?
Simple: They penalize different kinds of prediction error.
Technical: Cross-entropy compares predicted class/token distributions with targets; mean squared error measures squared numeric residuals; embedding objectives may use cosine similarity or contrastive losses. Select the objective according to the task and label semantics, then evaluate real task outcomes.
Example: Use cross-entropy for masked-token targets, not MSE between token IDs, because vocabulary IDs have no useful numeric distance.
Follow-up: What is contrastive learning? | It trains representations to bring related examples together and separate unsuitable matches according to a sampling/objective design.
Follow-up: Why do negative examples matter? | Easy negatives may teach little; incorrect hard negatives can teach the wrong distinction. Curate and evaluate them.

## What are precision-recall thresholds and class weights?
Simple: Thresholds choose when a score becomes a positive decision; class weights change how training penalizes classes.
Technical: For imbalanced tasks, tune thresholds on held-out data at the intended operational capacity. Class weighting or resampling can help learning but may change calibration. Report per-class performance and prevalence.
Example: An intent router can ask clarification when top scores are close rather than always choosing the highest class.
Follow-up: Why not force every query into a known intent? | Out-of-scope inputs need rejection or a fallback; otherwise the system confidently routes unrelated requests.
Follow-up: What is macro versus micro F1? | Macro averages class-level scores equally; micro aggregates counts before scoring. They emphasize different aspects under imbalance.

## What are dropout, weight decay and early stopping?
Simple: They are different ways to reduce overfitting or control training.
Technical: Dropout randomly suppresses selected activations during training; weight decay penalizes parameter magnitude under the optimizer formulation; early stopping chooses a checkpoint before validation performance degrades. Their effects depend on objective and architecture.
Example: Keep the checkpoint with the best validated extraction performance instead of automatically deploying the final epoch.
Follow-up: Is dropout active at inference? | Ordinary evaluation disables it; specialized uncertainty methods may deliberately enable it. State which mode you use.
Follow-up: Why monitor a downstream metric too? | A better language-model loss does not necessarily improve retrieval or classification, so choose the checkpoint with the relevant validation criterion.

documents.body:
# Plan before generating
Architecture: Natural-language question -> intent/entities -> authorized schema retrieval -> semantic definitions -> relationship graph and join candidates -> explicit query plan -> SQL generation -> dialect-aware AST/schema/policy validation -> coverage and calibrated confidence -> clarification or controlled execution boundary -> result checks and explanation. Execution is a design stage here; verify its actual deployment in your project before claiming it.
## Why planner-first Text-to-SQL instead of sending the whole schema to an LLM?
Simple: Make the meaning, tables and relationships explicit before producing SQL. This makes errors easier to detect and explain.
Technical: Retrieve relevant schema and business definitions, resolve entities, identify grain and measures, discover joins, then construct a plan with filters, aggregation and output requirements. A deterministic planner can constrain generation and expose missing information. Whole-schema prompting can work for small schemas, but becomes expensive and distracts the model as schema size and ambiguity grow.
Example: 'Top customers by revenue last quarter' requires a revenue definition, time zone, date field, refund treatment and ranking grain before selecting tables. SQL can be syntactically valid while answering the wrong business question.
Follow-up: Why not use only templates? | Templates are reliable for a narrow known query set but may not cover ad hoc combinations. A hybrid can route common tasks to templates and use constrained planning for broader cases.
Follow-up: What does a plan contain? | Required entities, measures, dimensions, filters, join keys, cardinalities, aggregation grain, ordering/limit and unresolved assumptions. Keep it structured and inspectable.
Metrics: Plan correctness, schema/column recall, join correctness, clarification quality and final semantic success.
## How do schema linking and business vocabulary resolution work?
Simple: Translate business language into authorized tables and columns without inventing missing fields.
Technical: Index table/column descriptions, aliases, data types, relationships and approved metric definitions. Combine exact lexical matches with embeddings when useful. Sample values can help entity resolution but may contain sensitive data; expose only permitted summaries or controlled lookups. Separate schema evidence from generic SQL examples.
Example: 'Active client' may map to customer_status='ACTIVE', but only if the business definition says so. 'Revenue' may require net amounts after refunds rather than summing a column named amount.
Follow-up: What if two columns both seem plausible? | Ask a targeted clarification or use an authoritative semantic definition. A confidence score should not conceal unresolved ambiguity.
Follow-up: Can Spider examples provide a missing enterprise column? | No. Generic examples can illustrate SQL patterns but cannot establish your private schema or business semantics. If a required attribute is absent, clarify or reject the unsupported request.
Trade-offs: Rich metadata improves linking but needs governance and freshness. Incorrect descriptions can systematically mislead the planner.
## How do you discover multi-table joins, and why is shortest path not enough?
Simple: Use known relationships to connect required tables, but choose joins according to business meaning and row cardinality.
Technical: Represent tables as nodes and validated relationships as edges with key columns, direction/cardinality and optional semantic labels. Search candidate connecting paths, then check whether they preserve the desired grain. The shortest graph path may use an irrelevant relationship or multiply rows. Inferred joins from similar column names require validation.
Example: Joining orders to order_items and payments can multiply each payment by each line item. Aggregate each one-to-many relation to order grain first or use a correct alternative plan before combining them.
Follow-up: How do bridge tables affect planning? | Many-to-many relationships often require a bridge and can change counting semantics. Decide whether to count rows, distinct entities or weighted allocations.
Follow-up: Why is table recall not enough? | You can retrieve every correct table and still choose wrong keys, omit filters or aggregate at the wrong grain. Evaluate joins and outputs separately.
Metrics: Required-table recall, unnecessary-table rate, edge/path correctness, cardinality violations and execution-equivalent results.
## How do you validate SQL safely beyond checking for SELECT?
Simple: Parse SQL, restrict what it can access and execute, and enforce limits in the database as well as the application.
Technical: Use a dialect-aware AST parser, require the intended single-statement form, allowlist accessible objects/functions and reject unsupported constructs. SELECT can still invoke dangerous functions, leak forbidden rows or run an expensive query. Use a least-privilege read-only account, row/column controls, timeouts, resource limits and result-size caps. Parameterize user values rather than concatenating strings.
Example: A SELECT from a sensitive payroll table is unacceptable for a user without permission even though it does not modify data. A Cartesian join over huge tables can exhaust resources without any write operation.
Follow-up: Why not regex alone? | SQL syntax includes nesting, comments, quoting and dialect-specific constructs. Regex checks are brittle; parsing plus database enforcement provides stronger boundaries.
Follow-up: Does AST validity prove correctness? | No. It checks structure and selected policies. Business meaning and result correctness require semantic validation or evaluation against expected outcomes.
Trade-offs: Strict allowlists reduce risk but limit expressiveness. Expose unsupported queries clearly instead of weakening controls silently.
## How do retries and confidence gates improve Text-to-SQL?
Simple: Use a specific error to repair a query, and stop when the problem requires clarification rather than another guess.
Technical: Feed constrained validator feedback into a bounded repair process. Distinguish syntax errors, unknown columns, missing requirements, ambiguous semantics and permission failures. Permission failures must not trigger attempts to bypass policy. Confidence should combine evaluated signals and be calibrated; a self-assigned score or deterministic heuristic is not a probability until validated.
Example: If the query omits a requested date filter, regenerate with that explicit requirement. If 'current exposure' has two business definitions, ask the user instead of repeatedly sampling SQL.
Follow-up: Can retries inflate success while harming latency? | Yes. Report first-attempt success, eventual success, attempts and latency/cost together. Additional retries may produce diminishing returns.
Follow-up: What if the corrected SQL changes the question? | Re-run coverage against the original request and preserve user-approved constraints. A valid but simplified query should not be labeled a successful repair.
Metrics: Repair success by error type, average attempts, semantic drift, false acceptance and p95 end-to-end latency.
## Explain SQL validity, execution accuracy and test-suite accuracy.
Simple: SQL validity asks whether a query passes defined checks. Execution accuracy asks whether its result matches the expected result. Neither should be confused with a generic success score.
Technical: Define validity precisely: parser validity, schema validity and policy validity are different. Result comparison needs handling for ordering, duplicates, nulls, numeric tolerance and nondeterministic functions. One database instance can make different queries accidentally produce the same result; multiple carefully chosen test databases can expose semantic differences. A benchmark's success field must be traced to its scoring code.
Example: SELECT COUNT(*) and SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) may match on a dataset with one row per customer, but differ when duplicates are introduced. Passing one execution result is weak evidence of general equivalence.
Follow-up: What is wrong with comparing SQL strings only? | Equivalent queries can use different aliases or join formulations. Structural comparison and execution-based tests are more informative, though each has limitations.
Follow-up: What should I say about my 120-case report? | It records 67.5% success, 78.33% validity, 79.17% join success and 93.15% average table recall. Establish the report's scoring definitions; do not rename its success as proven live-database execution accuracy.
Trade-offs: Execution evaluation is more realistic but requires safe datasets and careful expected-result design.
# SQL and DBA follow-ups
## INNER versus LEFT JOIN, WHERE versus HAVING, and COUNT variants?
Simple: INNER JOIN keeps matches; LEFT JOIN preserves left rows even without a match. WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups. COUNT(*) counts rows, while COUNT(column) ignores nulls.
Technical: SQL uses three-valued logic for nulls. A WHERE predicate on a nullable right-side column after a LEFT JOIN can remove unmatched rows and effectively change the intended outer-join behavior. COUNT(DISTINCT column) removes duplicate non-null values. Define the business grain before choosing a counting expression.
Example: To include customers with no orders, LEFT JOIN orders and place a qualifying order-status predicate in the join condition if unmatched customers must remain. Filtering that status in WHERE usually removes them.
Follow-up: Why does NULL = NULL not behave like ordinary equality? | NULL represents unknown/missing, so the comparison is unknown rather than true. Use IS NULL for null tests and understand dialect-specific null-safe comparisons.
Follow-up: Can HAVING replace every WHERE condition? | It may be inefficient or change meaning because filtering occurs after grouping. Apply row filters before aggregation when that matches the task.
Metrics: Validate edge cases with no matches, nulls, duplicate keys and multiple child rows.
## How do window functions differ from GROUP BY?
Simple: GROUP BY collapses rows into groups. Window functions calculate across related rows while retaining row-level output.
Technical: A window specifies partitioning, ordering and optionally a frame. ROW_NUMBER gives a unique sequence under a defined order; RANK and DENSE_RANK handle ties differently. Running totals depend on frame semantics; an implicit default can differ from the intended row-by-row calculation. Add deterministic tie-breakers when stable results matter.
Code:
SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY customer_id
           ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC
       ) AS rn
FROM orders;
EndCode:
Example: Use an outer query or CTE filtering rn=1 to get the most recent order per customer. The secondary order_id makes equal-date ordering deterministic under the chosen rule.
Follow-up: Why not MAX(order_date) alone? | It gives a date per group, not automatically the entire corresponding row, and ties may produce several rows when joined back.
Follow-up: What is a CTE? | A named query expression that improves structure and can support recursion in supported dialects. Do not assume it is always materialized or always faster; inspect the optimizer plan.
## How do indexes and EXPLAIN help a slow query?
Simple: An index can reduce the data scanned for selected access patterns. EXPLAIN shows how the database plans to execute a query.
Technical: Inspect estimated rows, access paths, join order, sorts and temporary work; compare estimates with observed execution where safe. Composite index usefulness depends on predicate/order structure and the engine. Indexes consume storage and slow writes. Non-sargable expressions, implicit casts and stale statistics can prevent good access plans.
Example: A query filtering tenant_id and created_at may benefit from a matching composite index, but the choice depends on selectivity and workload. Avoid adding an index merely because a column appears in a WHERE clause.
Follow-up: Why can an index be ignored? | A scan may be cheaper for a large fraction of the table; statistics, expression shape or ordering requirements may also matter. The optimizer's decision must be assessed with real cardinalities.
Follow-up: Should an LLM create indexes automatically? | It can propose candidates, but resource impact, write overhead and production rollout require controlled review and testing. An assistant should not receive unrestricted DDL rights.
Metrics: Rows examined, execution time, buffer/cache behavior, lock waits, write overhead and plan stability.
## Transactions, isolation, backups and DBA support: what must you know?
Simple: Transactions group changes reliably; isolation governs concurrent visibility; backups are useful only if restoration works.
Technical: Explain atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability without implying isolation always means serial execution. Know common anomalies such as dirty/nonrepeatable reads and phantoms, with engine-specific behavior. Investigate locks and deadlocks using database tools, keep transactions short and retry selected deadlock failures safely. Separate replication for availability from backups for recovery.
Example: DBA support may mean query troubleshooting, permissions, health checks and assisting restore tests. Do not claim ownership of cluster design or recovery objectives unless you actually had that responsibility.
Follow-up: RPO versus RTO? | RPO is the acceptable data-loss window; RTO is the target time to restore service. A backup schedule alone does not establish either without tested recovery.
Follow-up: Why can a read replica return stale data? | Replication may be asynchronous. Route tasks requiring current state appropriately and expose freshness when necessary.
Metrics: Backup/restore success, replication lag, slow-query rate, lock waits, recovery time and access-change auditability.
# Database foundations for Text-to-SQL

## What are primary keys, foreign keys and cardinality?
Simple: A primary key identifies rows; a foreign key expresses a reference; cardinality describes how many rows can relate.
Technical: One-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many relationships affect joins and aggregation. A column name ending in id is not proof of an enforced relationship. Inspect constraints and approved business semantics.
Example: Customers to orders is often one-to-many; orders to products may use an order_items bridge.
Follow-up: Can a foreign key be nullable? | Depending on schema rules, yes; missing relationships affect join semantics.
Follow-up: Why does cardinality matter for sums? | Joining multiple one-to-many tables can multiply rows and double-count amounts unless the plan preserves the intended grain.

## What are normalization and denormalization?
Simple: Normalization separates data to reduce certain redundancies; denormalization deliberately combines or duplicates data for access needs.
Technical: Choose based on consistency, write patterns and analytical performance. A normalized schema can require more joins, while a denormalized model can simplify reads but needs update correctness. Do not assume either is universally faster or more correct.
Example: A reporting table may precompute daily totals, while transactional data remains normalized.
Follow-up: Should a copilot use raw tables or a semantic layer? | A governed semantic/reporting layer can reduce ambiguity for common metrics, but its freshness and definitions must be explicit.
Follow-up: Can denormalization create stale answers? | Yes. Refresh lag and inconsistent updates must be measured and communicated.

## What is SQL injection and how do parameters help?
Simple: Injection occurs when untrusted input changes query structure instead of remaining a data value.
Technical: Bind values through the database driver rather than string concatenation. Identifiers such as table names often cannot be parameterized the same way, so validate them against an allowlist/schema. Generated SQL still needs AST, object and resource controls.
Example: A customer name containing quotes must remain a parameter value, not become part of executable SQL syntax.
Follow-up: Does parameterization make all generated SQL safe? | No. The query can still access forbidden data or be too expensive. Permissions and policy validation remain necessary.
Follow-up: Why not just escape quotes? | Manual escaping is dialect- and context-sensitive and easy to get wrong. Use supported binding APIs.

## What are subqueries, CTEs, UNION and UNION ALL?
Simple: They combine or structure query results in different ways.
Technical: Subqueries nest a query; CTEs name intermediate expressions; UNION combines compatible results and removes duplicates; UNION ALL preserves duplicates. Optimizer behavior and syntax vary by dialect. Choose according to intended semantics before performance.
Example: Combining transactions from two non-overlapping partitions may use UNION ALL, while deduplication requires a deliberate key policy.
Follow-up: Does a CTE guarantee caching? | No. Materialization/inlining depends on engine/version and query. Inspect the plan.
Follow-up: Why can UNION hide a bug? | Removing duplicate rows can conceal an incorrect join or unexpected duplication rather than fixing its cause.

documents.body:
# Deployment and operations
Architecture: Source commit -> CI checks and artifact build -> image/model registry -> staging and evaluation -> controlled rollout -> health/readiness checks -> traffic -> metrics/logs/traces -> rollback. Runtime services use scoped identities, managed secrets and durable data stores.
## How would you deploy a GenAI application on AWS?
Simple: Separate the web/API service, background ingestion, persistent data and model inference so each can scale and fail independently.
Technical: A possible design uses a load balancer, containerized API, object storage for documents, a durable queue for ingestion, a database for metadata and a model endpoint or GPU service. Select concrete services based on requirements; EC2, container platforms and managed inference have different control/operations trade-offs. Use private networking where appropriate, scoped IAM roles and centralized observability.
Example: An upload stores a file and enqueues a versioned job. The API serves queries without waiting for parsing. Inference capacity scales from active work/queue indicators, not simply the number of web requests.
Follow-up: Why not put everything on one server? | It may be fine for a small prototype. Production isolation, independent scaling and recovery requirements often justify separation. Explain the workload that makes the extra complexity worthwhile.
Follow-up: Why not serverless for every component? | Startup, execution duration, GPU requirements and dependency sizes can make some workloads unsuitable. Managed/serverless components remain useful where their limits fit.
Metrics: Availability, p95 latency, queue age, cost per task, deployment failure rate and recovery time.
## What Linux checks do you perform when an application is down?
Simple: Check the process, listening port, recent logs and resource pressure, then follow the failing dependency.
Technical: Inspect service status and journal logs, process/CPU/memory usage, disk space/inodes, network listeners, DNS and connectivity. Check configuration changes, permissions, certificate expiry and dependency health. Use targeted commands and preserve incident evidence; repeated restarts can hide the cause or worsen load.
Code:
# Read-only diagnostic examples; replace service and port.
systemctl status myapp --no-pager
journalctl -u myapp --since '30 minutes ago' --no-pager
ss -lntp
free -h
df -h
EndCode:
Example: The process is alive but readiness fails because database connections are exhausted. Restarting every instance simultaneously may create a reconnection storm; inspect pool sizing and slow transactions first.
Follow-up: Liveness versus readiness? | Liveness asks whether the process should be restarted. Readiness asks whether it should receive traffic. A dependency outage should not automatically trigger endless restarts if the process can recover.
Follow-up: What if disk is full? | Identify the responsible filesystem and files, check log rotation and retention, and follow an approved cleanup/recovery procedure. Do not blindly delete database files or active logs.
Metrics: Time to detect, time to mitigate, recurrence, resource saturation and customer-visible failures.
## What makes a Bash script safe and maintainable?
Simple: Validate inputs, quote variables, check failures and make reruns predictable.
Technical: Use explicit arguments, safe temporary files, cleanup traps and clear exit codes. set -euo pipefail can catch some errors but has shell-context exceptions and is not a substitute for explicit checks. Never use eval on untrusted input. Avoid logging secrets. Use locks or idempotent operations if scheduled runs can overlap.
Code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
url=${1:?Usage: healthcheck.sh URL}
if curl --fail --silent --show-error --max-time 5 "$url"; then
  printf '\nHealth check passed\n'
else
  printf 'Health check failed\n' >&2
  exit 1
fi
EndCode:
Example: A health-check script is a small unit you can explain completely. A deployment script should additionally record artifact version, validate configuration, verify readiness and support rollback.
Follow-up: Why quote "$variable"? | Unquoted expansion can cause word splitting and glob expansion, changing arguments unexpectedly. Quoting is especially important for paths and user-provided values.
Follow-up: Does set -e guarantee every error stops execution? | No. Its behavior depends on constructs such as conditionals and pipelines. Handle important failures explicitly and test the script under those paths.
Trade-offs: Shell is useful for orchestration, but complex data transformations and retry state are often clearer in Python.
## How do you deploy and roll back an application on a Linux server?
Simple: Deploy a versioned artifact, verify it before receiving traffic and keep a known-good version available.
Technical: Run under a dedicated low-privilege service identity, use a service manager, externalize configuration and secrets, and configure graceful shutdown. Apply migrations using a backward-compatible expand/contract strategy when possible. A code rollback cannot undo an incompatible database migration automatically. Separate deployment success from application readiness.
Example: Start the new release on a separate port, run health and representative functional checks, then switch the proxy or load balancer. Keep the prior artifact until rollback conditions are cleared.
Follow-up: What if requests are in flight? | Drain connections and allow a bounded graceful period. Durable jobs must be resumable; do not assume killing the process safely cancels external side effects.
Follow-up: Blue-green versus canary? | Blue-green switches between environments; canary gradually sends a subset of traffic to the new version. Both need compatibility, observability and a rollback plan.
Metrics: Deployment duration, error-rate/latency regression, rollback time and change-failure rate.
## What should a production Docker image contain?
Simple: Only the application and required runtime dependencies, built reproducibly and run with limited privileges.
Technical: Pin appropriate dependencies and base versions, use multi-stage builds where useful, exclude secrets and local caches, and run as a non-root user when possible. Image layers are immutable, so deleting a secret in a later layer does not make its earlier inclusion safe. Keep persistent data outside the container filesystem and set resource limits.
Example: Build the API separately from a large model artifact where that suits the deployment. Reproducible model downloads need checkpoint revisions and integrity checks, not an unpinned latest reference.
Follow-up: Is a container a VM? | No. It typically shares the host kernel while isolating processes and resources. Security and compatibility assumptions differ from a full virtual machine.
Follow-up: What is Docker Compose useful for? | Defining a reproducible local multi-service environment. It does not by itself provide every production scheduling, resilience and security capability.
Trade-offs: Smaller images reduce transfer and attack surface, but aggressive minimalism can complicate debugging; use controlled diagnostic tooling rather than adding secrets or compilers indiscriminately.
## What belongs in CI/CD for a GenAI system?
Simple: Test software behavior and model-system quality before promoting a change.
Technical: Run lint/type checks where useful, unit/contract tests, security/dependency checks, image builds and a representative evaluation suite. Version prompts, datasets, retrieval configuration and model adapters as deployable artifacts. Use regression gates for critical tasks and access-control behavior. Slow comprehensive evaluations can run separately from fast pull-request checks, but promotion criteria must be explicit.
Example: A prompt change passes code tests but reduces abstention on unsupported financial questions. The quality gate should catch it before a broad rollout.
Follow-up: How do you handle nondeterministic evaluations? | Use stable cases, repeated measurements where justified, tolerance bands and human adjudication for consequential changes. Avoid a flaky gate based on one sampled response.
Follow-up: Can I roll back only the prompt? | Yes if prompt/model/tool/schema versions remain compatible. Track the whole configuration bundle so a rollback restores a coherent system.
Metrics: Regression escape rate, evaluation variance, release lead time, deployment failures and rollback success.
# Frontend and end-to-end product questions
## React state, props, effects and rendering: what should you know?
Simple: Props pass data into components; state stores changing component data. Rendering describes the UI for the current inputs. Effects synchronize with systems outside rendering.
Technical: Keep state minimal and place it at the right shared owner. Use stable keys for list identity. Effects are not a general place for every derived calculation; derive values during rendering when appropriate. Handle cleanup and stale async responses so an older request does not overwrite a newer result.
Example: A SQL Copilot page stores the current question, request status and result. If the user submits a second query, cancel or ignore the first response using a request ID rather than letting the older SQL replace the new result.
Follow-up: Why not mutate state objects directly? | React relies on state updates and identity changes to schedule predictable rendering. Use updates that preserve the intended immutable data flow.
Follow-up: Why can an effect run more than expected in development? | Development checks and dependency changes can expose unsafe effects. Make setup/cleanup correct rather than relying on a single invocation assumption.
Trade-offs: State libraries can help complex applications, but small local state should remain simple. Your resume states basic React/Next.js knowledge, so demonstrate concrete implemented screens.
## Next.js server versus client components: what belongs where?
Simple: Server components can perform server-side work; client components handle browser interactivity and browser APIs.
Technical: Keep secrets and privileged service calls on the server. A client-side component boundary affects what code and serialized data reach the browser. Rendering and caching behavior depend on the Next.js version and route configuration, so verify the project's version. Server rendering does not automatically authorize data access; every server-side fetch still needs policy checks.
Example: Render a permitted schema summary server-side, while the query editor and streaming display run interactively in the browser. Do not embed API keys or unrestricted database credentials in client bundles.
Follow-up: Is hiding a button an authorization control? | No. Users can call backend endpoints directly. The server must enforce the action regardless of UI state.
Follow-up: Can server caching leak user data? | Yes if cache scope and keys ignore identity/permissions. Treat personalized responses differently from public static content and validate framework caching behavior.
Metrics: Initial load, interaction latency, bundle size, failed requests and unauthorized-data tests.
## How do you design a trustworthy SQL/chatbot UI?
Simple: Show what is happening, what evidence supports the answer and whether an action has actually completed.
Technical: Distinguish planning, validation, execution and final results. Present source citations, timestamps, clarifications and explicit incomplete/error states. Avoid displaying a heuristic confidence number as guaranteed accuracy. For privileged actions, show exact parameters and impact before the required approval. Keep technical implementation details out of ordinary user flows unless they aid a decision.
Example: A SQL preview should state that validation passed but execution has not occurred. A failed stream should not look like a completed answer with an empty final section.
Follow-up: How do you prevent duplicate submissions? | Disable accidental duplicate UI actions where appropriate, but rely on server-side idempotency for real protection. Browser controls alone cannot guarantee exactly one operation.
Follow-up: How do you collect feedback? | Attach feedback to a request/configuration ID and ask for actionable categories such as wrong source, wrong filter or missing detail. Sanitize free-text feedback and separate it from trusted instructions.
Metrics: Successful task completion, correction rate, abandonment, duplicate-action rate and time to resolve ambiguity.
## Node.js, Python and Java: how do you compare backend choices?
Simple: Choose based on the workload, ecosystem and team's ability to operate the service, not a blanket fastest-language claim.
Technical: Node.js has an event-loop model suited to many I/O workloads, while CPU-heavy JavaScript can block that loop without worker separation. Python has a strong ML ecosystem and several concurrency models. Java/Spring Boot offers a mature enterprise ecosystem with its own threading, resource and operational choices. Network calls, database plans and model inference often dominate language overhead.
Example: Retain a stable Java business service, provide a Python SDK for AI integration and use Next.js for the web UI. This is a defensible separation when contracts and observability are consistent.
Follow-up: Why use microservices instead of a monolith? | Independent ownership/scaling can justify them, but distributed failures, deployments and data consistency add cost. A modular monolith may be simpler for a small team or tightly coupled workflow.
Follow-up: What should I say about Soven Developer experience? | Explain one actual feature, API integration, bug and validation process. Do not inflate earlier Node.js/React exposure into ownership of systems you did not build.
Trade-offs: A polyglot system gains ecosystem fit but requires more build, deployment and debugging expertise.
# Cloud and operational foundations

## What are IAM roles, least privilege and secret management?
Simple: IAM controls access to cloud resources; least privilege grants only needed permissions; secret management keeps credentials out of code.
Technical: Prefer workload identities and short-lived credentials where supported. Scope roles by operation/resource, rotate secrets and audit access. Application-level tenant authorization remains necessary even when cloud IAM is correct.
Example: An ingestion worker can read its input bucket and write its index artifacts without admin access to the whole account.
Follow-up: Why not use one shared admin key? | It increases blast radius and weakens attribution. Separate responsibilities and identities.
Follow-up: Does encryption replace access control? | No. An authorized decrypting service can still disclose data incorrectly unless application policy is enforced.

## What are a load balancer, reverse proxy and API gateway?
Simple: They sit in front of services to route traffic or apply shared network/API behavior.
Technical: Load balancers distribute requests across healthy instances; reverse proxies forward requests and may terminate TLS; API gateways can add authentication integration, quotas and routing. Products overlap, so describe the functions used rather than assuming every feature exists.
Example: Multiple stateless API replicas share external state and are removed from traffic when readiness fails.
Follow-up: Does a load balancer make the app stateless? | No. You must externalize or deliberately partition durable state; sticky sessions do not fix crash recovery.
Follow-up: Where should rate limits apply? | At suitable global and per-tenant boundaries, with downstream-specific limits as well.

## What are horizontal scaling, vertical scaling and autoscaling?
Simple: Horizontal scaling adds instances; vertical scaling adds resources to an instance; autoscaling adjusts capacity from measured signals.
Technical: Select signals that reflect the bottleneck: queue age, active tokens or request concurrency may be more informative than CPU for LLM services. Account for startup time, cooldowns, maximum capacity and downstream limits.
Example: Adding API replicas does not help if a single model endpoint is already saturated.
Follow-up: Why can autoscaling oscillate? | Noisy signals and aggressive policies can repeatedly add/remove capacity. Use appropriate windows, hysteresis and minimum warm capacity.
Follow-up: Can scaling solve inefficient SQL? | Sometimes capacity buys time, but poor plans can overwhelm any reasonable scale. Fix the bottleneck as well.

## What are availability, durability, RPO and RTO?
Simple: Availability means the service can be used; durability means stored data survives; RPO/RTO define recovery objectives.
Technical: Replication improves some failure tolerance but can replicate corruption or deletion. Backups and tested restores address different risks. Specify which data may be lost and how long recovery may take, then validate with exercises.
Example: A vector index can be rebuilt from durable source files, but that rebuild time may exceed the desired recovery target.
Follow-up: Is a backup successful if upload completed? | Not enough. Verify integrity and restoration under realistic conditions.
Follow-up: Why distinguish index from source durability? | Indexes are derived artifacts; losing originals or metadata can make faithful reconstruction impossible.

## What are metrics, logs, traces and alerts in operations?
Simple: Metrics summarize trends, logs record events, traces connect a request across stages, and alerts notify on actionable conditions.
Technical: Use stable labels and correlation IDs, protect sensitive fields and define retention. An alert should identify an owner and response, not merely report every noisy fluctuation. Link high-level symptoms to detailed traces.
Example: An alert on queue age triggers investigation of model capacity; the trace shows whether time was spent waiting or generating.
Follow-up: Why not log every token and document? | Cost, privacy and data volume can overwhelm usefulness. Collect only what is needed and permitted.
Follow-up: What is alert fatigue? | Too many low-value notifications train responders to ignore them. Use actionable thresholds, grouping and runbooks.
