documents.body:
# How to use these scenarios
Note: These are proposed interview designs, not claims that you deployed them. All workload numbers are illustrative unless explicitly identified as resume evidence. Healthcare and finance examples focus on engineering and decision support; actual clinical, legal and financial workflows need their applicable professional and organizational governance. HIPAA is a US framework applicable to covered entities/business associates, not a universal label for every health application.
# Healthcare scenarios
## H1. Build a hospital policy assistant whose guidelines change frequently.
Simple: Retrieve the current approved policy and show the supporting section. Do not let the assistant silently turn an old guideline into current advice.
Architecture: Approved policy repository -> versioned parsing and metadata -> ACL-aware hybrid index -> query/scope resolution -> current/as-of policy retrieval -> reranking -> evidence and conflict checks -> cited draft -> reviewer/escalation path. Maintain audit and revocation controls alongside every stage.
Technical: First distinguish policy lookup from patient-specific clinical decision support. Store authority, approval state, effective dates, specialty and facility scope. Preserve superseded versions for historical questions, while defaulting to currently effective approved content. Restrict access before model processing, minimize any patient identifiers and keep them out of unnecessary logs. Require claims to map to source spans. When policies conflict or evidence is absent, expose the conflict or route to the responsible team.
Example: A nursing procedure changes on July 1. A June 20 incident review needs the policy effective on June 20, while a current operational question needs the new version. Sorting solely by upload date can answer one of these incorrectly.
Follow-up: Why RAG rather than fine-tuning? | Policies change and require traceable evidence. Retrieval supports versioning and deletion more directly than weight updates. Fine-tuning may improve style or extraction, but should not be the authoritative policy store.
Follow-up: Why not place every guideline in a long prompt? | It can be costly, exceed limits and mix conflicting versions. For a very small bounded policy set, a long-context baseline is reasonable; compare measured quality and freshness controls rather than assuming RAG always wins.
Follow-up: What if two approved sources disagree? | Apply an explicit authority/applicability policy and preserve both source references. If the policy cannot resolve it, abstain and escalate rather than synthesizing an unsupported compromise.
Follow-up: What if the model provider is outside the approved data boundary? | Restrict what data is sent, choose an approved deployment and contractual/data controls with the responsible team, or keep inference within the authorized environment. Encryption alone does not settle all governance questions.
Metrics: Evaluate current-version accuracy, citation support, contradiction detection, false answers on unanswerable questions, unauthorized releases and p95 latency. Use expert-labeled cases spanning facilities, effective dates and obsolete policies.
Trade-offs: Strict evidence requirements increase abstention but reduce unsupported answers. Local hosting may improve control while adding operations. Strong version consistency adds indexing and cache-invalidation work.
Say: I would scope this as a policy lookup assistant, use only approved versioned sources, and filter by facility, authority and effective date. I would retrieve and cite evidence, detect unresolved conflicts and escalate. RAG is appropriate because the knowledge changes and must be auditable. My evaluation would emphasize current-policy correctness and unsupported-answer risk, not only fluent responses.
## H2. Summarize a patient's longitudinal record without omitting critical facts.
Simple: Build a traceable timeline and summarize what the record says. Do not infer missing facts or convert an uncertain note into a confirmed diagnosis.
Architecture: Authorized record APIs -> patient identity verification -> encounter normalization -> structured timeline and document evidence -> completeness checks -> constrained summary -> claim-to-source links -> clinician review. Keep deterministic calculations and identity matching separate from generation.
Technical: Resolve patient and encounter identifiers before retrieval. Preserve timestamps, author, provenance, negation, uncertainty and medication status. Use structured fields where available and retrieve supporting notes for context. Hierarchical summarization can scale, but each compression step must retain critical facts and source links. Define required sections with clinicians and evaluate omissions as well as fabricated additions. Access control must follow the current care context and applicable policy.
Example: 'No evidence of condition X' and 'history of condition X' should not become the same extracted fact. A medication listed as discontinued must not be presented as currently active. The example illustrates information handling, not treatment guidance.
Follow-up: Why not ordinary RAG over all notes? | Pure top-k retrieval may miss low-similarity but mandatory facts. Combine structured completeness checks with targeted retrieval, and define the required information set rather than assuming relevance ranking ensures completeness.
Follow-up: Why not a single summary of the whole record? | Long inputs can dilute important details and exceed budgets. A timeline with source-linked sections offers inspection and targeted updates, but repeated summarization can lose detail and needs quality checks.
Follow-up: How do you handle conflicting medication lists? | Preserve source and time, identify the conflict and use an approved reconciliation workflow. The model should not independently resolve clinically meaningful discrepancies without sufficient authority.
Follow-up: How would you update the summary after a new encounter? | Process the new record version, invalidate affected derived sections, regenerate with provenance and rerun completeness/conflict checks. Keep an audit trail of changes.
Metrics: Clinician-rated factual precision, critical-fact recall, negation/temporal accuracy, unsupported additions, source-link accuracy and review time. Assess subgroup and document-format performance where relevant.
Trade-offs: A longer source-linked summary may be safer but harder to scan. Compression saves review time only if it preserves the required facts. Human review adds latency but is essential for consequential use.
Say: I would treat this as structured evidence synthesis, not just free-form summarization. I would verify identity, normalize a timeline, preserve negation and status, and combine required-field checks with retrieved notes. Every important statement would link back to evidence. I would measure critical omissions and temporal mistakes with clinicians, because a fluent summary can still be unsafe or incomplete.
## H3. Automate medical-document intake and coding suggestions from scanned forms.
Simple: Extract fields with confidence, validate them and send uncertain cases for review. A model suggestion should not silently become a final billing or clinical decision.
Architecture: Secure upload -> malware/type checks -> native-text/OCR routing -> layout and table extraction -> field schema -> deterministic validation/reference lookup -> coding suggestion with evidence -> human review -> audited export.
Technical: Separate extraction from classification/coding. Keep page coordinates and raw images so reviewers can inspect a field. Validate dates, identifiers, units and cross-field consistency, and use the approved current coding/reference source. Track OCR uncertainty separately from model classification uncertainty. Apply access and retention controls to original files and extracted data; deleting one copy does not remove the others.
Example: An OCR system confuses 0 and O in an identifier. A format check catches it, but should not guess the correction unless another authorized source confirms it. Route the field for review and preserve the original crop.
Follow-up: Why not use a multimodal LLM end to end? | It may be a useful baseline, but structured extraction and validation provide clearer error localization and auditability. Compare field accuracy, review cost and failure behavior on representative scans.
Follow-up: Why RAG here? | Retrieval can supply current coding definitions or document instructions. It should not replace OCR, identifier validation or a deterministic eligibility rule that already exists in a system of record.
Follow-up: What if OCR confidence is high but the value is wrong? | Confidence is not correctness. Evaluate against labeled fields and use format, cross-field and source consistency checks. Calibrate routing thresholds using actual error rates.
Follow-up: How do you prevent test leakage? | Split by patient/document template family and time where appropriate, so near-duplicate forms do not appear in both training and test. Keep private information protected in evaluation fixtures.
Metrics: Field-level precision/recall, exact-match accuracy for critical identifiers, coding suggestion agreement, false auto-accept rate, review workload and processing latency. Report critical fields separately from overall averages.
Trade-offs: More review reduces automated errors but increases cost. Aggressive preprocessing can improve OCR while destroying evidence; retain originals and reversible transformations.
Say: I would separate OCR, field validation and coding suggestions. Each extracted value would carry a page reference and uncertainty, with deterministic checks and review for consequential fields. Retrieval would supply approved current references, while the system of record remains authoritative. The acceptance threshold would be chosen from measured false-accept risk and review capacity.
# Cybersecurity scenarios
## C1. Design a SOC assistant for alert triage without overwhelming analysts.
Simple: Gather relevant evidence and help analysts prioritize. Do not treat a persuasive narrative as proof of an attack.
Architecture: SIEM alerts -> normalize/deduplicate -> asset and identity enrichment -> retrieval of approved runbooks/threat context -> bounded investigation tools -> structured hypothesis/evidence summary -> analyst decision -> feedback and audit.
Technical: Use deterministic detection/rules or trained classifiers for suitable high-volume signals, then use retrieval and generation to explain and assemble context. Link every finding to event IDs and timestamps. Separate observed facts, hypotheses and recommended next checks. Treat logs and external intelligence as untrusted input, restrict outbound tools and prevent text inside events from issuing instructions. Tune prioritization to analyst capacity and attack-cost asymmetry.
Example: A burst of failed logins may be an attack, a broken service account or a deployment error. The assistant should correlate source, timing, success events and change history rather than declaring compromise from one pattern.
Follow-up: Why not use RAG as the detector? | Retrieval finds similar records; it does not necessarily detect novel malicious behavior or provide calibrated risk. Use appropriate detection signals and evaluate the assistant's added triage value separately.
Follow-up: Why not fine-tune on all incident logs? | Labels may be noisy, incidents rare and data sensitive. Start with a curated dataset and retrieval baseline; tuning may help classification but does not remove the need for current context.
Follow-up: What if a log contains instructions to reveal credentials? | Treat it as data, redact secrets and enforce tool/network restrictions. A retrieved instruction cannot authorize an action.
Follow-up: How do you prove time savings? | Compare analyst effort on matched or randomized cases with quality guardrails, define start/stop boundaries and account for review time and case complexity. Do not attribute every reduction to the LLM.
Metrics: High-severity recall, alert precision, time to triage, evidence completeness, analyst correction rate, unsupported RCA claims and tool-policy violations. Report prevalence and review capacity.
Trade-offs: High recall creates more work; high precision may miss threats. Automated enrichment improves speed but can introduce stale asset context or noisy threat matches.
Say: I would build an evidence-gathering assistant around existing detection, not replace all detection with a chatbot. It would enrich alerts, retrieve approved procedures and present facts separately from hypotheses. Analysts would retain consequential decisions. I would measure detection coverage and triage time together, with explicit checks for prompt injection through logs.
## C2. A security agent can isolate a host. How do you make the action safe?
Simple: Make the proposed action precise, verify authority and require the appropriate approval before a disruptive change.
Architecture: Alert evidence -> host identity resolution -> proposed action and impact -> policy/risk gate -> bound human approval -> idempotent orchestration -> endpoint-control API -> status reconciliation -> audit and recovery path.
Technical: Confirm the exact asset and environment, including critical-service dependencies. Separate read-only investigation tools from action tools with narrower scopes. Bind approval to target, operation, parameters and expiration. Recheck permissions and current host state before execution. Use operation IDs, handle timeout ambiguity and define recovery procedures with the operations team. Do not assume an isolation can always be instantly reversed without consequences.
Example: The analyst approves isolating a workstation, but the agent's target resolves to a production database host after an inventory update. A target/version mismatch must invalidate the approval and trigger a fresh review.
Follow-up: Why not auto-isolate at a high confidence score? | Confidence must be calibrated and the cost of a false action understood. Some well-defined low-risk cases may be automated under explicit policy, but a generic LLM score is insufficient authorization.
Follow-up: What if the API times out after isolation succeeds? | Query operation/host status before retrying. The same idempotency key should reconcile the existing action, avoiding duplicate or conflicting changes.
Follow-up: Does a human-in-the-loop solve everything? | No. Reviewers need clear evidence and exact impact, and can approve mistakes. Keep least privilege, parameter checks and audit controls regardless.
Follow-up: How do you test without disrupting production? | Use simulated tools or a controlled lab with representative state transitions, then staged rollout and explicit operational authorization. Test stale approvals, wrong targets and duplicate delivery.
Metrics: Correct-target action rate, unauthorized/disallowed actions, duplicate effects, approval latency, reconciliation success and restoration time in controlled tests.
Trade-offs: Approval slows response but reduces unintended disruption. Automation can be tiered by risk, with deterministic policy determining which tier applies.
Say: I would separate investigation from execution privileges and bind approval to a specific verified host and action. Before executing I would recheck state and authority, then use an idempotent operation with status reconciliation. I would measure false-action risk and recovery behavior, not just how quickly the agent can call an isolation API.
## C3. Build a vulnerability and incident knowledge assistant with fresh intelligence.
Simple: Retrieve the right advisory and relate it to the actual asset inventory. Similar text does not prove that an asset is vulnerable.
Architecture: Trusted advisory feeds and internal incidents -> source/version validation -> lexical+dense index -> CVE/product/version resolution -> authorized asset inventory lookup -> applicability checks -> cited explanation and remediation workflow.
Technical: Preserve exact identifiers, affected version ranges, publication/update times and vendor authority. Use lexical matching for CVEs and error codes, with dense retrieval for descriptions. Asset versions and configuration come from current authoritative inventory. Distinguish vulnerability presence, exploitability and business exposure; a retrieved advisory does not settle all three. Validate remediation instructions before operational use.
Example: Two products share a similar name but only one is affected. Entity resolution and version-range checks prevent a semantically similar advisory from becoming an incorrect patch recommendation.
Follow-up: Why BM25 rather than dense search alone? | Exact CVE, package and version tokens are highly discriminative. Dense retrieval can help paraphrases but may blur identifiers. Evaluate both and their fusion on exact and semantic queries.
Follow-up: Why not always use the latest external article? | A newer article can be less authoritative or contain errors. Prefer verified vendor/advisory provenance and retain updates/retractions.
Follow-up: How do you handle poisoned intelligence? | Use source trust controls, ingestion validation, provenance, anomaly checks and bounded tool permissions. Retrieved content must not become executable instructions automatically.
Follow-up: What if inventory is stale? | Surface its timestamp, request a fresh authorized check or qualify the applicability assessment. Do not conceal freshness uncertainty behind a confident answer.
Metrics: Identifier resolution accuracy, applicability precision/recall, advisory freshness lag, citation support and false remediation suggestions.
Trade-offs: Frequent updates improve freshness but increase ingestion validation and reindexing work. Conservative applicability checks reduce false alarms but may require additional evidence collection.
Say: I would combine exact-identifier search with semantic retrieval, then verify applicability against current asset versions and configuration. RAG supplies traceable knowledge; deterministic checks establish whether it applies. I would expose stale inventory and uncertain evidence, and measure false applicability claims rather than only search relevance.
# Finance scenarios
## F1. Build a financial-services policy and compliance assistant.
Simple: Answer from the policy that applies to the user's jurisdiction, product and date, and show the source. Do not turn a general policy into a definitive case decision without the required facts.
Architecture: Approved policies and authoritative references -> jurisdiction/product/effective-date metadata -> permission-aware retrieval -> applicability and conflict checks -> grounded answer -> evidence audit -> compliance-team escalation where required.
Technical: Model authority and applicability separately from recency. Preserve amendments, supersession and as-of queries. Use client/tenant isolation and prevent private customer records from leaking through caches or traces. The assistant can explain source material and route ambiguous cases, while regulated or consequential decisions stay within the organization's approved workflow. Avoid assuming one country's regulation applies everywhere.
Example: A policy uploaded today becomes effective next month. A question about a transaction last week must use the rule effective then, together with the relevant jurisdiction and product scope.
Follow-up: Why RAG rather than training a 'compliance model'? | Rules change and require source traceability. Training may help language behavior, but a model's weights are not a complete auditable policy repository.
Follow-up: Why not a rules engine only? | Rules engines are appropriate for explicit deterministic decisions. RAG helps discover/explain text and exceptions. A combined system can retrieve the policy while a controlled rule service computes eligibility.
Follow-up: How do you handle a conflict between a public rule and internal policy? | Apply an approved authority/escalation policy and show the conflict. The engineer should not invent legal precedence inside a prompt.
Follow-up: How do you audit a past answer? | Store request identity within policy, source versions, configuration versions, evidence IDs and decision outputs. Retention and access must follow applicable organizational requirements.
Metrics: Applicability accuracy, correct as-of version, citation support, unsupported definitive answers, escalation quality and unauthorized disclosure.
Trade-offs: Strict applicability checks add clarification turns. That cost may be justified when a superficially correct general answer could be wrong for the specific case.
Say: I would make jurisdiction, product and effective date first-class filters, then produce cited explanations from approved sources. A rules service would handle explicit deterministic decisions where appropriate, and unresolved cases would go to the responsible team. RAG supports freshness and auditability, but it does not make the system a legal authority.
## F2. Let analysts ask natural-language questions about financial data.
Simple: Turn the question into an explicit business plan, validate the SQL and run it only within the user's data permissions and resource limits.
Architecture: Analyst identity -> question and semantic definitions -> authorized schema retrieval -> join/grain plan -> SQL generation -> AST/policy validation -> least-privilege query service -> numeric/result checks -> cited data timestamp and explanation.
Technical: Resolve currency, reporting period, time zone, gross/net definitions, restatements and aggregation grain. Use approved metric definitions and current schema rather than generic examples for missing fields. Enforce row/column access and read-only execution at the database. Apply query timeouts and result caps. Use deterministic arithmetic and preserve rounding conventions; the LLM explains the result rather than inventing totals.
Example: 'Revenue last quarter' may require net revenue in a reporting currency with refunds and a fiscal calendar. A query summing order amounts by calendar quarter can run successfully and still be wrong.
Follow-up: Why not vectorize the database and use RAG for totals? | Similarity search is not a reliable aggregation engine and may miss rows. Use SQL or a governed analytical API for exact calculations; retrieve definitions to guide the query.
Follow-up: Why not grant the model a database connection directly? | Credentials, policy checks and resource controls belong in a constrained service. The model proposes a query; the execution boundary decides whether it is permitted and bounded.
Follow-up: What if joins double-count amounts? | Check table grain and cardinality, aggregate child tables first when appropriate and test with counterexample datasets. Table recall and syntax validity will not detect every such error.
Follow-up: What if the user requests a missing field? | Clarify or explain the limitation. Do not substitute a similarly named field or a column from an unrelated Spider example.
Metrics: Business-semantic correctness, execution-equivalence on test data, numeric tolerance, join correctness, policy violations, query cost and end-to-end latency.
Trade-offs: Strong restrictions limit ad hoc expressiveness but improve safety and predictability. Clarification costs a turn while preventing confidently wrong financial outputs.
Say: I would combine schema retrieval with a governed semantic layer and explicit query planning. The critical checks are grain, joins, date/currency meaning and permissions, not just SQL syntax. Exact results come from the database under read-only controls, while the model explains them with timestamps and definitions. I would evaluate semantic equivalence on challenging datasets.
## F3. Design a fraud-investigation assistant. Is RAG the fraud model?
Simple: RAG can help investigators understand alerts and retrieve case evidence. Fraud scoring itself usually needs suitable statistical, rule-based or ML methods and carefully labeled outcomes.
Architecture: Transaction/event pipeline -> governed risk model/rules -> alert queue -> authorized case and relationship retrieval -> investigation summary with evidence -> analyst review -> case action service -> outcome labels and monitoring.
Technical: Separate scoring, explanation and action. Fraud labels can be delayed or biased by prior investigations, creating feedback and selection effects. Use time-based evaluation, prevent future-information leakage and monitor changing transaction patterns. Retrieve policies, previous cases and entity links for investigators, but do not infer guilt from similarity alone. Customer-impacting actions require the organization's approved decision and appeal processes.
Example: A transaction resembles previous fraud cases but belongs to a legitimate new travel pattern. The assistant should list supporting and contradictory evidence and ask for the missing authorized check rather than asserting fraud.
Follow-up: Why not fine-tune an LLM to classify every transaction? | It may be expensive, difficult to calibrate and poorly matched to structured high-volume data. Compare against suitable tabular/time-series baselines and use language models where unstructured evidence adds value.
Follow-up: Why not optimize accuracy? | Fraud is often rare, so a trivial negative classifier can appear accurate. Evaluate precision/recall at investigation capacity, expected loss and customer-impact guardrails.
Follow-up: How do you avoid leakage? | Split by time and related entities as appropriate, use only information available at prediction time, and separate confirmed future outcomes from input features.
Follow-up: How do you explain a model decision? | Provide validated contributing evidence and limitations, not a fabricated causal narrative. A generated explanation should be checked against actual model/features and case records.
Metrics: Precision at analyst capacity, recall of confirmed cases, false-positive customer impact, calibration, time to disposition, evidence correctness and drift. Report outcome-label delay and review bias.
Trade-offs: Aggressive blocking may reduce loss while harming legitimate users. A useful assistant lowers investigation effort without hiding uncertainty or automating unsupported judgments.
Say: I would keep fraud scoring separate from the GenAI investigation assistant. The scoring system handles structured risk signals, while retrieval assembles permitted case evidence and the model produces a checked summary. I would evaluate rare-event performance and analyst workload together, account for delayed labels, and retain controlled decision paths for customer-impacting actions.

# Read this before rehearsing
Note: Prepared from your four local resume versions, attached interview prompt and selected local SQL Copilot code/reports. This guide does not change any resume. 'Resume-reported' means supplied in your material, not independently verified from production records. Sample wording is a rehearsal template: use first-person ownership only for work you personally performed. Do not disclose confidential client names, data or credentials in interviews.
Note: Evidence inspected: D:/Resume/ShashankSingh_AIEngineer, D:/Resume/ShashankSingh_AIEngineer_GPU, D:/Resume/ShashankSingh_AIEngineer_TwoPage and D:/Resume/ShashankSingh_AIEngineer_OnePage_ATS; the supplied Pasted text.txt; D:/Projects/EnterpriseSQLCopilot/reports/enterprise_query_planning_before_after.md and nvidia_gpt_oss_20b_evaluation.md, dated 2026-08-10; selected backend and orchestration files. The report snapshot is not a newly rerun production benchmark.
# Introduction and ownership
## Tell me about yourself in 60-90 seconds.
Simple: Lead with your current work, two concrete projects and the engineering problems you solve. Keep the technology list secondary.
Technical: Your supplied background is B.Tech CSE, Siksha 'O' Anusandhan University, 2020-2024, CGPA 8.50; TCS from October 2024, and earlier Soven Developer work from June-September 2024. The materials use AI/ML Developer and GenAI Engineer descriptions; use your exact official title where required and explain your functional role accurately.
Say: I work on enterprise AI and backend integration at TCS in the financial-services domain. My main areas are retrieval and schema-grounded SQL generation, conversational workflows using Rasa and MCP, and Python service integration. I focus on making model outputs usable through validation, permissions and observability. I can go deepest on the SQL Copilot planning pipeline and Python SDK/backend integration, including their limitations and the evaluation evidence available.
Follow-up: Why should we consider you for a senior-level technical discussion? | Explain the design decisions, failure handling and ownership you can defend. Do not equate preparing for senior questions with having held a senior title. Demonstrate depth through specific trade-offs and measured evidence.
Follow-up: What did you personally own? | Prepare a project-by-project boundary: designed, implemented, tested, deployed, operated or assisted. Name team interfaces without taking credit for others' work.
## How do you distinguish tools used from tools only studied?
Simple: Keep an implementation ledger. A skill list is not evidence that every project used every listed technology.
Technical: For each tool record project/component, purpose, code/config reference, environment, date and personal contribution. Current SQL Copilot material supports BM25/FAISS and a schema-relationship graph; the prompt also lists Qdrant/Pinecone, but their use in this project is not established by the inspected evidence. Treat them as broader skills or proposals unless you can show the implementation.
Example: Say, 'The implementation I can demonstrate uses FAISS. I understand how I would compare a managed vector service for filtering and operations, but I would not claim that migration as completed.'
Follow-up: What if I used the tool in a prototype only? | Say prototype, explain the experiment and result, and distinguish it from production deployment. That is still valid experience.
Follow-up: What if asked a configuration I cannot recall? | State what you know and identify the evidence needed. Do not invent an HNSW index, embedding dimension or deployed model size because it sounds plausible.
Trade-offs: A narrower accurate claim is easier to defend than a broad stack list with no implementation story.
# SQL Copilot deep-dive
## Explain your SQL Copilot architecture in two minutes.
Simple: Explain how the system turns a question into a schema-grounded plan and validated SQL, then clearly identify the actual execution boundary.
Architecture: Question -> intent/entity resolution -> schema linking -> semantic resolution -> graph-based join discovery -> query planning -> SQL generation -> validation -> coverage audit -> confidence/clarification. Optional model assistance and the web interface surround this pipeline.
Technical: The materials describe Python, BM25/FAISS, relationship-based join discovery, a ten-stage LangGraph workflow and optional GPT-OSS-20B via NVIDIA. The current inspected web backend uses Flask with an ASGI arrangement and Next.js frontend; broader resume claims mention FastAPI. Confirm whether FastAPI belongs to an earlier iteration, separate service or integration layer before explaining both as one deployment. A safe SQL execution stage is discussed in your prompt, but the inspected evidence does not establish a complete deployed execution path.
Say: The core is planner-first: I resolve the question against schema and business definitions, identify relationships and a query plan, then generate and validate SQL. Coverage checks look for missing requested elements, and uncertain cases should clarify rather than guess. The current deterministic benchmark is separate from optional model-assisted behavior. I distinguish the demonstrated generation/validation pipeline from any execution integration that needs additional evidence.
Follow-up: Why not let the LLM generate SQL directly? | Planning exposes ambiguous metrics, missing columns and incorrect join grain before generation. It supports deterministic validation and more localized debugging.
Follow-up: What is your biggest current limitation? | The saved benchmark shows a large drop on five-plus-table cases. Discuss join/semantic planning improvements and evaluation, not an unsupported claim that all complex queries already work.
## Reconcile 87.5% success with the saved benchmark.
Simple: Do not combine unverified and measured numbers into one result. The local saved report shows 67.5% success across 120 cases, not 87.5%.
Technical: The report lists success 67.5%, SQL validity 78.33%, join success 79.17%, average table recall 93.15%, average planner latency 20.839 ms and p95 planner latency 31.537 ms. Rounded counts correspond to 81/120 successes, 94/120 valid cases and 95/120 join successes if the report uses those denominators. Average table recall is a mean of per-case values, not 112 correct cases. The 87.5% claim would imply 105/120 and requires a separate reproducible report and definition.
Example: Say, 'The report I can substantiate is the deterministic planner run on 120 cases. An older 87.5% figure appears in my material, but I would not present it as verified without the separate run and scoring definition.'
Follow-up: Is 67.5% live execution accuracy? | Not established merely by the report's success label. Inspect its scoring code and whether real result equivalence was tested. Do not rename it end-to-end production accuracy.
Follow-up: Does 31.54 ms include NVIDIA inference and the UI? | No evidence supports that interpretation. It is the deterministic planner boundary in the saved report. The NVIDIA evaluation report explicitly says the provider was not run.
Follow-up: Can I claim a before/after improvement? | The report states historical pre-change metrics were unavailable. Without a comparable baseline, report the current result and avoid invented speedups or percentage gains.
Metrics: Bring the report date, exact configuration, case categories, definitions and denominators. Do not quote a percentage without those boundaries.
## Why does your planner struggle on complex joins, and what would you improve?
Simple: More tables create more possible relationships and more ways to get the business meaning or row grain wrong.
Technical: The saved categories have 20 cases each. Reported success is 95% for edge/safety/clarification, 85% single-table, 80% two-table, 60% three-table, 50% four-table and 35% five-plus-table. Inspect failures individually: missing tables, wrong edges, ambiguous measures, filters and row multiplication need different fixes. Use graph constraints and semantic definitions, then evaluate on a held-out complex-query set.
Example: A proposed improvement is to score candidate join plans using validated relationships and required entities, then reject plans that violate known cardinality or leave requirements unresolved. This is a next-step design, not a completed measured improvement.
Follow-up: Why not increase top-k schema retrieval? | It may recover missing tables but also add distractors. First determine whether the correct tables were missing or whether planning failed despite their presence.
Follow-up: Why not add retries? | Repeating a flawed plan without new evidence can increase latency without fixing semantics. Use error-specific feedback or clarification.
Metrics: Compare per-category success, join-path correctness, table/column recall, unnecessary joins and latency with the same evaluation boundary.
## What did LangGraph actually do, and are ten stages ten agents?
Simple: Ten named stages are not automatically ten independent agents. Explain where real computation and branching happen.
Technical: The inspected orchestration file defines ten workflow nodes. Its node-runner helper records stage visits; this alone does not prove each callback independently performs the corresponding reasoning. Distinguish the logical pipeline, graph orchestration and underlying deterministic engine. If another version contains substantive node logic, bring that code and describe the version clearly.
Example: An interview diagram can show intent, linking, planning and validation stages while your explanation says which are deterministic functions and which invoke a model. Do not label every box an autonomous agent.
Follow-up: What would justify LangGraph here? | Explicit state, conditional repair/clarification branches, tracing and potentially durable execution. Demonstrate the features actually used rather than listing every framework capability.
Follow-up: How do you prevent a repair loop? | Bound attempts and time, preserve original requirements and detect no-progress states. Verify whether 'three retries' means three additional attempts or three attempts total in your code.
Trade-offs: A graph improves visibility when branching is meaningful; simple sequential logic may need less orchestration.
## What is GraphRAG in your SQL project, and what is the Spider dataset issue?
Simple: Your SQL use case can use a graph of table relationships for join planning. That differs from document knowledge-graph summarization systems sometimes also called GraphRAG.
Technical: State what nodes and edges mean and how their provenance is validated. Generic SQL examples can guide syntax, but cannot supply enterprise columns or relationships missing from the actual schema. The attached prompt says 'Spider's 80,034 examples'; official Spider 1.0 describes 10,181 questions and 5,693 unique complex SQL queries across 200 databases. A local CSV with another row count needs its own provenance, version and transformation history.
Example: Say, 'I used a schema relationship graph for join discovery and a separate generic SQL-pattern corpus. I need to verify the corpus lineage before attributing its row count to Spider.'
Follow-up: Is the benchmark schema of approximately 18-20 tables verified? | That range is supplied in your prompt. Before quoting an exact number, identify the actual schema snapshot used by the 120-case benchmark.
Follow-up: Can fallback examples answer an unknown attribute? | No. A missing private-schema attribute should lead to clarification or a limitation, not a fabricated mapping from a public dataset.
Trade-offs: Generic examples can improve syntax patterns but create grounding and leakage risks if treated as authoritative schema evidence.
## How do you defend GPT-OSS-20B and the Gemini variant?
Simple: Separate an optional configured capability from a completed model evaluation, and keep distinct project variants separate.
Technical: The saved NVIDIA report explicitly states GPT-OSS-20B was not run because the provider was not configured/available in that process. It reports no NVIDIA accuracy, latency, token or hallucination numbers. Your resume also describes a Gemini variant using Antigravity, ADK, Vertex AI Agent Engine, Firestore and AST validation. These are supplied claims; prepare a runnable demo, deployment/config evidence and your exact contribution before asserting details.
Example: Do not attribute the deterministic planner's 31.54 ms p95 to a hosted 20B model. Explain the optional provider path and the conditions under which it is called or bypassed.
Follow-up: How would you evaluate model assistance? | Run the same held-out cases with and without it, record prompts/model version, latency/tokens, validity and semantic success, then analyze which failures it fixes or creates.
Follow-up: Did you fine-tune GPT-OSS-20B? | The inspected report does not establish that. Distinguish API integration, local inference and fine-tuning; claim only the work you can evidence.
Metrics: Keep each variant's dataset, configuration and outcome report separate. No model-provider result is invented in this guide.

# Rasa, SDKs and enterprise integration
## Explain the Rasa/MCP conversational chatbot project.
Simple: This project is included as a major deep-dive. Explain intent handling, backend discovery and controlled tool execution rather than treating it as a small supporting bullet.
Architecture: User -> Rasa intent/dialogue state -> action mapping -> authorized API/tool discovery -> Python SDK/FastAPI integration -> enterprise backend -> validated result -> conversational summary.
Technical: Your materials describe a six-step conversational flow and a four-stage interpretation/discovery/execution/summary view. Map these as levels of abstraction and verify the actual components. AWS-hosted MCP tools, Streamable HTTP and application discovery are resume-reported. Prepare exact server/client roles, transport version, tool schemas and a representative end-to-end trace.
Example: A user asks about an application without a required identifier. The dialogue collects it, verifies access and calls a typed status method. The answer summarizes returned facts with a timestamp; it does not guess a status.
Follow-up: Why use Rasa with an LLM? | Rasa can provide structured intents, slots and predictable flows while an LLM handles flexible interpretation/summarization. Explain which responsibilities you actually assigned to each.
Follow-up: What was multi-agent about the design? | Identify distinct roles, state and routing if they exist. A chain of four steps or several tools is not by itself proof of multiple autonomous agents.
Metrics: Prepare actual intent/task success, clarification and tool-failure measurements if available. None are supplied here as verified production figures.
## What exactly did you implement in Python SDKs, FastAPI and access control?
Simple: Explain one concrete backend capability from Python method to service response, including how identity and permissions are checked.
Technical: You requested this experience be added: Java/Spring Boot services integrated through reusable Python SDKs, exposed backend capabilities through FastAPI, and used MCP for chatbot development with authentication and authorization. Clarify whether you wrapped existing REST APIs or rewrote selected service logic. Identify token acquisition/validation, scopes, object-level checks, retries, timeouts and error translation from actual implementation.
Example: A strong demonstration is a sanitized sequence diagram plus one SDK method and its tests: authorized success, forbidden object, expired token, timeout and duplicate request handling.
Follow-up: Where is authorization enforced? | At the backend/tool boundary for the requested resource, with verified principal/tenant context. A frontend check or prompt instruction is insufficient.
Follow-up: What if the model changes the account ID? | The server must reject access to an unauthorized object even when the tool name and schema are valid. Explain your implemented protection or label it as a necessary improvement.
Trade-offs: A reusable SDK reduces duplicated integration code but needs versioning and contract tests to avoid spreading one bug to every tool.
# KEDB, logs, BERT and GPU claims
## Defend the KEDB: 100K+ reports, under two seconds, 27% and 120 hours.
Simple: Explain retrieval behavior, then define how each impact figure was measured. These numbers are resume-reported, not independently verified by the inspected benchmark files.
Technical: BM25 supports exact error identifiers, FAISS semantic similarity and Redis repeated lookup acceleration. Explain preprocessing, duplicates, permissions, query classes and cache invalidation. 'Under two seconds' needs a percentile, boundary, concurrency, hardware and cache-hit mix. Duplicate reduction needs a baseline/time window and denominator; time savings need the number of users/cases and a measurement method.
Example: A defensible calculation might compare matched-case median triage time before and after, multiplied by verified monthly case volume, minus review overhead. This is an example methodology, not evidence for your 120-hour figure.
Follow-up: Why hybrid retrieval? | Exact codes and stack identifiers benefit from lexical matching; paraphrased symptoms benefit from semantic similarity. Show an ablation if available, or describe it as the evaluation you would run.
Follow-up: Is 27% a percentage-point reduction? | Clarify. A drop from 100 duplicate cases to 73 is a 27% relative reduction; a rate from 40% to 13% is 27 percentage points. Do not interchange them.
Metrics: Prepare relevance labels, latency distributions, cache breakdown, duplicate-definition rules and productivity evidence.
## Defend AI log analysis and 4-5 hours saved per engineer/week.
Simple: Distinguish a useful summary from a verified root cause and a proposed fix from an automatically executed change.
Technical: Your material names Qwen3.5 and LLaMA 3. Confirm exact checkpoints/API IDs, dates, quantization, deployment and which model served which stage. Describe log parsing, secret redaction, deduplication, time-window correlation, context limits and structured output. A root-cause hypothesis needs supporting evidence and should not be presented as causally proven merely because the model generated it.
Example: A summary links repeated timeout events to a deployment window and suggests checking a dependency. That is an evidence-based investigation step; it is not proof the deployment caused the outage.
Follow-up: How was time saved measured? | Bring baseline task time, sample size, user count, study window and quality checks. Self-reported estimates should be labeled as such, and review/correction time included.
Follow-up: How did you prevent dangerous fixes? | Explain actual controls: approved runbooks, read-only investigation, validation and operational gates for changes. Do not claim automatic remediation if the system only recommended actions.
Metrics: Summary factuality, key-event recall, root-cause agreement with incident reviews, unsupported remedies and analyst time with quality preserved.
## Defend the BERT model trained on 1,000+ FSD documents.
Simple: State that the dataset was documents, then explain initialization, objective and the downstream task.
Technical: The material says PyTorch, Hugging Face and masked-language modeling. Confirm whether training started from a pretrained BERT checkpoint, which would ordinarily be domain-adaptive continued pretraining. Prepare usable token count, deduplication, train/validation/test split, tokenizer, sequence length, steps, optimizer, learning rate and held-out results. Do not invent these values. BERT is an encoder, not a standard causal chatbot.
Example: Explain why domain terms and specifications motivated adaptation, then compare the adapted encoder against the original on the actual downstream task. Without that comparison, describe the training exercise and its limitations honestly.
Follow-up: Why not train from scratch? | A small document collection usually makes reuse of pretrained representations a more plausible baseline. Scratch training needs sufficient token diversity and compute; the actual initialization determines the correct claim.
Follow-up: What proves it improved? | Held-out objective performance and downstream task evaluation, with leakage controls and a baseline. A lower training loss alone is insufficient.
Metrics: Collect MLM validation loss, task-specific metrics, data-split evidence and base-versus-adapted results.
## Defend LoRA/QLoRA, DGX Spark, TensorRT and vLLM on the GPU version.
Simple: Bring one reproducible optimization experiment, not just the list of tools.
Technical: These are resume-reported capabilities. The inspected files do not establish exact adapter ranks, datasets, model revisions, engine versions, hardware configuration or before/after results. Separate training from inference, API usage from local serving, and TensorRT-related experiments from vLLM experiments. Verify GB10 platform compatibility and the actual memory design.
Example: Your evidence ledger should show the bottleneck, baseline configuration, single changed variable, measured quality and latency/memory results, and rollback decision. If the work was exploratory, call it an experiment.
Follow-up: What was your LoRA rank and why? | Use the real configuration. If unavailable, say it needs verification and explain how you would choose rank through validation. Do not substitute the guide's rank-8 arithmetic example as your project setting.
Follow-up: How much faster was vLLM? | Only quote a measured comparison with the same model, precision, workload and timing boundaries. The library's published benchmark is not your personal result.
Metrics: Peak memory, TTFT/TPOT, throughput at a latency target, task-quality regression and training-resource use, with reproducible artifacts.
# Broader experience and final rehearsal
## What can interviewers ask about Linux, Bash, DBA support and Soven Developer?
Simple: They will ask for a specific incident, script, query or feature you handled and how you knew it worked.
Technical: For Linux, prepare deployment, service/log inspection and rollback examples. For Bash, explain input handling, quoting, failure paths and idempotency. For DBA support, identify responsibilities such as query troubleshooting, permissions or maintenance; do not imply ownership of full recovery architecture without evidence. For Soven, choose a JavaScript/Python/API feature and describe your role, testing and debugging.
Example: Structure an incident answer as symptom, evidence, hypothesis, action, verification and prevention. Use a real case with sanitized details rather than inventing a dramatic outage.
Follow-up: What if I only assisted the DBA? | Say assisted and specify the work you performed. Supporting analysis and implementing a reviewed fix are credible contributions.
Follow-up: What if asked about React/Next.js depth? | State your basic/intermediate scope, explain implemented screens and request handling, and distinguish conceptual knowledge from production ownership.
Metrics: Use real incident duration, query timing or feature outcomes if recorded. Otherwise describe observable verification without fabricated impact numbers.
## What evidence should I collect before sending these resumes again?
Simple: Resolve ambiguous metrics and prepare proof for the claims most likely to be challenged.
Technical: Priority items are the 87.5% SQL claim, generic SQL dataset provenance, actual execution deployment, Flask/FastAPI component history, LangGraph node behavior, exact model/provider runs, BERT training configuration and GPU optimization results. For KEDB/log productivity figures collect baseline, sample size and timing definitions. Verify official job title and certification names/issuers against your records; a certification is not proof of every associated implementation skill.
Example: Keep a private ledger with claim, evidence file, date, denominator, boundary, your contribution and remaining uncertainty. Use sanitized diagrams and synthetic examples for interviews, never confidential production extracts.
Follow-up: Should I remove all metrics until perfect evidence exists? | Use figures you can substantiate and qualify estimates or user-reported impact. Correct known inaccuracies before use; this guide itself does not edit the resumes.
Follow-up: What is the strongest way to answer a gap? | State the limitation, explain how you would measure or fix it, and connect that plan to the observed failure. This demonstrates judgment without inventing completed work.
Metrics: Every numeric claim should have a source, definition and scope. Every tool claim should have an identifiable component or a clearly labeled learning context.

documents.title: Mock interviews and revision
documents.subtitle: Five practice rounds, answer keys and a four-week rehearsal plan
documents.body:
# Practice one question at a time
Note: Cover the answer, speak for two minutes, then draw the architecture and attempt the follow-ups. In a live mock session ask the mentor to reveal one question at a time and critique your answer before moving on. These answer keys are for self-study, not a script to recite without understanding.
## Round 1: Your RAG assistant fails after a policy update. Diagnose it.
Simple: Trace the policy from source to final response and locate stale or conflicting state.
Architecture: Source version -> ingestion job -> active index -> retrieval -> evidence selection -> answer cache -> generation -> final version check.
Technical: Check publication versus effective date, failed ingestion, mixed chunks, stale replicas, permissions and cache keys. Replay an affected query with current oracle evidence and with cache disabled in a controlled test. If oracle evidence fixes the answer, focus on retrieval/freshness; otherwise inspect generation and conflict handling. Repair the first failing boundary and serve a clear degraded response where needed.
Example: The new index is correct, but a response cache lacks corpus version in its key. Invalidating the index alone cannot repair cached answers.
Follow-up: What if only some users fail? | Compare tenant/role filters, cache partitions and regional replicas. It may be permission-specific or a selective-filter recall issue rather than a global model regression.
Follow-up: What catches this earlier? | Freshness lag, correct-version answer rate and canary questions for recently changed policies, alongside cache/version telemetry.
Metrics: Correct-version rate, stale-answer rate, ingestion/cache lag and incident recovery time.
Trade-offs: Strong freshness checks add latency and dependencies; weaker checks permit stale answers. Choose by data risk.
Say: I would localize the stale version across ingestion, retrieval and caches, use an oracle-evidence experiment, and repair the first failing boundary. Then I would add version-aware keys and update canaries.
## Round 2: Double serving throughput without materially hurting quality or p95.
Simple: Identify the bottleneck, then improve capacity at a fixed latency and quality target.
Architecture: Load generator -> admission/queue -> prefill/decode scheduler -> GPU -> streamed result -> complete outcome metrics.
Technical: Inspect active tokens, KV occupancy, prefill/decode balance, CPU preprocessing and batching. Test continuous batching, token-budget tuning and prefix reuse where applicable. Consider quantization only with quality evaluation, or replicas if capacity is genuinely saturated. Do not declare success by dropping long requests or excluding errors.
Example: If shared prompts dominate prefill, prefix caching may reduce work. If decode bandwidth dominates with unrelated prompts, the same change may do little.
Follow-up: What if throughput rises but p99 doubles? | The change may violate user experience despite a better average. Adjust admission/fairness or separate batch workloads; report the full trade-off.
Follow-up: How do you estimate concurrency memory? | Add weight/runtime memory to per-sequence KV estimates using actual layers, KV heads, dimension, precision and retained tokens.
Metrics: Throughput at the SLO, TTFT/TPOT, error rate, peak memory, quality and cost per successful task.
Trade-offs: Larger batches improve utilization but increase waiting. Replicas cost money; lower precision can change quality.
Say: I would optimize the measured bottleneck and compare at the same offered workload, quality gate and p95 constraint. Successful work within the service target is the objective.
## Round 3: An agent creates two tickets after a timeout. Fix the design.
Simple: The retry duplicated a business action. Introduce durable operation identity and reconcile uncertain results.
Architecture: User action -> stable operation ID/payload hash -> authorization -> idempotent ticket service -> committed result -> workflow checkpoint -> response/status lookup.
Technical: The same business request must reuse its ID across retries. Atomically bind the ID to the effect where possible, reject changed payloads and handle in-progress operations. If the downstream cannot support this, add reconciliation and acknowledge the remaining race; a Redis cache written after creation cannot guarantee duplicate prevention by itself.
Example: The ticket is created but the response is lost. Retrying with the original ID returns the existing ticket instead of creating a new one.
Follow-up: Is at-least-once delivery the bug? | It is an expected delivery model. The bug is treating duplicate delivery as a new non-idempotent action without a recovery design.
Follow-up: Does a graph checkpoint solve it? | It preserves workflow state, but a crash can occur between the effect and checkpoint. External action semantics need separate design.
Metrics: Duplicate effects, unresolved outcomes, retry amplification and recovery under injected failures.
Trade-offs: Idempotency state needs retention and cleanup; coordination adds latency. Scope guarantees precisely.
Say: I would treat the timeout as an unknown outcome, reuse a durable operation ID and query the existing result before retrying. Checkpointing helps orchestration; exactly-once business effects need explicit service design.
## Round 4: Your resume says 87.5% SQL success. Show the evidence.
Simple: Acknowledge the mismatch and give the substantiated result with its boundary.
Technical: The saved deterministic report shows 67.5% success across 120 cases, 78.33% validity, 79.17% join success, 93.15% average table recall and 31.54 ms planner p95. The optional NVIDIA provider was not run in its saved report. A separate 87.5% claim needs its own run and scoring definition; it cannot be merged into this result.
Example: Correct the unsupported number rather than rationalizing it as a different metric without evidence.
Follow-up: Why is table recall higher than final success? | Retrieving correct tables is necessary but insufficient. Joins, semantics, filters, aggregation and validation can still fail.
Follow-up: What would you improve first? | Inspect five-plus-table failures, where success is 35%, and separate missing-schema problems from planning/cardinality errors.
Metrics: Use counts and definitions. Keep planner latency distinct from end-to-end model/application latency.
Trade-offs: Accurate scope may sound less impressive than an inflated number, but creates a defensible engineering discussion.
Say: The result I can substantiate is the saved deterministic planner run. I would bring the report and explain each metric separately, including complex-query limitations and the unmeasured provider path.
## Round 5: Design an assistant that explains account data and submits a request.
Simple: Separate reading/explaining data from performing an action, with stronger controls at the action boundary.
Architecture: Identity -> intent/clarification -> authorized read tools and policy RAG -> proposed request -> policy checks -> required approval -> idempotent action API -> status/audit -> response.
Technical: Use current APIs for account values, retrieval for definitions and a constrained service for submission. Bind each call to resource permissions. Separate evidence from authority, reject instructions in retrieved content and recheck stale approvals. Define compensating actions only where the business operation supports them.
Example: Explain an option from approved policy, fetch the permitted account state and show the exact proposed change before the workflow's required approval.
Follow-up: Why not one all-powerful tool? | Narrow tools/scopes reduce accidental effects and make tests/audits clearer. Broad capabilities increase the impact of prompt injection.
Follow-up: What if the action succeeds but the final answer fails? | Preserve operation status and return it on retry. Do not repeat the action just to regenerate the explanation.
Metrics: Authorized completion, wrong-object actions, duplicates, clarification quality, audit completeness and latency by path.
Trade-offs: Gates slow actions but protect consequential operations. Keep information lookup efficient while applying controls by action risk.
Say: I would use RAG for definitions, authoritative APIs for live data and a separate authorized idempotent action service. The model can propose; server-side policy decides what it may execute.
# Four-week rehearsal plan
Note: Week 1: Resume prep, SQL Copilot and RAG; explain one real project daily and resolve the evidence ledger. Week 2: Agents/MCP, SDK/backend, Python exercises and access-control scenarios. Week 3: LLM foundations as needed, GPU arithmetic, LoRA/QLoRA and BERT; reproduce a small measured experiment if available. Week 4: Domain scenarios, cloud/Linux/frontend and five mock rounds, with targeted review of weak answers.
Note: Daily structure: recall without notes; one architecture sketch; two main questions with all follow-ups; one calculation or coding exercise; a short error log. Use the 12-point rubric in Start here. A question is mastered when you can change a constraint, explain a rejected alternative and evaluate the revised design.

documents.title: LlamaIndex, LangSmith, Grafana and tooling
documents.subtitle: What each tool does, how components connect and how to defend your choices
documents.body:
# Tool map
Architecture: LlamaIndex/LangChain help application construction; LangGraph coordinates state and control; LangSmith helps inspect and evaluate application runs; OpenTelemetry propagates standardized telemetry; Prometheus stores/queries operational metrics; Grafana visualizes connected data. Choose components for requirements rather than using every product.

# Framework and observability questions

## What is LlamaIndex?
Simple: LlamaIndex is a framework for building applications that connect language models to external data.
Technical: Its abstractions include documents/nodes, ingestion, indexes, retrievers and query engines. The framework coordinates components; it is not itself a model or a universal replacement for a vector database. Inspect what an integration actually stores and retrieves.
Example: Load approved documents, create nodes with source metadata, retrieve candidates and synthesize a cited answer.
Follow-up: Why not use direct Python calls? | Direct code can be clearer for small pipelines. A framework helps when connectors and reusable retrieval abstractions reduce work without hiding needed controls.
Follow-up: Does it guarantee accurate RAG? | No. Parsing, evidence quality, permissions, prompts and evaluation remain your responsibility.

## What are Documents and Nodes in LlamaIndex?
Simple: A Document represents source material; a Node is a smaller unit used in processing/retrieval with metadata and relationships.
Technical: Stable source/node identities support updates, citations and parent-child relationships. The exact types and fields depend on the release. Preserve original source references rather than treating an embedding row as the entire document.
Example: A PDF document yields paragraph/table nodes linked to page and section metadata.
Follow-up: Can a node contain more than plain text? | Framework integrations can support multimodal or structured representations; verify the specific component and model support.
Follow-up: Why does metadata matter? | It controls filtering, provenance and updates. Losing it can make a relevant answer unauthorized or impossible to cite.

## What are an index, retriever and query engine in LlamaIndex?
Simple: An index organizes searchable data, a retriever returns candidates, and a query engine combines retrieval with response production.
Technical: Keep the abstraction boundaries visible so you can test retrieval without generation and change synthesis separately. A query engine may include postprocessors/rerankers and response synthesis; examine its configuration rather than assuming a default architecture.
Example: Call the retriever alone to inspect whether the correct policy is present before blaming the LLM answer.
Follow-up: Is an index always a vector index? | No. The broader term covers different structures and query strategies; identify the actual backend.
Follow-up: Why separate these components? | It enables focused tests, clearer metrics and swapping one stage without rebuilding everything.

## What are ingestion transformations and node postprocessors?
Simple: Ingestion transformations prepare data before indexing; postprocessors adjust retrieved candidates before synthesis.
Technical: Parsing, splitting, metadata enrichment and embedding belong to ingestion. Filtering, reranking and context selection may occur after retrieval. Version both stages because changing either affects output and caching.
Example: A postprocessor removes duplicate nodes then reranks remaining authorized evidence.
Follow-up: Should access filtering wait until synthesis? | No. Enforce permissions before unauthorized content reaches a model or external processor, and recheck when needed.
Follow-up: Can postprocessing recover missing evidence? | Not unless it explicitly triggers more retrieval. Reordering an incomplete candidate set cannot create the missing document.

## LlamaIndex versus LangChain versus LangGraph: what is the distinction?
Simple: They overlap, but emphasize data/retrieval integration, application integrations and explicit stateful orchestration respectively.
Technical: Avoid rigid claims that one can only do RAG or another only agents. Compare required connectors, control flow, observability, deployment complexity and team familiarity in pinned versions. You can combine them, but overlapping abstractions can complicate debugging.
Example: Use a retriever inside a graph node while keeping its input/output contract framework-independent.
Follow-up: Should I learn all APIs by memory? | Understand responsibilities and implement a small example. Exact imports and flags change; verify them against the installed version.
Follow-up: How do I justify my project choice? | Describe the requirement it solved and the simpler alternative you evaluated, not just popularity.

## What is LangSmith?
Simple: LangSmith helps observe and evaluate LLM application behavior using traces, datasets and experiments.
Technical: Trace retrieval, model and tool steps with relevant versions and sanitized metadata. It supports multiple frameworks; using LangGraph is not a prerequisite. Enabled tracing still needs access, retention and data-redaction decisions.
Example: Inspect a failed SQL request to see whether schema retrieval, generation or validation caused the failure.
Follow-up: Is LangSmith the same as LangGraph? | No. LangGraph orchestrates execution; LangSmith provides observability/evaluation capabilities around applications.
Follow-up: Does an installed dependency mean tracing worked? | No. Verify configuration and actual trace delivery. The resume should distinguish available instrumentation from observed production coverage.

## What is a trace, span, run and experiment?
Simple: A trace follows one execution; spans/runs represent its steps; an experiment evaluates a configuration over a dataset.
Technical: Names vary by tool, but parent-child timing and causal relationships are the key. Record request IDs, stage, model/prompt version and outcomes. A trace is not itself proof of correctness; connect outcomes to a scoring rubric.
Example: A retrieval span contains candidate source IDs and timing, while a generation span records token counts and the model revision.
Follow-up: What if asynchronous tasks lose trace context? | Propagate the context through queues and SDK boundaries and link resumed work explicitly.
Follow-up: Why separate experiments from production traces? | Experiments provide controlled comparisons; production traces reveal real workload failures. Each has different sampling and privacy needs.

## How do you build a LangSmith dataset and evaluation experiment?
Simple: Create versioned examples and expected outcomes, run a fixed configuration and attach appropriate evaluators.
Technical: Separate development and held-out data, keep reference evidence and use deterministic checks alongside calibrated model judges. Store configuration and dataset versions so comparisons are reproducible. Review failures by category rather than only aggregate scores.
Example: Compare hybrid retrieval with and without a reranker on the same policy questions and report latency as well as quality.
Follow-up: Can user thumbs-up be the only label? | No. It is useful feedback but may reflect style, convenience or selection bias rather than factual correctness.
Follow-up: How do you protect private prompts? | Minimize/redact content, restrict access and choose retention/deployment controls appropriate to the data.

## What are Prometheus and its metric types?
Simple: Prometheus is an operational monitoring system built around labeled time-series metrics.
Technical: Counters accumulate events, gauges represent values that can rise/fall, histograms bucket observations, and summaries provide client-side distribution statistics with specific aggregation limits. Choose labels with bounded cardinality. Exact query/metric behavior depends on configuration.
Example: Count requests/errors, gauge queue depth and record request duration in a histogram.
Follow-up: Why not use a counter for current queue size? | Queue size decreases as well as increases; a gauge represents it directly.
Follow-up: Why avoid user ID labels? | Each unique label combination creates a series, causing cost and performance problems and potentially exposing identifiers.

## What is Grafana, and does it collect every metric itself?
Simple: Grafana displays and explores data from connected sources and can support alerting workflows.
Technical: Dashboards query configured sources such as a metrics backend, log store or trace store. Grafana is not automatically the producer of every signal. Instrument the application and provision data sources, retention and access controls deliberately.
Example: A dashboard shows p95 request duration, error ratio, queue age, GPU memory and cost by model version.
Follow-up: Grafana versus LangSmith? | Operational dashboards and application-level LLM traces/evaluations answer overlapping but different questions. Link them using request/version metadata rather than assuming one replaces all of the other.
Follow-up: What makes a good dashboard? | It answers an operational question, has units and time windows, and links symptoms to actionable diagnosis rather than filling screens with decorative charts.

## How do you calculate p95 from histogram metrics?
Simple: Use the histogram distribution across requests, not the average of separate p95 values.
Technical: Aggregate compatible bucket counts across instances for the intended window, then estimate the quantile using the metric backend function. Bucket resolution affects accuracy. Client-computed summary quantiles generally cannot be meaningfully averaged into a global percentile.
Example: Two replicas with very different traffic volumes cannot be combined by averaging their displayed p95 values.
Follow-up: Why do bucket boundaries matter? | Wide buckets near the SLO can produce coarse percentile estimates. Choose boundaries suited to the latency range.
Follow-up: What about failed requests? | Define whether they are included and report them separately; excluding timeouts can make latency look artificially good.

## What are OpenTelemetry, logs, traces and correlation?
Simple: OpenTelemetry provides APIs and conventions for generating and transporting telemetry across services.
Technical: Propagate trace context across HTTP, jobs and tools; export signals to chosen backends. Sampling reduces volume but can hide rare events, so preserve critical errors/audit events under a deliberate policy. Do not place credentials or full private documents in attributes.
Example: A browser request, API call and model-service span share trace lineage, allowing queue time to be distinguished from inference time.
Follow-up: Does observability prove causality? | It provides evidence for diagnosis, but correlation alone is not a causal proof. Use controlled experiments or additional evidence.
Follow-up: Why keep audit records separately? | Security/business audits may require stronger completeness, retention and access guarantees than sampled debugging traces.

## What alerts would you configure for a GenAI service?
Simple: Alert on user-impacting failures and leading indicators that someone can act on.
Technical: Examples include error-budget burn, sustained queue age, provider failures, ingestion freshness lag and unauthorized access attempts. Use appropriate thresholds/windows, owners and runbooks. Model-quality alerts need calibrated labels or reliable proxies, not arbitrary confidence drops.
Example: A rising queue-age alert tells the owner to inspect downstream capacity and admission control before requests time out.
Follow-up: Why not alert on every single error? | Transient noise causes fatigue. Group and prioritize, while preserving immediate handling for critical security conditions.
Follow-up: How do you test alerts? | Inject controlled failures and verify detection, routing, context and recovery notifications.

## How do you choose tools without creating an unnecessary stack?
Simple: Choose the smallest set that satisfies data, control-flow, evaluation and operations requirements.
Technical: Build a responsibility map and identify overlaps. A small app may need direct SDK calls plus ordinary traces; a complex durable agent may justify graph orchestration and a dedicated evaluation platform. Assess maintenance, migration and data-governance cost.
Example: Do not add LlamaIndex, LangChain and a second vector database just to list them; add a component when a specific gap is demonstrated.
Follow-up: What is vendor lock-in here? | Dependence on proprietary schemas, APIs, storage or evaluation workflows can make migration costly. Keep domain logic and data contracts portable where useful.
Follow-up: What should I say if I only studied a tool? | Describe conceptual understanding and a proposed application, not a production integration. Your actual implementation evidence remains the boundary.
