documents.body:
# How to answer a production scenario
Note: These designs expand the examples you supplied. Begin with requirements and assumptions, draw the architecture, explain what each layer does, then handle the follow-ups. They are proposed designs, not assertions that every component is deployed in your SQL Copilot. The current inspected backend is Flask/ASGI; FastAPI replicas below are a hypothetical scaling option or a separate service design.
# Concurrency and ingestion
## How would you scale SQL Copilot for 100 simultaneous users?
Simple: Share stable infrastructure, isolate each user's state and bound work at every scarce dependency. One hundred users should not create one hundred uncontrolled model calls and database connections.
Architecture: Browser -> gateway/auth/rate limits -> stateless API replicas -> isolated graph execution and durable state -> shared authorized schema retrieval -> global model admission queue -> LLM service -> validated read-only query service -> result/audit. Metrics and traces cover every boundary.
Technical: First clarify whether 100 means connected users, in-flight requests or requests/second, and define input/output sizes and latency targets. Keep sessions/checkpoints outside API processes and authorize every thread lookup. Share immutable versioned schema indexes where safe; keep conversation history, retrieved private results and permissions isolated. Apply provider-wide concurrency and token/rate limits, not only a semaphore per process. Use bounded queues with deadlines and fair tenant scheduling. Database pool capacity must be budgeted across all API replicas. If execution is included, use least-privilege credentials, statement timeouts and resource caps. Long-running jobs belong in durable workers, and in-flight operations need explicit failure/retry semantics.
Example: Suppose the provider allows 20 active calls and 100 requests arrive at once. At most 20 enter inference; the remaining 80 wait only if queue capacity and their deadlines permit. Reject or defer excess work cleanly. Do not claim all requests will finish in five seconds without a service-time distribution and load test.
Follow-up: Why multiple API instances? | Stateless replicas allow horizontal scaling and failure isolation. They help only if the bottleneck is at the API layer or available downstream capacity exists. External state allows any healthy replica to continue a request or conversation under authorization.
Follow-up: What is Redis doing? | It may support caching, short-lived state and rate-limit coordination. Assign each use a durability/failure policy. Durable business records or checkpoints should use a store whose guarantees match the requirement; do not treat an optional cache as the only permanent truth.
Follow-up: How do you isolate LangGraph state? | Use separate authenticated tenant/conversation execution IDs, validate ownership before checkpoint access and avoid a global mutable state object. An ID naming convention alone is not authorization.
Follow-up: Why is a local semaphore insufficient? | Five processes each allowing 20 calls can send 100 calls in total. Coordinate a global limit through a gateway/shared admission service or distribute a safe quota across replicas, with failure behavior defined.
Follow-up: What if SQL becomes the bottleneck? | Inspect pool wait, query plans, locks and execution time. Improve queries, cap expensive work and use suitable read replicas only where their lag is acceptable. More API workers can make the database problem worse.
Follow-up: What if an instance crashes? | The load balancer stops new traffic to it. Durable work resumes from recorded state, while uncertain side effects use idempotency/status reconciliation. A retry is not proof the previous attempt had no effect.
Follow-up: How do you prove it supports 1,000 users? | Use representative ramp, burst and sustained-load tests, recording offered versus achieved load, queueing and errors. Test long prompts and provider/database slowdowns, not only cached short requests.
Metrics: p50/p95/p99 end-to-end and stage latency, model queue age, token throughput, pool wait, timeouts, tenant fairness, cross-user isolation tests and cost per completed correct task.
Trade-offs: More replicas increase cost and connection demand. Caches reduce work but add freshness and isolation requirements. Longer queues absorb bursts but worsen tail latency; controlled rejection may protect existing work.
Say: I would make the API stateless, keep every user's graph state isolated and centralize limits around model and database capacity. Shared schema indexes can be reused under authorization, while conversation state cannot. I would define deadlines and bounded queues, recover durable work after crashes and validate the design with realistic load tests rather than equating replicas with capacity.
## How would you ingest and index 100,000 mixed documents?
Simple: Inventory the corpus, route files to suitable parsers and process them through a restartable pipeline. Document count alone does not determine size or cost.
Architecture: Source inventory -> original object storage and manifest -> durable queue -> format-specific workers -> normalization/OCR quality -> structure-aware chunks -> bounded embedding batches -> lexical/vector/metadata stores -> validation -> active-version publication.
Technical: Sample files by type, size, language and quality. Record source ID/version, checksum, permissions, bytes/pages, status and processing configuration. Preserve originals and parse PDF, Office, HTML and scans appropriately; avoid OCR when native text is reliable. Keep headings, tables, units and source coordinates. Use stable document/chunk IDs and separate stage status so retries resume safely. Batch embeddings by token/request limits, with backpressure from downstream storage. Quarantine repeatedly failing files in a DLQ with actionable errors. Validate source counts, metadata, sample extraction and retrieval quality before exposing a new index version.
Example: For an illustrative 500 million tokens, 400-token windows and 50-token overlap imply roughly 1.43 million chunks before real boundary effects. At 1,536 float32 dimensions, raw vectors are about 8.8 GB decimal; metadata, indexes, replicas, files and headroom are additional.
Follow-up: Why inventory before processing? | It reveals unsupported formats, duplicates, oversized files, access rules and cost drivers. It also provides a reconciliation ledger so missing documents are visible.
Follow-up: Why store original files separately? | Search indexes are derived artifacts. Originals and metadata allow reprocessing, citations, audit and recovery when an index or parser changes.
Follow-up: Why not send all documents in one embedding request? | Provider token/payload limits, memory and failure recovery make that impractical. Use bounded batches with per-record identity and result validation.
Follow-up: What if one 500-page PDF is huge? | Process pages/sections incrementally with resource limits and a document manifest. Preserve cross-page relationships where needed, but do not require the whole file's decoded content in memory.
Follow-up: How do you handle identical files with different ACLs? | Share storage only with separate source references and permissions. Deduplication must not merge access rights or erase provenance.
Follow-up: How do you handle an embedding worker crash? | Retry the same versioned job, detect completed chunk IDs and upsert missing work. Publish only when the document version meets completeness and quality checks.
Follow-up: How does this differ from SQL schema ingestion? | SQL Copilot primarily indexes tables, columns, keys, relationships and business definitions. Keep general document knowledge separate and route questions appropriately rather than pretending every PDF is schema truth.
Metrics: Inventory reconciliation, document/page/chunk throughput, queue age, parse/OCR failures, embedding cost, freshness/deletion lag, retrieval relevance and answer quality by source type.
Trade-offs: More workers can overwhelm parsers, model quotas or storage. High throughput is not success if extraction loses tables or permissions. Start with a representative benchmark before scaling the full corpus.
Say: I would build an inventory and versioned manifest, preserve originals, and use asynchronous format-aware workers. Chunking and OCR would follow document structure. Stable IDs, bounded embedding batches and backpressure make retries safe. I would validate both completeness and retrieval quality before publication, and estimate capacity from sampled token counts rather than file count alone.
## A technical manual contains prose, APIs, code and tables. Which chunking do you choose?
Simple: Use a strategy matched to the content rather than one arbitrary fixed size everywhere.
Architecture: Parsed blocks and headings -> content-type classification -> prose splitter / API-code units / table row groups -> parent-child links -> token-limit checks -> retrieval benchmark -> selected configuration.
Technical: Begin with structure-aware boundaries. For ordinary prose, a recursive baseline can preserve available separators; configure token counting separately. Keep API endpoint, parameters and response semantics together. Split large tables into row groups with repeated headers/units and stable identifiers. Preserve code syntax/context and parent sections for expansion. Compare a small set of chunk sizes/overlaps on representative queries while keeping other components fixed. Recursive splitting is a heuristic and still needs inspection.
Example: Splitting 'threshold applies except to corporate accounts' after 'except' can reverse interpretation. Parent context or a larger structural unit may be necessary, even when the smaller chunk has a strong similarity score.
Follow-up: Why not fixed-size? | It is an inexpensive baseline but can break logical units. It can still win on uniform text; judge by evidence recall and answer quality rather than a universal preference.
Follow-up: Why not semantic chunking? | It adds embedding/threshold work and can create variable sizes or poor boundaries in code/tables. Use it when measured benefits justify the cost.
Follow-up: How do you choose overlap? | Start modestly, enforce overlap smaller than size and measure boundary recall against duplicate storage/context. Tables often need repeated headers rather than arbitrary token overlap.
Follow-up: What if chunks are too small or large? | Small chunks lose context and increase count; large chunks dilute relevance and consume prompt budget. Parent-child retrieval can balance localization with context, but expansion must preserve permissions.
Follow-up: How do you choose the winner? | Evaluate retrieval and end-to-end answers by document type, including exceptions, numeric tables and long sections. Report token/storage/latency cost alongside quality.
Metrics: Evidence Recall@k, answer correctness, citation span precision, duplicate context ratio, mean/percentile chunk tokens and ingestion/query cost.
Trade-offs: A specialized pipeline takes more engineering but preserves meaning. A simple baseline is easier to operate and should remain the comparison point.
Say: I would preserve structure first, use recursive splitting for suitable prose and specialized handling for APIs, code and tables. I would tune sizes and overlap through a controlled evaluation, using parent expansion where small chunks lose necessary conditions.
# Retrieval and answer failures
## A reversal query retrieves settlement documents. How do you debug it?
Simple: Find the stage that lost or misranked the actual reversal procedure.
Architecture: Source inspection -> parsed chunks -> query/rewrite -> lexical and dense candidate inspection -> authorized filters -> fusion/reranking -> context selection -> answer. Compare the correct source at each boundary.
Technical: Verify the source exists, is current and accessible. Inspect extracted text and chunk context before changing the model. Compare lexical and dense results independently, including exact identifiers and synonyms. Check whether a rewrite changed reversal into settlement, whether filters excluded the source, or whether reranking/truncation dropped it. Use an oracle-context answer test to separate retrieval from generation failures. Fix the observed stage and rerun a held-out slice.
Example: The reversal policy was ingested, but its heading was removed and the chunk contains only 'this process'. Restoring title/section context may help more than a stronger generator.
Follow-up: Why hybrid retrieval? | Exact procedure/API terms and semantic paraphrases provide complementary signals. Compare the union's recall before assuming fusion helps.
Follow-up: What if the correct chunk is ranked 40? | Increasing candidate depth and reranking may help, but measure added cost. Also inspect why the first-stage rank is poor.
Follow-up: What if it is never retrieved? | A reranker cannot recover it. Fix parsing, indexing, embedding/query alignment or filters, or search additional authorized sources.
Follow-up: Would query rewriting help? | Only if language mismatch is the cause. Preserve product, date, negation and identifiers, and retain original-query retrieval as a baseline.
Follow-up: How do you avoid overfitting the fix? | Test other procedure families and exact-code queries on held-out examples, not only the one failure you just inspected.
Metrics: Candidate recall, reranker retention, final-context coverage, answer correctness and latency by query class.
Trade-offs: More candidates improve recall but can increase reranker cost and distraction. Better metadata may be cheaper and more reliable than extra model calls.
Say: I would inspect the missing source through every stage, compare lexical/dense paths and run an oracle-context experiment. The fix depends on whether the source was absent, filtered, misranked or dropped; changing the LLM first would not isolate the problem.
## Retrieval has high recall but low precision. Should you reduce top-k?
Simple: The system finds needed material but also too much noise. Reducing top-k is one option, not an automatic solution.
Architecture: Candidate retrieval -> relevance labels -> fusion -> reranker -> diversity/deduplication -> evidence budget -> answer evaluation.
Technical: Measure candidate recall separately from selected-context precision. Improve ranking, metadata applicability and duplicate handling before simply cutting candidates. A high candidate top-k followed by a small precise context can preserve recall. Evaluate multi-hop tasks that require several sources and unanswerable questions where all candidates may be weak.
Example: Fifty candidates include all three required policies, but the top five are near-duplicates. Diversifying after relevance ranking can recover the other evidence without sending all 50 to generation.
Follow-up: Why not set top-k to one? | A single-source task may tolerate it, but multi-hop or exception questions may require several sources. Tune for the task distribution.
Follow-up: Can a score threshold solve it? | Scores need calibration and vary by query/model. A single unvalidated threshold may reject relevant evidence unevenly.
Follow-up: What role does a reranker play? | It assesses query-candidate interaction more closely, within the retrieved set. Validate domain performance and latency.
Follow-up: How do you measure redundancy? | Track repeated source/span overlap and unique required evidence retained. Diversity is useful only when relevance stays adequate.
Metrics: Precision@k, Recall@k, nDCG, required-evidence coverage, selected-context tokens and final answer correctness.
Trade-offs: Tight context reduces noise/cost but can omit qualifiers. Optimize the full answer, not one retrieval metric in isolation.
Say: I would preserve a high-recall candidate pool, then improve ranking and context selection. I would reduce final context only after checking evidence coverage, especially on multi-source questions.
## The model answers confidently when no source contains the answer. What changes?
Simple: Make missing evidence an explicit outcome and teach the system to clarify or abstain.
Architecture: Authorized retrieval -> evidence sufficiency/coverage -> grounded generation or clarification -> claim support/citation checks -> answer or abstention -> evaluation and feedback.
Technical: Build answerable and unanswerable test sets, including tempting near-matches. Use source quality, relevance, coverage and conflict signals calibrated against labels. Require important claims to be supported and avoid treating a model's self-reported confidence as a probability. Prompt instructions help but cannot guarantee compliance. Keep deterministic checks for source IDs and sensitive operations outside the model.
Example: A policy mentions review frequency but no guaranteed approval deadline. The answer should say the deadline is not established in the available evidence rather than infer one.
Follow-up: Is temperature zero enough? | No. The most likely continuation can still be an unsupported guess.
Follow-up: Can a second LLM verify it? | It can help but may share the same blind spot. Calibrate against humans and include contradictions and plausible unsupported claims.
Follow-up: What if the source itself is wrong? | Grounding can be faithful to bad evidence. Validate source authority/freshness and measure factual correctness separately.
Follow-up: How do you avoid excessive refusal? | Tune the risk-coverage trade-off and offer targeted clarification or an appropriate source/escalation path.
Follow-up: Does citing a page prove support? | No. Check whether the specific passage entails the claim, including units, dates and exceptions.
Metrics: Unsupported-claim rate, false answers on unanswerable tasks, accepted-answer correctness, coverage, false abstention and citation precision.
Trade-offs: Conservative answering reduces unsupported claims but may frustrate users. Calibrated thresholds and useful clarification can improve that balance.
Say: I would evaluate missing-evidence cases explicitly, add a calibrated sufficiency gate and verify important claims against sources. I would measure both unsafe guessing and unnecessary abstention, because a useful system needs the right balance.

# Reliability, latency and quality changes
## Users wait 8-10 seconds for a RAG answer. How do you reduce latency?
Simple: Measure where time goes before optimizing. Queueing, retrieval, reranking and generation require different fixes.
Architecture: Arrival -> queue -> query embedding/rewrite -> parallel lexical+dense search -> reranking -> context assembly -> model prefill/decode -> delivery. Trace each stage and retain failed/time-out outcomes.
Technical: Define end-to-end boundaries and separate TTFT from completion time. Inspect prompt/output lengths, provider throttling, queue age and cache mix. Parallelize independent retrieval, reuse safe connections and cache valid repeated work. Reduce reranker candidates only after checking recall. Trim irrelevant context without removing required evidence. For self-hosting inspect batching/KV pressure; for APIs inspect provider quotas and network timing. Streaming improves perceived progress but does not reduce total work or suit every output-validation requirement.
Example: Retrieval takes 100 ms while 5 seconds are spent waiting for a model slot. Replacing the vector index will not solve the dominant delay.
Follow-up: Why not immediately use a smaller model? | It may help generation but reduce quality and leave queueing elsewhere unchanged. Measure and evaluate the end-to-end trade-off.
Follow-up: Can I cache every answer? | Only when identity, permissions, source freshness and input semantics permit. Financial values and personalized answers need stricter controls.
Follow-up: What if p50 is good but p99 is bad? | Inspect bursts, long prompts, slow dependencies, retries and noisy tenants. Use bounded admission and fairness rather than hiding slow cases in averages.
Follow-up: How do you test the fix? | Replay representative workload at fixed offered load with long/short requests, failures and cold/warm cache conditions. Report quality and errors alongside speed.
Follow-up: How do you set the latency budget? | Allocate an illustrative target across stages, then revise using measurements and dependencies. A budget is a design constraint, not a claim of achieved performance.
Metrics: End-to-end p50/p95/p99, stage spans, queue age, TTFT/TPOT, output length, errors and cost per correct completed task.
Trade-offs: Faster models and smaller contexts can hurt quality; more capacity costs money; caching adds invalidation work. Optimize under explicit quality and reliability constraints.
Say: I would trace the whole path, separate waiting from work and fix the dominant stage. I would compare the change under realistic load, keeping answer quality and timeouts visible rather than reporting only faster successful requests.
## You changed both chunking and embeddings. How do you prove the system improved?
Simple: Compare controlled versions on a held-out dataset and inspect which change caused which effect.
Architecture: Versioned corpus and gold cases -> baseline -> chunking-only candidate -> embedding-only candidate -> combined candidate -> retrieval/answer/cost evaluation -> review -> shadow/canary -> rollout or rollback.
Technical: Freeze data snapshots, source permissions and generation configuration for a controlled comparison. Reindex correctly for each embedding/chunking configuration. Evaluate exact-code, paraphrase, table, multi-hop and unanswerable slices. Use paired query comparisons and uncertainty estimates rather than treating tiny score differences as definitive. Keep tuning separate from the final test and preserve a rollback-compatible index.
Example: The combined system improves average recall but harms error-code queries. An ablation shows the new embedding caused the regression while chunking helped prose; this suggests a targeted fix rather than accepting the average gain blindly.
Follow-up: What is a golden dataset? | Curated questions with expected outcomes and evidence, versioned with a clear labeling rubric and reviewed for leakage/staleness.
Follow-up: Can I use an LLM judge? | Yes as a calibrated instrument. Compare with human labels, randomize answer order in pairwise judging and record judge/prompt versions.
Follow-up: Why not use production thumbs-up only? | Feedback is biased toward users who respond and may reflect style or convenience. Combine it with controlled quality checks and operational guardrails.
Follow-up: What if the new index is more expensive? | Report quality at matched latency/cost budgets and decide whether the incremental value justifies the resource increase.
Follow-up: What triggers rollback? | Predefined critical-slice, access, error or latency regressions, with the old compatible configuration retained during the rollout window.
Metrics: Paired win/loss, Recall@k/nDCG, supported/correct answers, false abstention, cost, latency and permission test outcomes.
Trade-offs: Full factorial experiments cost more but clarify interactions. A smaller representative evaluation is useful initially, provided uncertainty is acknowledged.
Say: I would separate the changes through ablations, evaluate on an untouched representative set and inspect critical slices. I would then shadow or canary the complete configuration, with explicit rollback gates and measured cost-quality trade-offs.
## Redis becomes unavailable. Which parts of your application should continue?
Simple: The answer depends on whether Redis is a cache, a coordinator, a queue or the only copy of state. Define failure behavior for each role.
Architecture: API -> cache with bounded fallback -> authoritative stores/services. Global limit and job coordination -> durable/fail-safe alternative or controlled rejection. Circuit breakers isolate Redis failure from unrelated read paths.
Technical: Inventory every Redis use. A cache miss can often fall back to the source with concurrency protection, but a failed global rate limiter must not unleash unlimited provider calls. Durable job/state recovery depends on actual persistence/replication guarantees. Use short dependency deadlines, circuit breakers and bounded local degradation where safe. Avoid a cache outage causing every replica to stampede the database.
Example: Schema cache failure can use a validated local immutable snapshot, while sensitive permission checks must still query an authoritative policy service or fail closed. This is a proposed fallback, not permission to use stale ACLs.
Follow-up: Can I fail open for rate limiting? | Only under an explicit safe policy and residual capacity bound. For strict external quotas use conservative limits or controlled rejection when coordination is unavailable.
Follow-up: What happens to sessions? | If Redis was the only session store, continuity may be lost according to its configured durability. Design that deliberately rather than assuming every Redis deployment is durable.
Follow-up: Should I retry Redis rapidly? | No. Use bounded backoff/circuit behavior and protect downstream services from amplified load.
Follow-up: How do you test recovery? | Inject unavailability, latency and partial network failure; verify fallback limits, state consistency and return to normal without a burst.
Metrics: Degraded completion rate, database amplification, provider-limit violations, state loss, recovery time and error/latency changes.
Trade-offs: More fallback paths add complexity and stale-state risk. Sometimes a clear temporary rejection is safer than a misleading partially correct response.
Say: I would define Redis's role per feature. Optional caches can degrade with bounded source access, but authorization and global capacity controls need conservative behavior. I would test the outage and recovery rather than assuming Redis is simply optional everywhere.
## A worker crashes mid-batch and a document is later deleted. How do you keep indexes consistent?
Simple: Use stable versioned identities and a durable lifecycle so retries cannot resurrect deleted data.
Architecture: Source event -> document lifecycle/version ledger -> stage jobs -> idempotent artifacts -> publication check -> active pointer. Deletion tombstones invalidate indexes, summaries and caches; reconciliation verifies completion.
Technical: Store the intended document version and lifecycle state on each job. Before publishing, compare with the authoritative current state. A late retry for a deleted/superseded version must be ignored or cleaned up. Track artifacts across lexical/vector/metadata stores and process deletion idempotently. Keep retention/backup handling aligned with policy, and audit incomplete cleanup. A queue acknowledgment alone does not prove all stores agree.
Example: Version 2 embedding completes after a delete event. The publish check sees the tombstone and refuses to activate it, then removes orphaned artifacts.
Follow-up: Why not use random chunk IDs on retry? | It creates duplicates and makes deletion/reconciliation harder. Derive stable identity from source/version/configuration and chunk position or content policy.
Follow-up: Can a transaction span every store? | Usually not cheaply. Use a versioned state machine, idempotent steps and reconciliation rather than pretending a cross-service atomic transaction exists.
Follow-up: What if one deletion path fails? | Keep the tombstone authoritative so queries exclude the item, retry cleanup and surface deletion lag. Verify no derived cache still exposes it.
Follow-up: How do you change the embedding model? | Build a separate versioned index, re-embed compatible source data, sync updates/deletes, evaluate and cut over with rollback. Do not mix unaligned spaces.
Metrics: Duplicate/orphan artifacts, deletion lag, stale-version hits, job recovery rate and reconciliation backlog.
Trade-offs: Versioning and tombstones add storage/state complexity but make asynchronous recovery explainable and auditable.
Say: I would make the lifecycle ledger authoritative and require every publish/retry to check the current version and deletion state. Stable IDs make retries safe, while tombstones and reconciliation keep multiple indexes and caches consistent.
## Your documents contain tables, charts and scanned numerical values. What changes?
Simple: Preserve structure and exact data instead of converting everything into an undifferentiated text string.
Architecture: Format/quality detection -> native parser or OCR/vision -> layout/table/chart interpretation -> structured numeric store plus searchable descriptions -> source-linked retrieval -> deterministic calculation -> grounded explanation.
Technical: Keep headers, units, currencies, row identities and chart axes/scales. Use summaries for discovery and structured values for arithmetic. OCR confidence is only a signal; validate critical identifiers/numbers against the page or authoritative source. Preserve coordinates and originals so reviewers can inspect ambiguous extraction. Chart interpretation requires attention to labels, scales and uncertainty, especially when exact values are not printed.
Example: A revenue table is labeled 'INR thousands'. Summing extracted cells as rupees is wrong by a factor of one thousand even if every digit was recognized correctly.
Follow-up: Why not embed the table and ask the model to add values? | Retrieval may omit rows and generation may make arithmetic mistakes. Query structured data and compute deterministically when exact totals are required.
Follow-up: What if OCR changes Qwen3.5 to Qwen35? | Flag it with domain/format checks and inspect the original crop before correction. A dictionary should not invent an unverified model version.
Follow-up: Why not OCR all PDFs? | Native text can be more accurate and cheaper. Use quality-based routing, since OCR may introduce new errors.
Follow-up: How do you cite a chart answer? | Link the page/figure and describe the basis and uncertainty; do not claim exact values when only an approximate visual reading is available.
Metrics: Field/cell accuracy, header/unit association, OCR error, numeric calculation correctness, source-link support and review workload.
Trade-offs: Structured extraction costs more engineering but enables accurate calculations. Vision models help difficult layouts while adding uncertainty and expense.
Say: I would retain the original visual evidence, extract structure and units, and separate retrieval from calculation. Exact numerical answers should come from validated structured data with source links, with low-confidence extraction routed for review.
## SQL is syntactically valid but the business answer is wrong. What do you investigate?
Simple: Valid syntax does not prove the right entities, joins, dates or aggregation were used.
Architecture: Original request -> semantic definitions -> retrieved schema -> join/grain plan -> generated SQL -> AST/policy checks -> controlled test execution -> expected-result comparison -> repair or clarification.
Technical: Inspect required columns and tables, relationship keys/cardinality, filters, fiscal/date semantics, units and metric definitions. Use adversarial test data with duplicates, nulls, missing relations and boundary dates to expose accidental equivalence. Distinguish parser validity, schema validity, policy validity and semantic correctness. For missing private attributes, ask clarification rather than importing a column from a generic example corpus.
Example: An order-to-items-to-payments join multiplies payment amounts. The SQL runs and references valid tables, but totals are inflated because the plan violated order-level grain.
Follow-up: What if the correct table was not retrieved? | Improve schema metadata, lexical/semantic linking or candidate coverage first. A generation repair cannot reliably invent missing schema evidence.
Follow-up: How do you prevent bad joins? | Use validated relationship edges and cardinality-aware plans, then test result semantics. Similar column names and shortest paths alone are insufficient.
Follow-up: Why not execute every generated query to see? | Execution needs least privilege, timeouts, object policy and resource controls. Some syntactically valid reads can be expensive or disclose unauthorized data.
Follow-up: What does the current benchmark prove? | Only its defined measured outcomes. Your saved report's success and validity are distinct; do not promote planner timing or validity into unmeasured live execution accuracy.
Follow-up: What if confidence is high? | A heuristic can be overconfident. Validate/calibrate it against semantic outcomes and reject unresolved ambiguity despite a high score.
Metrics: Semantic/result correctness, join correctness, required-column/table recall, unsafe-query rejection, repair success and end-to-end timing.
Trade-offs: Strong semantic constraints may limit flexible ad hoc questions, but reduce plausible wrong answers. Clarification is preferable to silently choosing an unsupported metric definition.
Say: I would inspect the business plan and row grain before treating valid SQL as success. I would test with counterexample data and evaluate result semantics, while keeping execution safe. Missing or ambiguous schema meaning should lead to clarification, not a confident guess.

# Architecture and development incident drills
## Scenario: A deployment succeeds but users see a blank page. How do you debug it?
Simple: Separate asset loading, JavaScript execution, routing and data failures before changing application code randomly.
Architecture: Browser/network evidence -> entry document -> versioned assets -> runtime errors -> route/data checks -> rollback or targeted repair
Technical: Inspect the console and network responses, status/content types, base paths, CSP, cache versions and runtime configuration. Verify direct links as well as the landing route. Check that HTML references assets in the deployed publish directory and that stale caches do not mix versions. Reproduce the deployed artifact locally, then repair the failing layer or roll back the exact release.
Example: A static host publishes the repository root while index.html and scripts are inside dist. The build succeeds but the wrong directory is served.
Metrics: Successful page loads, JS error rate, asset failures, route success and time to recovery.
Trade-offs: Broad cache invalidation can restore consistency but increases origin traffic; versioned assets and an uncached entry point offer a controlled release strategy.
Say: I would inspect the deployed network/runtime evidence and artifact paths, then fix the verified failure or restore the previous artifact.
Follow-up: Can every missing asset use a single-page-app fallback? | No. Returning HTML for a missing JS file hides the error and causes parse/MIME failures. Configure fallback only as appropriate for routes.
Follow-up: Why might refresh fail on a deep URL? | History-based routing needs suitable server fallback rules. Hash routing avoids that particular server lookup issue.
Follow-up: Is a successful build proof of deployment correctness? | No. Artifact paths, configuration, cache and runtime behavior need release checks.
## Scenario: Users submit the same job twice after a slow response. How do you prevent duplicate work?
Simple: Give the intended operation a stable identity and make repeat submission return its existing status/result.
Architecture: Client request key -> authenticated scope -> durable idempotency record -> one job -> status endpoint -> result
Technical: Bind the key to the user/tenant and normalized request semantics, detect conflicting reuse and persist the operation state before scheduling. Use a unique constraint or atomic operation, then handle enqueue/DB consistency with an outbox or appropriate transaction pattern. Define key retention, in-progress responses and failure retry policy.
Example: Repeated clicks on 'ingest document' reuse the same upload/job identity rather than scheduling two embedding runs.
Metrics: Duplicate effects, deduplicated submissions, stuck operations, enqueue reconciliation and completion latency.
Trade-offs: Persistent identities add storage and lifecycle complexity but protect cost and user-visible correctness.
Say: I would make job creation idempotent with a scoped durable key, not rely only on disabling the button.
Follow-up: Is hashing the full prompt always enough? | No. Identical text can represent separate intended operations, while equivalent requests can differ in formatting. Use explicit operation identity and documented semantics.
Follow-up: What if the key is reused with a different body? | Reject the conflict instead of returning an unrelated old result or executing a second effect silently.
Follow-up: What if the database write succeeds but enqueue fails? | Persist an outbox/reconciliation record and retry delivery safely rather than losing or duplicating the job.
## Scenario: A retry policy turns a small failure into a full outage. What do you change?
Simple: Bound retries, slow them down and protect dependencies from amplified traffic.
Architecture: Failure classification -> deadline/retry budget -> exponential backoff with jitter -> circuit/admission controls -> fallback -> recovery probe
Technical: Retry transient failures only when operation semantics permit it. Respect Retry-After where applicable, cap attempts and total duration, and avoid retries at every layer multiplying each other. Apply bulkheads/connection budgets and a circuit-breaker policy with bounded recovery probes. Preserve idempotency for effects and cancel work the caller no longer needs when possible.
Example: Three retries at API, SDK and worker layers can multiply downstream attempts far beyond the original request count.
Metrics: Attempt amplification, dependency error/latency, queue age, open circuits, useful success and dropped/expired work.
Trade-offs: Fewer retries expose transient failures to users; uncontrolled retries make recovery harder. Define a user-visible degraded path.
Say: I would centralize retry responsibility, enforce a total budget and recover with jittered bounded probes rather than synchronized storms.
Follow-up: Should 401 and 400 errors be retried like 503? | Generally no. Correct credentials/validation under a deliberate bounded flow; unchanged requests usually repeat deterministic failures.
Follow-up: What is a bulkhead? | A resource partition, such as separate bounded pools, that stops one dependency or tenant from consuming all capacity.
Follow-up: Does a circuit breaker replace a timeout? | No. Timeouts bound individual waits; a breaker governs calls during a failing dependency period. They work together.
## Scenario: An API streams tokens but users receive duplicated or missing text. How do you fix it?
Simple: Give stream events stable sequence identities and define reconnect behavior explicitly.
Architecture: Run ID -> ordered event sequence -> persisted/cursored delivery where required -> client deduplication -> terminal status
Technical: Distinguish a transport reconnect from starting a new generation. Use event IDs/sequence numbers, deduplicate client appends and preserve final authoritative output when the contract needs recovery. Detect partial failure and mark incomplete answers. Tune proxy buffering and timeouts, and test deploy/connection interruption. Do not claim resumable generation unless the server actually supports it.
Example: A reconnect resends the last event; the client ignores its already-seen sequence number instead of appending the same phrase twice.
Metrics: Duplicate/missing event rate, reconnect success, incomplete outputs, final-output consistency and TTFT.
Trade-offs: Persistent event history costs storage; simple restart may be acceptable for read-only chat but can repeat cost and cannot repeat external effects safely.
Say: I would define event ordering and run identity, deduplicate on reconnect and distinguish a resumed delivery from a new model run.
Follow-up: Does SSE automatically persist events? | No. Transport features do not create durable replay storage or application resume semantics by themselves.
Follow-up: Why keep a terminal event? | Clients need to distinguish completed output from a dropped connection that merely stopped producing bytes.
Follow-up: What if the server cannot resume? | Disclose the interrupted answer and offer a controlled restart; do not silently splice unrelated generations.
## Scenario: A cache returns another user's answer. What is the architecture failure?
Simple: Cache reuse crossed an authorization or personalization boundary.
Architecture: Verified identity/scope -> authorization-aware cache key -> current policy/freshness check -> permitted result -> audit
Technical: Stop unsafe reuse, identify exposed records and inspect key dimensions: tenant, user/resource scope, prompt/model/retrieval versions, policy version and relevant personalization. Shared caches are appropriate only when content is truly shareable under the permission model. Hashing a question alone is insufficient, including for semantically similar questions. Revalidate permission-sensitive data at required boundaries and purge affected cache entries.
Example: Two users ask 'What is my account balance?' The text is identical; the permitted resource and answer are different.
Metrics: Cross-scope hits/exposure, cache effectiveness within scope, stale-policy hits and incident containment time.
Trade-offs: More precise keys lower hit rate and increase storage. That cost is part of maintaining correct access boundaries.
Say: I would contain the leak, repair scope-aware keys and authorization checks, then evaluate cache correctness before re-enabling sharing.
Follow-up: Does encryption fix a wrong cache key? | No. An application with decryption access can still serve the wrong user's plaintext.
Follow-up: Can semantic caching be safe? | It needs strict permission/personalization partitioning and evaluated equivalence. Similar wording does not establish identical allowed answers.
Follow-up: Is prompt version needed in the key? | Often yes when output depends on it. Define all relevant configuration and freshness dimensions explicitly.
## Scenario: A new release changes agent state schema. How do you migrate running workflows?
Simple: Version the workflow contract and preserve a compatible path for existing runs.
Architecture: Graph/state version -> compatibility check -> old-run drain or explicit migration -> validated resume -> new-run release
Technical: Store graph, state, prompt and tool versions with run provenance. Prefer backward-compatible additions, defaults and typed validation. Test old checkpoints against the new code, or keep the old worker version for draining. For incompatible migrations define a deterministic transform and rollback plan; quarantine unsupported states rather than guessing. Reconcile pending external operations before restarting or migrating.
Example: Renaming approved to approval_status without a migration may send old checkpoints down the wrong branch. Add a versioned transform and verify permitted transitions.
Metrics: Migration success, unsupported checkpoint count, duplicate effects, resume correctness and drain time.
Trade-offs: Keeping versions side by side costs operational effort; forced restart can lose context or repeat actions.
Say: I would treat persisted agent state as a versioned production contract and test migration/resume, not just new-run unit behavior.
Follow-up: Can we delete old fields immediately? | Only after the compatibility window and all relevant readers/runs have migrated or drained. Use an expand/contract strategy.
Follow-up: What if rollback code cannot read migrated state? | Plan reversible or forward-compatible transitions, retain appropriate backups and constrain rollback claims to what is actually supported.
Follow-up: Why include tool versions too? | A valid graph can still fail or create wrong effects if argument/result schemas changed underneath it.
