documents.body:
# ML fundamentals: choose the right problem
Note: Study data quality before model selection and evaluation before deployment. Numerical examples are illustrative, not resume benchmark claims.
## What is machine learning, and how do supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning differ?
Simple: Machine learning learns patterns from examples to make predictions or decisions. The training signal determines the learning setup.
Technical: Supervised learning fits inputs to labeled targets. Unsupervised learning discovers structure without a supplied target, such as clusters. Reinforcement learning optimizes actions from rewards over interactions and must account for delayed consequences. Self-supervised learning constructs targets from the data, such as predicting the next token; it still has a defined loss.
Example: Ticket priority prediction is supervised classification; grouping similar unlabeled tickets is clustering; learning a control policy from rewards is reinforcement learning.
Follow-up: Why start with a baseline? | Simple rules, majority prediction or a linear model establish whether complexity adds measurable value under the same split and costs.
Follow-up: Does self-supervision mean there are no targets? | No. Targets are constructed automatically from the data instead of manually annotating every example.
## What is classification versus regression versus clustering?
Simple: Classification predicts a category, regression predicts a number, and clustering groups similar observations.
Technical: Classification can be binary, multiclass or multilabel. Regression estimates a continuous target. Clustering depends on representation, distance and assumptions about group shape. Cluster IDs have no inherent business meaning, and numeric regression predictions do not have classification accuracy without a separately defined tolerance or bucket rule.
Example: Fraud/not-fraud is classification, claim amount is regression, and spending-profile segmentation is clustering.
Follow-up: Can I turn regression into classification? | Yes, by defining buckets, but this discards information and adds arbitrary boundaries. Match the output to the decision.
Follow-up: How do I evaluate unlabeled clusters? | Assess stability, separation and domain usefulness. A high silhouette score alone does not prove a useful business segmentation.
## What are features, labels, parameters and hyperparameters?
Simple: Features are inputs, labels are desired outputs, parameters are learned values, and hyperparameters configure learning.
Technical: Coefficients and neural weights are fitted using training data. Tree depth, regularization and learning rate are selected using a validation procedure. Preprocessing has learned state too: means, vocabularies and feature selection must be fitted inside the training partition rather than using the entire dataset.
Example: Past usage is a churn feature, future churn is the label, fitted coefficients are parameters, and regularization strength is a hyperparameter.
Follow-up: Is a decision threshold a model weight? | Usually it is a separate decision policy selected on validation data using costs or capacity. Do not tune it on the final test set.
Follow-up: Can a post-outcome field be a feature? | Only if it is actually available at prediction time. Otherwise it leaks the answer even if its column name sounds legitimate.
# Missing values and data contracts
## How do you handle null or missing values?
Simple: Find why data is missing, then choose a treatment that preserves the field's meaning.
Technical: Profile missingness by field, time and cohort. Distinguish unknown, not applicable, sensor failure and valid zero. Compare justified row/column removal, numeric mean or median, categorical missing tokens, indicators, model-native handling or multivariate imputation. Fit all learned imputation on training folds only, apply the same transform at serving time, and monitor missingness drift.
Example: Salary zero means no salary; null means unknown. Replacing both with zero erases that distinction. Median plus a missing indicator is a baseline to compare, not a universal answer.
Follow-up: When is mean imputation a poor choice? | It is sensitive to extreme values and changes variance and correlations. Median is more robust for skew, but neither restores the true uncertainty.
Follow-up: What if a whole column disappears in production? | Enforce the data contract, alert on the feed failure and use a tested fallback or reject safely. Do not silently invent a new rule during inference.
Follow-up: Can missing target labels be filled like missing features? | Guessed targets are not ground truth. Resolve annotation or use an explicitly evaluated semi-supervised method, retaining genuine held-out labels for evaluation.
## What do MCAR, MAR and MNAR mean?
Simple: They describe whether missingness is unrelated to the data, explained by observed data, or related to the missing value itself.
Technical: MCAR means missing completely at random. MAR means missingness is independent of the missing value conditional on observed variables. MNAR means dependence remains on unobserved values. These are assumptions about the data-generating mechanism, not categories a histogram can reliably prove. Domain knowledge and sensitivity analysis matter.
Example: Random logging loss may approximate MCAR. Missing salary explained by observed job group may fit MAR. High earners preferentially withholding salary is a possible MNAR process.
Follow-up: Does a missing indicator solve MNAR? | It may help prediction, but it does not identify the missing distribution or remove selection bias. Check cohorts and sensitivity to assumptions.
Follow-up: Why can dropping incomplete rows be biased? | The retained population may systematically exclude certain users or conditions, changing the actual task.
## How do you encode missing and unseen categories?
Simple: A missing value and a previously unseen category are different situations and should be handled predictably.
Technical: Mode imputation can suppress rare groups. A dedicated missing token preserves absence. An unknown-category path handles new values without crashing or changing column order. For high-cardinality categories compare hashing, embeddings or cross-fitted target encoding. Keep the training and serving vocabulary and schema consistent.
Example: Missing occupation and a new occupation named robotics auditor should not both become the most frequent occupation.
Follow-up: Why is naive target encoding dangerous? | A category average computed with the row's own label or held-out labels leaks the target. Use training-fold/cross-fitted encoding and a fallback for rare categories.
Follow-up: Can I use zero as a generic missing constant? | Only if the semantics and model behavior are understood. Zero may be a valid value, requiring a separate indicator or representation.
# Outliers, anomalies and robust treatment
## How do you identify outliers?
Simple: Look for observations that differ strongly from the expected pattern, then determine whether they are errors or meaningful rare cases.
Technical: Start with range, unit, duplicate and timestamp checks; inspect histograms, boxplots, quantiles and cohort-aware scatterplots. IQR fences use Q1-1.5*IQR and Q3+1.5*IQR. Z-scores rely on mean and standard deviation and can be misleading with heavy tails; median absolute deviation is a robust alternative. For multivariate relationships compare Isolation Forest, LOF or domain rules. Fit thresholds on training/reference data and validate flags with experts.
Example: A payment of 50,000 can be extreme for a student account and routine for a business account. Segment before treating all large transactions as abnormal.
Follow-up: Is every point outside an IQR fence wrong? | No. It is an investigation candidate. Valid heavy-tailed distributions naturally produce extreme observations.
Follow-up: Why can univariate tests miss an outlier? | Height and weight can each be plausible but unusual together. Multivariate detection considers the relationship.
Follow-up: Is an absolute z-score above three a universal rule? | No. It is a distribution-dependent heuristic. Validate false alerts, tail behavior and domain costs.
## How do you handle outliers in ML?
Simple: Correct documented errors, preserve meaningful rare events, and use robust methods for valid extreme values.
Technical: Verify mixed units, sensor faults, duplicates and labels first. Options include correcting known errors, excluding invalid records, transforming skew, capping with training-derived quantiles, robust scaling and robust losses/models. Audit every treatment and compare ordinary and tail cohorts. Never remove fraud merely because it is unusual. Apply exactly the same validated preprocessing during serving.
Example: Fix a documented cents-versus-dollars mismatch. For valid long-tailed income compare log1p and robust loss rather than deleting high earners automatically.
Follow-up: What is winsorization? | Replace values beyond chosen bounds with those bounds. It limits influence but destroys some tail information; learn bounds on training data and justify the trade-off.
Follow-up: Should I remove target outliers? | Only if they are invalid under a documented rule. Removing real large claims can make the model underestimate the risk it must predict.
Follow-up: What about production values beyond training bounds? | Monitor their prevalence and quality, distinguish corruption from a new valid regime, and use a documented fallback or retraining path.
## Anomaly versus outlier: are they the same?
Simple: An outlier is statistically unusual; an anomaly is unexpected in a system's context. The terms overlap and are not universally separated.
Technical: An anomaly can be a single unusual point, a contextual violation or a collective sequence of individually normal observations. An outlier can be harmless. Novelty detection generally fits a mostly clean reference population and scores new observations, whereas outlier detection may fit data already containing contamination. Neither score alone proves fraud or a security incident.
Example: A 3 AM login is routine for a night-shift employee but unusual for another account. A coordinated series of small transfers can be anomalous without any extreme amount.
Follow-up: Can an ordinary-looking value be anomalous? | Yes. Timing, identity, order and relationships can make it suspicious even when its magnitude is normal.
Follow-up: How do you choose the alert threshold? | Use known incidents where available, analyst capacity, false-positive costs and time-aware validation. A contamination setting is an assumption about the cutoff, not established prevalence.
## Isolation Forest, LOF and one-class models: when do you use each?
Simple: Isolation Forest finds easily isolated points, LOF compares local density, and one-class methods learn a boundary around normal behavior.
Technical: Isolation Forest is a useful tabular baseline. LOF may detect local density deviations but depends on neighbors, scale and dimensionality. One-Class SVM requires careful scaling and can be costly on large samples. Compare incident recall, ranking stability, alert volume and deployment cost on representative time splits rather than assuming one algorithm is best.
Example: A sparse point beside a dense cluster may have high LOF, while a legitimate separate sparse cluster should not automatically be labeled malicious.
Follow-up: Can ordinary LOF automatically predict on new samples? | In scikit-learn, novelty mode has distinct fit/predict semantics. Configure it for new observations and follow the pinned version's documentation.
Follow-up: How do you evaluate without labels? | Review ranked alerts with experts, test historical incidents and carefully justified simulations, then monitor prospectively. Internal anomaly scores are not ground-truth accuracy.
## Scaling, standardization, normalization and robust scaling: what changes?
Simple: Scaling prevents arbitrary units from dominating a model; different transformations solve different problems.
Technical: Standardization uses training mean and standard deviation. Min-max scaling uses the training range, but future values may fall outside that range. Robust scaling uses statistics such as median and IQR. Unit-vector normalization changes each sample's norm. Distance models and regularized linear models often need scaling; tree split decisions usually do not require it.
Example: Income in rupees and age in years can distort nearest-neighbor distance. Fit a scaler on training data and reuse it unchanged.
Follow-up: Does standardization make a feature Gaussian? | No. It changes location and scale, not the distribution's shape.
Follow-up: Why not fit scaling before splitting? | The transformation would learn validation/test distribution information. Fit within each training fold.
# Model selection and statistical reasoning
## How do train, validation, test, time and group splits differ?
Simple: Training fits a model, validation chooses settings, and a final test estimates generalization. Split structure should reflect deployment.
Technical: Random splitting is suitable only when its assumptions match the task. Group splits separate the same patient/customer/document family. Time splits train on past data and assess future periods, with gaps where labels overlap. Fit preprocessing inside training folds. Repeated tuning using the test result turns that set into validation.
Example: Duplicate tickets from one incident in train and test inflate results. Group by incident before splitting.
Follow-up: What if a future split has different class balance? | That may be the real challenge. Report it rather than reshuffling away the distribution shift.
Follow-up: Is cross-validation always better than one split? | It can estimate variability but is costly and must respect grouping/time. Random folds cannot repair a mismatch with the deployed task.
## What is data leakage, and how do you detect it?
Simple: Leakage supplies information that would not be available at the time of a real prediction.
Technical: Audit feature timestamps, post-outcome columns, duplicate families, whole-dataset preprocessing and label-informed sampling. Use ablation tests, temporal evaluation and suspicious-feature review. A field created after ticket resolution is unavailable at ticket creation even if the training table includes it. Pipeline-based fold fitting prevents many preprocessing leaks.
Example: Cancellation_date cannot fairly predict whether a customer will cancel in the future.
Follow-up: Is high accuracy proof of leakage? | No. It is a reason to investigate. Validate feature availability and the deployment-matched split.
Follow-up: Can oversampling cause leakage? | Yes, if performed before splitting. Synthetic observations can share source information across folds. Resample training folds only.
## What are overfitting, underfitting and the bias-variance trade-off?
Simple: Underfitting misses useful patterns; overfitting learns details that do not generalize.
Technical: Compare train/validation curves, cohort performance and repeated splits. High errors on both can indicate insufficient signal or capacity. A large gap may arise from excessive complexity, leakage or distribution mismatch. Compare regularization, simpler models, representative data and early stopping after diagnosing the cause.
Example: A deep tree memorizes 200 tickets with perfect training results but fails on new incidents. Limiting depth and improving coverage can help.
Follow-up: Does more data always help? | More representative correctly labeled data often helps; duplicates, corruption and biased samples may not.
Follow-up: Is the textbook bias-variance curve universal? | No. Modern models, optimization and regularization interact more subtly. Use empirical validation rather than treating the simplified diagram as a law.
## What are L1, L2, dropout and early stopping?
Simple: These constrain learning or choose a checkpoint before it becomes overly specialized to training data.
Technical: L1 penalizes absolute coefficient magnitude and can yield sparsity; L2 penalizes squared magnitude and shrinks coefficients. Dropout masks activations during configured training. Early stopping selects a checkpoint using validation criteria. Strengths and stopping rules are hyperparameters, and feature scaling affects coefficient penalties.
Example: Save the best validation checkpoint when validation loss starts rising rather than deploying the last epoch automatically.
Follow-up: Is dropout normally active at inference? | Ordinary deterministic inference disables it. Monte Carlo dropout is an explicit uncertainty technique, not the default.
Follow-up: Does L1 find the true causal features? | No. Correlation and sample variation affect selection. Predictive feature selection does not establish causality.
## How do logistic regression, trees, random forests and boosting differ?
Simple: Linear baselines are straightforward; trees model interactions; forests aggregate trees; boosting improves an objective sequentially.
Technical: Logistic regression is linear in log-odds for the specified features. Trees partition feature space. Random forests average decorrelated trees to reduce variability, while gradient boosting adds learners sequentially. Compare leakage-safe task quality, calibration, explainability, missingness behavior and serving cost. Tabular boosting is often competitive, but no model wins universally.
Example: Compare regularized logistic regression and boosted trees on structured risk features before introducing a large neural network.
Follow-up: What is bagging versus boosting? | Bagging aggregates models trained using resampling; boosting fits learners sequentially to improve an objective. Dependencies and error behavior differ.
Follow-up: Does logistic regression require probability to be linear? | It models log-odds as linear in the chosen features. Nonlinear feature transformations can expand that representation.
## What is gradient descent, and what does learning rate do?
Simple: Gradient descent updates parameters using the loss gradient; learning rate controls the step size.
Technical: Full-batch, stochastic and mini-batch methods use different gradient estimates. Excessive steps can diverge or oscillate; tiny steps can waste the training budget. Adaptive optimizers still need a suitable schedule and monitoring of loss, gradient norms and numerical precision. Training loss need not equal the final business metric.
Example: If loss becomes non-finite after a learning-rate change, inspect the rate, bad batches, gradient norms and precision rather than just training longer.
Follow-up: Why can cross-entropy improve while recall falls? | The loss assesses probabilities under its weighting, while recall depends on the selected threshold and positive cases. Evaluate the deployed decision too.
Follow-up: Why shuffle batches? | Shuffling can reduce order-induced optimization bias when assumptions allow it. Time-dependent data still requires time-safe evaluation.
## PCA versus feature selection: what is the difference?
Simple: Feature selection keeps original variables; PCA constructs lower-dimensional combinations of them.
Technical: PCA finds orthogonal directions explaining variance after the chosen preprocessing. High variance is not necessarily predictive signal. Label-based feature selection must be fitted inside training folds. Compare downstream performance, memory, stability and explainability rather than assuming dimension reduction always helps.
Example: A low-variance sensor indicator may identify rare failures even when PCA removes it to retain high-variance directions.
Follow-up: Does PCA use labels? | Standard PCA is unsupervised, but choosing its settings using test performance still leaks evaluation information.
Follow-up: Why scale before PCA? | Units can dominate variance. Whether standardization is appropriate depends on the meaning of the measurements.
# Algorithms and statistics interview essentials
## K-nearest neighbors versus K-means: why are they not the same algorithm?
Simple: KNN predicts using nearby labeled observations; K-means groups unlabeled observations around learned centers.
Technical: KNN is an instance-based supervised method whose prediction depends on distance, neighbor count and weighting. K-means minimizes a within-cluster squared-distance objective under its representation, using iterative assignments and center updates. Both are affected by scaling and high-dimensional geometry, but their objectives and meanings of k differ.
Example: KNN predicts a ticket category from similar labeled tickets. K-means groups tickets into similarity clusters whose IDs require interpretation.
Follow-up: How do you select k? | Use supervised validation for KNN; for clustering compare stability, separation and business usefulness. Do not assume one elbow plot proves a universally correct cluster count.
Follow-up: Why can KNN become expensive at serving time? | It compares with retained examples or a search structure. Indexing/approximation, representation and dataset size affect latency and quality.
## What is an SVM, and what does the kernel trick do?
Simple: An SVM learns a separating boundary with a margin; a kernel lets it represent nonlinear relationships through similarity computations.
Technical: Regularization and loss control the trade-off between margin and training violations. Kernel choice and parameters affect the boundary, and feature scaling matters. Kernel methods can become expensive as sample counts grow. Compare a linear baseline and suitable alternatives under representative validation rather than assuming nonlinear kernels are always better.
Example: An RBF-kernel model can separate nonlinear feature patterns but needs tuning and scaling that a simple linear text classifier may not justify.
Follow-up: Is SVM output automatically a calibrated probability? | No. Scores/margins require separate evaluated calibration when reliable probabilities are needed.
Follow-up: What does a large C generally encourage? | Under common formulations it penalizes training violations more strongly, potentially fitting the training set more tightly. Select it using validation, not a universal rule.
## What is Naive Bayes, and why can its independence assumption still be useful?
Simple: Naive Bayes combines class probabilities with feature evidence under a simplifying conditional-independence assumption.
Technical: The assumption is conditional on the class, not that features are independent in every sense. Common variants fit different input types, such as token counts or continuous features. Smoothing avoids zero-likelihood issues for unseen events under the chosen formulation. It can be an efficient text baseline even when independence is imperfect; probability calibration still needs checking.
Example: Token counts can support a fast ticket-routing baseline, while duplicated correlated phrases may cause overconfident evidence accumulation.
Follow-up: Does violating independence make all predictions useless? | No. Classification can still work well empirically. Evaluate predictive quality and probability reliability separately.
Follow-up: What if a new token was never observed? | Use the configured smoothing/vocabulary strategy and validate out-of-vocabulary behavior rather than allowing accidental zero likelihood to dominate.
## How do decision trees split data, and what are Gini impurity and entropy?
Simple: A tree repeatedly asks feature-based questions to make child groups more useful for predicting the target.
Technical: Classification trees can choose splits using impurity reductions, including Gini impurity or entropy. Regression trees use suitable numeric objectives. Greedy local splits do not guarantee a globally optimal tree. Depth, leaf size, feature choices and pruning affect generalization; small data changes can produce different trees.
Example: A tree may split first on transaction amount and then on account age if those partitions reduce label impurity in the training data.
Follow-up: Are feature importances always causal explanations? | No. They describe model behavior under a method and can be affected by correlation and split opportunities. They do not establish causal effect.
Follow-up: Why does a random forest reduce variance? | Averaging diverse trees can reduce instability compared with one tree. Highly correlated trees reduce that benefit, so diversity matters.
## Correlation versus causation: what can a model legitimately claim?
Simple: Correlation means variables vary together; causation means changing one produces a change in another under a defined intervention.
Technical: Confounding, selection bias, reverse causality and leakage can create predictive relationships without causal effects. Prediction quality alone cannot identify an intervention's outcome. Use an appropriate experiment or defensible causal assumptions/design when making treatment or policy claims. Feature importance and SHAP-type explanations explain aspects of predictions, not causality by default.
Example: Customers receiving more support calls may churn more because they already have problems. It does not prove that reducing support calls will reduce churn.
Follow-up: Is zero correlation proof of no relationship? | No. Linear correlation can miss nonlinear relationships, and subgroup patterns can cancel in aggregate.
Follow-up: Why can randomization help? | Under a well-run experiment it reduces systematic confounding between treatment assignment and pre-existing factors. Execution, attrition and outcome measurement still require care.
## What are a p-value and a confidence interval, and what should you avoid saying?
Simple: They quantify evidence and uncertainty under a statistical procedure, not certainty about a claim.
Technical: A p-value describes how incompatible the observed statistic or a more extreme one is with the specified null model and assumptions. It is not the probability the null is true. A frequentist confidence procedure has its stated long-run coverage under assumptions; a realized interval is not automatically a probability distribution over a fixed parameter. State the sampling unit, dependence assumptions and multiple-testing context.
Example: Testing many prompt variants until one achieves p<0.05 can produce false discoveries. Use a preplanned comparison and a held-out evaluation.
Follow-up: Is statistical significance the same as useful improvement? | No. A tiny effect can be significant with large samples. Report effect size, uncertainty and practical cost/quality impact.
Follow-up: Can correlated examples be bootstrapped as independent rows? | That can understate uncertainty. Resample at an appropriate group/unit level or use a method accounting for dependence.
## What are backpropagation, activation functions and softmax?
Simple: Backpropagation computes parameter gradients; activations add nonlinear transformations; softmax converts a vector of logits into a normalized distribution.
Technical: Backpropagation applies the chain rule through the computation graph and is distinct from the optimizer that updates weights. Nonlinear activations enable richer functions than stacked linear maps alone. Softmax outputs depend on all logits and sum to one over the specified axis, but these values are not guaranteed calibrated confidence. Use numerically stable implementations.
Example: A classifier produces logits for three classes, applies softmax for probabilities and trains using a compatible cross-entropy implementation that may accept logits directly.
Follow-up: What is a vanishing gradient? | Gradients can become very small through parts of a network, making learning difficult. Architecture, activation, normalization and initialization affect this behavior.
Follow-up: Should softmax be manually applied before every cross-entropy function? | Follow the library's API. Many losses expect raw logits and apply stable internal operations; applying softmax twice is wrong.
## How do you tune hyperparameters without overfitting the evaluation?
Simple: Search using training/validation data, reserve the final test, and compare quality against compute cost.
Technical: Choose a search space based on the model and budget, then compare grid, random or Bayesian methods using a deployment-matched split. Fit preprocessing inside folds and track seeds, data/model versions and failed trials. Repeated manual choices can overfit validation too, so use nested evaluation or a fresh holdout when estimating selected-model performance.
Example: Tune tree depth and regularization on training folds, select a candidate and threshold on validation, and evaluate once on the untouched future test period.
Follow-up: Why can random search outperform a huge grid under a budget? | It can explore more distinct values along influential dimensions when only some parameters matter. It is not universally superior.
Follow-up: Should the highest metric always win? | Consider uncertainty, latency, memory, interpretability and business constraints. A tiny uncertain gain may not justify a much larger operating cost.
# Metrics: measure the decision
## How do you measure accuracy, and when does accuracy fail?
Simple: Classification accuracy is the fraction of correct predictions. It can hide failure on rare but important classes.
Technical: For binary classification, accuracy=(TP+TN)/(TP+TN+FP+FN). Define the positive class, dataset, sampling unit and held-out split. Add confusion counts, precision, recall, F1 and cohort breakdowns. Balanced accuracy averages per-class recall. For regression use suitable numeric errors; for LLMs use a task rubric, execution success and groundedness instead of an undefined universal accuracy score.
Example: With 10 frauds among 1,000 transactions, predicting every transaction as legitimate yields 99% accuracy but zero fraud recall.
Follow-up: What should SQL Copilot accuracy mean? | Specify whether success is syntactic validity, execution correctness or semantic business correctness. Report successful cases/total cases, with the exact dataset and evaluator.
Follow-up: Is F1 always better? | No. It ignores true negatives and expresses a particular precision/recall balance. Choose metrics according to error costs and capacity.
Follow-up: How do you express uncertainty? | State sample sizes and confidence intervals using an appropriate sampling unit, and compare models using paired cases when possible.
## What are precision, recall, F1, specificity and a confusion matrix?
Simple: Precision asks how many alerts are correct; recall asks how many actual positives were found.
Technical: Precision=TP/(TP+FP), recall=TP/(TP+FN), specificity=TN/(TN+FP), and F1=2PR/(P+R) when defined. State zero-denominator behavior and macro/micro/weighted averaging for multiclass work. The confusion matrix preserves counts that percentages can hide.
Example: TP=8, FP=2, FN=12 and TN=978 gives precision 80%, recall 40%, specificity about 99.8% and F1 about 53.3%.
Follow-up: Can precision and recall both improve? | A better representation or ranking can improve both. Changing only the threshold on a fixed model often creates a trade-off.
Follow-up: Why inspect absolute alert counts? | Even a small false-positive rate can overload reviewers when the negative population is huge.
## ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, calibration and threshold: how do they differ?
Simple: Ranking, reliable probabilities and the final action rule are separate properties.
Technical: ROC-AUC summarizes ranking across false-positive/true-positive trade-offs. Precision-recall analysis often reveals rare-positive performance more directly, and its baseline depends on prevalence. Calibration checks whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies. Choose thresholds on validation data using costs or workload; do not optimize them on final test results.
Example: A model can rank fraud well yet assign unreliable 0.9 probabilities. It may need calibration and a review threshold matched to analyst capacity.
Follow-up: Does high AUC imply good probabilities? | No. Monotonic score transformations can preserve ranking while changing probability meaning.
Follow-up: What changes when prevalence shifts? | Precision and calibration may change even with similar ranking behavior. Recheck current outcomes and workload.
## What are MAE, RMSE, R-squared and MAPE?
Simple: They evaluate numeric predictions and emphasize different errors.
Technical: MAE averages absolute errors in target units. RMSE emphasizes large errors through squaring. R-squared compares squared error with a mean-prediction reference and can be negative on new data. MAPE divides by actual magnitudes, making zero/near-zero targets problematic. Inspect signed residuals and important cohorts alongside averages.
Example: RMSE can expose costly large-claim misses that MAE smooths over. MAPE is a poor unexamined choice for demand with frequent zeroes.
Follow-up: Is negative R-squared necessarily a bug? | No. The evaluated model can perform worse than predicting the evaluation set's mean under that comparison.
Follow-up: Can low mean error hide harm? | Yes. Systematic underprediction in expensive cases or one population can disappear inside an aggregate average.
# Production ML incident scenarios
## Scenario: A model is 99% accurate but misses almost every fraud. What changes?
Simple: Replace aggregate accuracy with a detection objective that respects false-alert cost and reviewer capacity.
Architecture: Label audit and time split -> baseline and ranking evaluation -> cost-aware threshold -> shadow deployment -> analyst feedback
Technical: Confirm labels and detection delays, then inspect prevalence and confusion counts. Compare class weighting or training-only resampling, useful features and candidate models. Choose a threshold on validation data for recall, precision or review capacity, then evaluate on unresampled future data. Monitor delayed truth, calibration and subgroup performance.
Example: With capacity for 200 reviews/day, compare fraud recall and precision within that workload and estimate loss avoided. An all-negative predictor fails regardless of its 99% accuracy.
Metrics: Fraud recall, precision at review capacity, PR curves, expected loss, daily false alerts and detection delay.
Trade-offs: Higher recall may increase customer friction and analyst workload. Delayed labels and changing adversaries constrain automated tuning.
Say: I would inspect counts, define a cost- and capacity-aware target, select the policy on validation data and verify it on future cases.
Follow-up: Should SMOTE be applied before splitting? | No. Synthetic examples can share information across folds. Resample training folds only and verify interpolation is meaningful for the features.
Follow-up: What if labels are extremely sparse? | Use expert review, historical incidents and uncertainty-aware reporting. Do not claim reliable recall from a handful of positives.
Follow-up: What if recall improves but complaints rise? | Measure intervention harm and introduce stepped actions or manual review instead of blocking every alert.
## Scenario: A feature becomes 70% null after release. What do you do?
Simple: Treat sudden missingness as a data incident before treating it as a training problem.
Architecture: Data-contract alert -> source and lineage inspection -> tested fallback -> upstream repair -> replay -> monitored recovery
Technical: Slice missingness by producer, time and model version. Check parsing, schema changes and units. Use a last-known-good model or tested missing-feature path if safe; otherwise abstain or route for review. Repair the feed and reprocess affected records. Evaluate the actual missingness pattern before restoring full traffic.
Example: A renamed JSON key makes salary null. Fixing the parser is more defensible than silently replacing every salary with zero and retraining.
Metrics: Source-level missingness, affected request count, fallback coverage, impacted-cohort quality and recovery time.
Trade-offs: Abstention reduces coverage but can avoid harmful predictions. Final impact may require labels that arrive later.
Say: I would isolate the feed regression, activate a tested fallback, repair the source and verify affected cohorts before normal service resumes.
Follow-up: Why not use the training median immediately? | It can be an approved fallback, but new missingness may differ from training. Alert and measure its impact rather than hiding the incident.
Follow-up: Should the model retrain immediately? | First determine whether this is corruption or a valid new regime. Fix upstream corruption before learning from it.
Follow-up: How do you prevent recurrence? | Version schemas, run producer/consumer contract checks and monitor field-level missingness and payload parity.
## Scenario: Deleting outliers improves the test score. Can you ship it?
Simple: Only if the exclusion rule matches valid deployment scope and does not hide important rare cases.
Architecture: Tail audit -> error versus valid-event review -> training-only treatment -> representative evaluation -> cohort guardrails
Technical: Investigate errors, rare valid events and disputed labels. If exclusions were selected by looking at test outcomes, that test is no longer untouched. Compare robust transforms/models without deleting valid tails, and define how extreme serving inputs are handled. Report quality and coverage on the full intended population.
Example: Removing expensive insurance claims reduces RMSE but can destroy the model's usefulness for financial risk.
Metrics: Overall and tail MAE/RMSE, signed bias, excluded population share, rejection rate and expected loss.
Trade-offs: Robust treatment loses some tail detail; retaining corruption harms fit. Domain adjudication is necessary.
Say: A better filtered score is insufficient. I would justify exclusions and verify the untouched deployment population, especially costly tails.
Follow-up: Can target caps use test quantiles? | No. That leaks evaluation information and changes the task. Define target handling using training procedures and domain requirements.
Follow-up: What if tails are explicitly out of scope? | Enforce that scope with a fallback/rejection path and report coverage alongside conditional accuracy.
Follow-up: What if labels are disputed? | Review them with experts, retain uncertainty and test sensitivity to plausible corrections instead of silently deleting them.
## Scenario: Offline quality is strong but production quality falls. How do you debug it?
Simple: Compare evaluation conditions with the actual inputs, decisions and labels in production.
Architecture: Version inventory -> feature parity -> split and timestamp audit -> drift and cohort analysis -> shadow comparison -> rollback or targeted repair
Technical: Verify preprocessing, model, feature and threshold versions. Reproduce permissible live examples and inspect training-serving skew, leakage, delayed labels, new user groups and concept drift. Roll back a release regression; retrain when representative new labels demonstrate a changed relationship. Drift indicators do not themselves prove task-quality deterioration.
Example: Training uses final daily balance while serving predicts at noon. The feature contains future information offline and cannot be fixed by adding API replicas.
Metrics: Labeled task quality, feature parity failures, missingness, calibration, cohort errors and serving latency.
Trade-offs: Drift indicators arrive before truth but may be inconclusive. Logging must support reproducibility while respecting privacy.
Say: I would reproduce failures and establish data/version parity before choosing between rollback, upstream repair and retraining.
Follow-up: Is all drift harmful? | No. Inputs can shift without changing the target relationship. Connect drift alerts to observed outcomes.
Follow-up: What if labels arrive a month later? | Use leading operational indicators, sampled expert review and shadow comparisons, then backfill mature-label quality.
Follow-up: Should every drift alert trigger retraining? | No. Gate it on data quality, representative labels and a release evaluation so corruption is not amplified.

# AWS vocabulary: start with the building blocks
Note: If you meant SKS, the common AWS terms here are SQS (queues) and EKS (managed Kubernetes). They solve different problems. Architectures are design exercises, not claims about your resume implementation.
## What are an AWS Region, Availability Zone and edge location?
Simple: A Region is a geographic deployment area, an Availability Zone is an isolated infrastructure location within it, and edge locations serve nearby users.
Technical: Design across multiple AZs for many local infrastructure failures, and across Regions only when recovery, residency and latency requirements justify the added complexity. A multi-AZ application can still fail if a shared database, credential or release is broken. Edge caching can reduce delivery distance but does not automatically move all application logic to the edge.
Example: Place API replicas in two AZs behind a load balancer and use a suitable multi-AZ database configuration. Serve static assets through CloudFront.
Follow-up: Does multi-AZ mean multi-Region? | No. AZs belong to one Region. Regional disasters and cross-Region data replication require separate design.
Follow-up: Can every service be deployed identically in every Region? | No. Service/model availability and configuration vary. Verify the chosen Region rather than assuming parity.
## What is EC2, and when do you use it?
Simple: EC2 provides virtual servers whose operating system and application runtime you manage.
Technical: Choose an instance family for CPU, memory, network or GPU needs, then configure an image, storage, networking, IAM role and lifecycle management. Use immutable images or automation, health checks, patching and recovery. EC2 gives control but leaves more operational work than a managed container/serverless path.
Example: A custom vLLM server with specific GPU drivers can run on a suitable GPU instance while the web API scales independently.
Follow-up: Is stopping an instance the same as terminating it? | No. Lifecycle and attached-storage behavior differ. Check volume deletion settings and persistence before changing instance state.
Follow-up: Does one powerful EC2 instance provide high availability? | No. It remains one failure domain. Use redundant capacity and external durable state where the availability requirement calls for it.
## What are S3, buckets, objects, prefixes and presigned URLs?
Simple: S3 is object storage. A bucket contains objects identified by keys; a presigned URL grants time-limited access under a signer's permissions.
Technical: Use S3 for documents, model artifacts, logs or static assets, not as a mounted transactional database. Prefixes organize key names rather than acting as ordinary folders. Define bucket policies, IAM, encryption, versioning and lifecycle rules. Presigned URLs are bearer-like capabilities: keep expiry and scope narrow and avoid leaking them in logs.
Example: Upload a PDF directly to a restricted object key, enqueue an ingestion job, and store extracted metadata separately.
Follow-up: S3 versus EBS versus EFS? | S3 is object storage, EBS is block storage attached to EC2 under its attachment model, and EFS provides a managed shared file system. Choose from access semantics, latency, sharing and durability needs.
Follow-up: Does encryption make a bucket private? | No. Encryption and authorization are distinct. A badly configured policy can expose encrypted objects to principals allowed to read them.
Follow-up: Is S3 always eventually consistent? | Do not repeat that outdated blanket statement. S3 provides strong consistency for object operations covered by its documented model; caches, replication and application indexes still have separate freshness behavior.
## What is SQS, and what are visibility timeout, acknowledgment and DLQ?
Simple: SQS stores messages until workers can process them, helping smooth bursts and decouple services.
Technical: A worker receives a message, processes it, and deletes it after durable success. Visibility timeout temporarily hides a received message; extend it with a bounded heartbeat for long jobs. Standard queues support at-least-once delivery, so consumers must be idempotent. Configure dead-letter handling for repeatedly failing messages, age/backlog alarms and safe redrive procedures.
Example: A document-upload API enqueues an object ID. An ingestion worker extracts, embeds and upserts deterministic chunk IDs, then deletes the message.
Follow-up: What if the worker crashes before deleting the message? | After visibility expires it can be delivered again. Durable job state and idempotent writes prevent duplicated business effects.
Follow-up: Does FIFO mean every external side effect is exactly once? | No. Ordering/deduplication features do not create an atomic transaction across a queue and arbitrary downstream systems. Use idempotency and reconcile ambiguous outcomes.
Follow-up: What if visibility is too short or too long? | Too short can create overlapping retries; too long delays recovery after failure. Set it using job behavior and extend within a bounded processing deadline.
## SQS, SNS, EventBridge and Kinesis: how do they differ?
Simple: SQS buffers work, SNS fans out notifications, EventBridge routes events, and Kinesis supports streaming use cases.
Technical: Choose by consumption model, ordering needs, replay, throughput, routing and retention. SNS can fan one event to multiple queues. EventBridge routes events using rules and integrations. Stream consumers may process ordered partitions and replay retained records. These systems can complement each other; they are not interchangeable labels for an async API.
Example: An upload event fans out to an ingestion queue and an audit queue. A high-volume ordered telemetry stream may need a streaming design instead.
Follow-up: Why not let every worker read the same SQS message? | A work queue distributes competing work. Use fan-out with separate subscriptions/queues when independent services must each process the event.
Follow-up: Should events contain full sensitive documents? | Prefer references and necessary metadata, enforce access on dereference, and avoid duplicating sensitive payloads unnecessarily.
## What are ECS, EKS, Kubernetes and Fargate?
Simple: ECS orchestrates AWS containers, EKS provides managed Kubernetes, and Fargate supplies serverless container compute for supported workloads.
Technical: An orchestrator handles scheduling and service lifecycle; a compute option supplies capacity. EKS reduces control-plane management but does not remove cluster, networking, upgrade and workload responsibilities. ECS can be simpler for an AWS-focused team. Choose from operational skills, portability requirements, integrations and workload constraints. Verify current hardware/runtime support before assuming a GPU workload can use any option.
Example: A stateless FastAPI service can use managed container tasks while a GPU inference fleet has a separately selected capacity path.
Follow-up: Is EKS the same thing as EC2? | No. EKS is managed Kubernetes; EC2 is virtual-server compute that can provide node capacity. The layers have different responsibilities.
Follow-up: When is Kubernetes unnecessary? | A small team with simple container services may be better served by a simpler managed path. Added orchestration must solve a demonstrated requirement.
## What are Lambda, API Gateway and Step Functions?
Simple: Lambda runs functions, API Gateway exposes managed API interfaces, and Step Functions coordinates explicit workflow steps.
Technical: Serverless reduces some infrastructure management but still has runtime, concurrency, payload and execution constraints. Use short event handlers appropriately, return job IDs for long work and coordinate durable multi-step jobs with a workflow/queue design. Verify current limits rather than assuming any LLM or document job fits a synchronous function request.
Example: An API validates an upload and returns a job ID; durable workers process OCR and embeddings asynchronously while clients check status.
Follow-up: Why not run a large GPU model in a short function? | Hardware, initialization, memory and duration requirements may not fit. Separate lightweight orchestration from the inference serving platform.
Follow-up: Does a workflow engine remove the need for idempotency? | No. Retries and ambiguous downstream outcomes still occur. Steps that create effects need durable identity and reconciliation.
## What are ALB, NLB and load balancing?
Simple: Load balancing distributes requests or connections across healthy targets instead of sending everything to one server.
Technical: An Application Load Balancer works at the application layer with HTTP-oriented routing. A Network Load Balancer addresses transport-layer needs. Configure target health, TLS, timeouts and draining. A load balancer distributes available work but does not create new application capacity or fix a saturated database.
Example: Route /api requests to stateless API replicas and keep a long-running ingestion worker fleet behind queues rather than HTTP requests.
Follow-up: Do WebSockets or streaming responses need special attention? | Yes. Idle timeouts, connection draining and reconnect/resume behavior must fit the application. Test rolling releases with active streams.
Follow-up: Are sticky sessions a substitute for external state? | No. They may support a specific routing requirement, but shared durable state and recovery are still needed when targets fail.
## What is Auto Scaling, and how is it different from load balancing?
Simple: Load balancing shares traffic; Auto Scaling changes the amount of capacity.
Technical: Scale on a metric related to work: request demand, concurrency, queue age/backlog per worker or custom saturation. Configure minimum/maximum capacity, warm-up, cooldown/stabilization, draining and quotas. CPU alone may be misleading for I/O-bound APIs or GPU token workloads. Scale dependencies and enforce admission limits as well.
Example: Add ingestion workers when backlog per ready worker rises, while API replicas scale separately for request traffic.
Follow-up: What is horizontal versus vertical scaling? | Horizontal adds instances/replicas; vertical increases resources per instance. Horizontal scaling needs state isolation and coordination; vertical scaling has finite hardware ceilings.
Follow-up: Why can scale-out make an outage worse? | New replicas can amplify connection storms, retries or database load. Respect bottlenecks, connection budgets and downstream limits.
## What are a VPC, subnet, route table and NAT gateway?
Simple: A VPC defines a private network; subnets partition it; routes choose paths; NAT can support outbound access from private resources.
Technical: Public reachability depends on routes, addressing and controls, not a subnet name. Place services and databases according to their exposure requirements. A private service may use managed endpoints for supported AWS services instead of internet egress. Design AZ resilience, address capacity, DNS and egress cost explicitly.
Example: A public load balancer reaches private API tasks, which access private databases and restricted S3 objects using an appropriate endpoint path.
Follow-up: Does a NAT gateway allow unsolicited inbound internet access? | It is not an inbound reverse proxy. Public inbound service exposure requires its own route and controls.
Follow-up: Can a private subnet still access the internet? | Yes, with an appropriate outbound route such as NAT. Private does not mean air-gapped.
## What are security groups, NACLs and least-privilege networking?
Simple: Network controls restrict which traffic can reach resources, but they are only one layer of security.
Technical: Security groups are stateful resource-level controls; network ACLs are stateless subnet-level controls. Define necessary ports and sources, keep databases non-public where appropriate and authenticate application requests. A network allow rule does not authorize a user to access a document or tool.
Example: Permit database connections from the API's security group instead of from every internet address, while still enforcing database credentials and user-level policy.
Follow-up: Is a private network sufficient for MCP authorization? | No. Verify workload identity, audience/scope, tenant and resource permissions even inside a private network.
Follow-up: Why can traffic fail despite an allow rule? | Check routes, DNS, target health, other controls, return paths, listeners and application binding. Diagnose the whole path.
## What are IAM users, roles, policies, STS and KMS?
Simple: IAM controls identities and permissions; roles provide assumed identities; STS issues temporary credentials; KMS manages cryptographic keys.
Technical: Prefer workload roles and temporary credentials over hardcoded long-lived keys. Restrict actions and resources with necessary conditions, understand explicit denies and cross-account trust, and audit access. KMS encryption permissions are separate from access to the encrypted object. Application user authorization remains distinct from the application's AWS role.
Example: An ingestion task role can read only the required document prefix and write only its intended index metadata.
Follow-up: Why not put an AWS secret key in frontend JavaScript? | Every visitor can retrieve client assets. Keep privileged operations on an authorized backend and use narrow presigned capabilities when justified.
Follow-up: Is authentication the same as authorization? | Authentication establishes who a principal is; authorization decides which actions on which resources it may perform.
## What are Secrets Manager, Parameter Store and environment variables?
Simple: They are configuration mechanisms with different secret-management and operational features.
Technical: Store secrets using an appropriate managed service, restrict runtime access, rotate credentials and avoid logging values. Environment variables are a delivery mechanism, not automatically a safe vault: they may leak through diagnostics or process configuration. Plan cache expiry and connection refresh during rotation. Compare feature, cost and encryption needs rather than choosing by name alone.
Example: The API reads its database credential through its role and refreshes connections safely when the secret rotates.
Follow-up: Should secrets be committed in a private repository? | No. Private access can change and history persists. Use runtime secret management and rotate an accidentally exposed value.
Follow-up: Can frontend environment variables hide keys? | Variables embedded into a browser build are visible in the resulting assets. Keep privileged keys server-side.
## RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB and ElastiCache: how do you choose?
Simple: Relational databases support structured relationships and transactions, DynamoDB is a managed key-value/document database, and ElastiCache provides caching capabilities.
Technical: Start with access patterns, constraints, transactions, consistency and query needs. RDS/Aurora support relational workloads under engine-specific behavior. DynamoDB requires deliberate partition/access design. Cache data must have expiry, invalidation and authorization-safe keys; it is not the sole durable store for important jobs or agent state unless a fully justified durability design exists.
Example: Store job status and relational application records in a suitable database, cache permitted schema metadata and keep source documents in S3.
Follow-up: Does adding read replicas fix write bottlenecks? | Not generally. They can offload suitable reads, but write throughput, locks and transaction patterns need separate analysis.
Follow-up: How does a hot DynamoDB key affect scaling? | An uneven key/access pattern can concentrate demand. Revisit partition design and access patterns rather than assuming capacity automatically spreads it.
## What are CloudFront, Route 53, ACM and WAF?
Simple: CloudFront delivers content through edge locations, Route 53 provides DNS capabilities, ACM manages supported certificates, and WAF filters web requests.
Technical: Design origin protection, TLS, caching behavior, DNS records and request filtering deliberately. Private content must not enter shared caches without correct authorization-aware policy. WAF helps with classes of unwanted web traffic but does not validate business logic or guarantee prompt-injection safety.
Example: Serve versioned static assets through a CDN while authenticated APIs use correct cache-control and per-request authorization.
Follow-up: Why does a deployment show stale JavaScript? | Check browser/CDN cache headers, asset names and invalidation. Prefer content/versioned assets and short/no-cache entry documents.
Follow-up: Does DNS failover guarantee immediate recovery? | No. Caching, TTLs, client behavior and health decisions affect recovery time. Test the complete path.
## CloudWatch, CloudTrail and X-Ray: which question does each answer?
Simple: CloudWatch covers operational telemetry, CloudTrail records AWS API activity, and tracing services help follow requests across components.
Technical: Use metrics, structured logs and correlated traces for reliability. Use audit trails for who changed or accessed supported AWS control-plane/data-plane operations under the configured trail. Set retention, sensitive-data filtering and useful alerts. Trace request IDs across API, queue, worker, retrieval and generation without placing unbounded IDs in metric labels.
Example: CloudWatch shows queue age rising, distributed traces reveal a slow embedding call, and CloudTrail helps investigate a permission-policy change.
Follow-up: Should every trace ID be a Prometheus label? | No. High-cardinality labels can explode storage and cost. Keep IDs in logs/traces and use bounded metric dimensions.
Follow-up: Does a dashboard alone provide monitoring? | No. Define SLOs, actionable alerts, ownership and response procedures as well as visualization.
## What are SageMaker and Bedrock, and how do they relate to self-hosted models?
Simple: Managed ML/model services reduce some platform work; self-hosting provides more runtime control with more operational responsibility.
Technical: SageMaker supports managed ML development/serving workflows; Bedrock offers managed foundation-model capabilities and related features. Compare current Region/model availability, data controls, quotas, observability, latency, cost and customization needs. Self-hosted vLLM exposes control over weights and serving settings but requires capacity, security and upgrades.
Example: A team can evaluate a managed model endpoint against self-hosted inference using the same task set and load profile before choosing.
Follow-up: Does managed hosting eliminate evaluation? | No. Model correctness, groundedness, authorization, prompt quality and end-to-end SLOs remain your application responsibilities.
Follow-up: Why avoid quoting a universal token price? | Prices and charging models change by model, Region and deployment mode. Estimate with current published pricing and actual token/load measurements.
## What are RTO, RPO, high availability and disaster recovery?
Simple: RTO is the recovery-time objective; RPO is the acceptable data-loss window. Availability and disaster recovery address different failure scopes.
Technical: Define objectives from business needs, then choose replication, backups, failover, restore and testing accordingly. A backup is useful only if restoration works. Multi-AZ protects certain infrastructure failures; cross-Region recovery adds cost and consistency complexity. Synchronous versus asynchronous replication changes latency and potential loss.
Example: A one-hour RTO with fifteen-minute RPO requires a tested recovery procedure and suitable data protection, not simply a statement that backups are enabled.
Follow-up: Can a replica replace all backups? | No. Accidental deletions or corruption can replicate. Keep appropriate versioned/point-in-time recovery mechanisms.
Follow-up: Why run restore drills? | They reveal missing credentials, incompatible schemas and unrealistic timing before an incident.
## How do you deploy safely with blue-green, canary and rolling releases?
Simple: These limit release disruption by controlling which version receives traffic and how rollback works.
Technical: Rolling updates replace instances gradually; blue-green switches between separate environments; canary exposes a small cohort before expansion. Validate health, task quality and dependency compatibility, drain streams and use backward-compatible schema/state changes. Keep model, prompt, retriever and index versions in the release inventory.
Example: Send a small permitted traffic cohort to a prompt/model release, compare errors and quality guardrails, then expand or roll back the version pointer.
Follow-up: Can database migrations break rollback? | Yes. Use expand/contract compatibility and test old/new application behavior before destructive schema changes.
Follow-up: Is HTTP 200 enough to promote a GenAI canary? | No. Include task correctness, citation support, authorization and cost/latency guardrails.
# AWS architecture incident scenarios
## Scenario: Your FastAPI chatbot suddenly receives ten times the traffic. How do you scale it?
Simple: Protect the service, find the limiting resource and scale the relevant tier rather than blindly adding servers.
Architecture: DNS/TLS -> ALB -> stateless API replicas -> authorized retrieval/cache -> rate-limited model endpoint -> durable shared state
Technical: Apply per-tenant quotas and bounded admission, inspect request concurrency, queueing and dependency limits, then scale warmed API replicas across AZs. Externalize thread state and constrain database pools. Model-provider quotas or GPU tokens may be the true bottleneck, requiring a separate serving scale plan. Use async job/status flows where interactive latency is inappropriate, and define overload behavior explicitly.
Example: Doubling API replicas while every replica opens 50 database connections can exceed a 300-connection budget. Allocate a fleet-wide budget and load-test dependency saturation.
Metrics: End-to-end p95, TTFT, queue age, active requests, rejection rate, database saturation and per-tenant fairness.
Trade-offs: Spare warmed capacity costs money, while slow scale-out harms bursts. Caches help repeated permitted work but require authorization-safe keys and freshness.
Say: I would bound demand, identify the saturated tier, scale APIs and inference independently, and protect shared dependencies with explicit budgets.
Follow-up: Why not use CPU as the only scaling metric? | I/O waits, long streams and GPU token pressure can saturate user experience at modest API CPU. Choose metrics tied to work and latency.
Follow-up: How do you avoid losing conversations during scale-in? | Keep durable state outside instances, drain active connections and support safe reconnect/resume behavior.
Follow-up: What if the model provider quota is fixed? | Rate-limit, prioritize fairly, reduce unnecessary work and offer an approved fallback or delayed job path. More API replicas cannot create provider capacity.
## Scenario: An SQS ingestion backlog keeps growing. What do you inspect?
Simple: Determine whether workers are too few, too slow or repeatedly failing before increasing capacity.
Architecture: S3 upload -> SQS -> idempotent ingestion workers -> embedding/index writes -> durable completion -> delete message
Technical: Inspect arrival rate, oldest-message age, processing percentiles, ready-worker count, retries and DLQ. Trace OCR/embedding/index latency and quotas. Scale on useful backlog-per-worker or age targets, batch where safe and separate expensive document classes. Extend visibility for active jobs and cap total attempts/deadlines. Deterministic job/chunk IDs and completion records make redelivery safe.
Example: If arrivals are 100 jobs/minute and each worker sustains 5 jobs/minute, twenty workers merely match average arrivals and provide no burst/variance headroom. Measure real throughput and dependency capacity before selecting a target.
Metrics: Oldest-message age, arrival/completion rate, retry/DLQ volume, worker utilization and cost per successful document.
Trade-offs: More workers can trigger embedding throttles; bigger batches improve efficiency but can increase per-item delay and failure scope.
Say: I would compare arrival and service capacity, fix slow or poisonous work, and scale within downstream quotas while preserving idempotency.
Follow-up: Why not delete messages on receipt? | A crash would lose unfinished work. Delete only after durable success or an explicit durable terminal handling path.
Follow-up: What if one bad document retries forever? | Classify deterministic failures, use bounded attempts and DLQ with diagnostic metadata, then fix and redrive safely.
Follow-up: Can queue length alone estimate user waiting time? | Not reliably when jobs vary widely or workers are throttled. Combine age, service-time distribution and ready capacity.
## Scenario: One AZ fails while your chatbot is serving streams. How does it recover?
Simple: Route new work to healthy capacity and recover interrupted work from durable state.
Architecture: Multi-AZ targets -> health-based routing -> external thread/job state -> reconnect/resume -> dependency failover
Technical: Provision multiple healthy targets and enough surviving capacity, avoid AZ-local single points of failure and test target health/draining. Clients must handle broken streams and resume using a request/job ID without repeating external effects. Verify database failover and connection refresh under the chosen engine. Recovery must preserve authorization and idempotency.
Example: A streamed response disconnects. The client queries the persisted run state and reconnects or restarts generation under the same safe request identity rather than submitting an irreversible tool call twice.
Metrics: Failed/interrupted requests, recovery duration, surviving-tier saturation, duplicate effects and state-loss window.
Trade-offs: Redundancy and headroom cost money. Seamless continuation is harder than merely returning a fresh HTTP response.
Say: I would make APIs replaceable, persist recovery state and rehearse actual stream and database failure paths across AZs.
Follow-up: Is multi-AZ sufficient for regional loss? | No. Regional recovery needs separate objectives, data replication/restore and traffic failover design.
Follow-up: What if the remaining AZ cannot carry the load? | Apply admission controls and degrade optional work while scaling available capacity. Plan failover headroom explicitly.
Follow-up: Can retries immediately restore every request? | Blind retries can amplify overload and duplicate effects. Use bounded backoff, jitter and idempotent semantics.
## Scenario: Scaling the API makes the database slower. How do you fix it?
Simple: The database is a shared bottleneck; API scale-out must respect its capacity.
Architecture: Admission budget -> bounded connection pools -> query/index analysis -> permitted cache -> read/write capacity plan
Technical: Measure active/waiting connections, slow queries, locks, transaction duration, CPU and I/O. Budget connections across all replicas, use pooling appropriately, shorten transactions and fix poor query/index patterns. Cache only safe data with correct tenant scope/invalidation. Read replicas help suitable reads but not all writes or consistency-sensitive requests.
Example: Fifty replicas each creating a large independent pool can exhaust the database even though each API server is lightly loaded.
Metrics: Connection wait, query p95, lock time, database CPU/I/O, cache hit rate and end-to-end latency.
Trade-offs: Tighter pools may queue requests but protect stability. Replicas add lag/consistency decisions, and caches add freshness complexity.
Say: I would cap fleet-wide database pressure and fix query/access patterns before increasing request concurrency again.
Follow-up: Can Redis replace the database? | It can serve defined cache/state roles but is not a universal substitute for the required durable transactional model.
Follow-up: Why not raise max connections indefinitely? | Connections consume memory and scheduling resources, and the actual query workload can still exceed CPU/I/O or lock capacity.
Follow-up: What if reads must reflect a just-completed write? | Route using an explicit consistency policy rather than assuming every replica has the latest value.
## Scenario: A RAG system's AWS bill doubles with unchanged traffic. What do you investigate?
Simple: Break cost down per request and pipeline stage before changing architecture.
Architecture: Cost allocation -> request/token/job telemetry -> version comparison -> waste diagnosis -> controlled optimization
Technical: Compare model/input-output token mix, retries, agent steps, index ingestion, embedding duplication, instance utilization, egress/NAT and storage retention. Trace a release that lengthened prompts or disabled caching. Use deterministic ingestion identity and retention/lifecycle policies. Evaluate quality after batching, prompt compression, model routing or capacity changes.
Example: A retry regression doubles embedding calls and repeated agent loops triple output tokens even though user request counts stay flat.
Metrics: Cost per successful answer/document, tokens per stage, retries, steps, cache effectiveness, utilization and quality guardrails.
Trade-offs: Cheaper models and compression may lower quality. Aggressive caching can leak scope or serve stale answers unless keys and freshness are correct.
Say: I would attribute cost to stages and releases, remove duplicate work first, then optimize serving under the same quality requirements.
Follow-up: Should everything use Spot capacity? | Only workloads with suitable interruption/retry behavior and a capacity strategy. Interactive availability or long stateful work needs a deliberate design.
Follow-up: Why measure successful answers rather than requests only? | Cheap failures can make per-request cost look good while increasing total cost to obtain a useful outcome.
Follow-up: Is a budget alert a hard spending cap? | Do not assume so. Verify the configured service's behavior and implement explicit quotas/admission controls where needed.
